prosody.emphasis: How to Read This Book

p.prosody: This is a satirical, absurdist novel with a strong dose of British humour. You need to know no physics at all to read it, and nothing in the story requires homework.
But it is also an honest book, and it is built in two layers.

Lolly is thirty, has a PhD in physics, and wrote her doctoral work about quantum electrodynamics. The awkward part is that she eventually realised she could calculate and explain quantum mechanics without actually understanding it in the deep sense she wanted. So she left physics and, allegedly, worked in an organic grocery shop. Then she came across Feynman making essentially the same point in his own inimitable way: anyone who says they understand quantum mechanics has probably misunderstood the question. That sent Lolly back into physics — in a decidedly non-standard way. Which is, obviously, rather Wren.

The novel is the story of Lolly Wren, a Transit Reconciliation Officer, Third Grade, who earned a PhD in physics, wrote about quantum electrodynamics, and then discovered the much more inconvenient fact that she did not understand quantum mechanics, and who discovers that her department has been making reality simpler by pushing the difficult parts of it into a black hole in regional infrastructure.

The Physics Notes do not interrupt the story. They are gathered into a single Appendix at the very end of the book, after the Epilogue, where the Ministry could keep an eye on them. Within the Appendix they are filed into sections clearly labelled by chapter, so the notes for Chapter 7 live in the section marked Chapter 7 and nowhere more surprising than that. Each one takes the quantum-mechanical idea its chapter has just dramatised and explains it properly, starting from nothing, in plain English, for a reader with roughly high-school science.
Each Physics Notes section is laid out the same way, so you always know where you are:
In one breath — the whole idea in a sentence or two.
Start here — an everyday analogy, no jargon.
The idea, step by step — the argument assembled in order.
What this chapter was actually showing you — the story and the science locked together.
Where the popular version goes wrong — the misconception you have probably been taught, corrected.
Going deeper — the real machinery, the equations, the named experiments. Explicitly skippable.
What the reader learns — takeaways you can tick off.
One-line summary — the sentence to keep.
Three honest ways to read this book.
For the story alone: read the chapters straight through and ignore the Appendix entirely. You will lose nothing. Not a single plot point lives in the Physics Notes.

To learn quantum mechanics properly: read each chapter, then turn to the Appendix and read the section labelled for that chapter, in order, before going on to the next. The sixteen notes are built as a course. Chapter 1 assumes nothing; Chapter 13 assumes Chapter 12. By the end you will genuinely understand superposition, measurement, entanglement, uncertainty, decoherence, Bell’s theorem and why black holes are a problem — and you will know which of the things you have heard about quantum physics are false.

If you are impatient: the Physics Prologue that follows summarises the entire scientific content of the book in bullet points, drily, in about ten minutes. It was written by a civil servant for other civil servants and it gives away nothing except the physics.

One promise, kept throughout: where the science is genuinely unsettled — and a great deal of it is — this book says so plainly rather than tidying it away. Tidying things away is what the Ministry does, and look where that got them.

p.prosody: The Whole Book, Briefly
The following document was recovered from the Ministry’s internal circulation system. It is reproduced here because it is, unexpectedly, correct.

MINISTRY OF EVENTUALITIES INTERNAL SUMMARY — QUANTUM MECHANICS Circulation: Restricted Purpose: To permit officers to discuss the physics without reading any of it Prepared by: L. Wren, Transit Reconciliation, Third Grade Status: Unapproved
Part One: What the universe is actually doing (Chapters 1–5)
A thing’s state is the complete list of what can be said about it. It is not a location, an opinion, or an entry in a register.
A state may be a superposition : it has no definite value for some property until that property is measured. This is not the thing hiding its value. There is no value to hide.
Measurement is a physical interaction, not an act of attention. Nothing in the universe requires a witness, a clipboard, or a member of staff.

The result you can get depends on the question you ask. Asking a different question is not asking the same question more carefully. There is no basis-independent true answer waiting to be transcribed.
Measurement is an intervention. It changes the thing measured. Officers who measure repeatedly in order to be thorough should be aware that they are not observing a system; they are pinning one.

Between measurements, states evolve smoothly, predictably and reversibly, according to the Schrödinger equation. This is the least mysterious part of the entire subject and is routinely reported as the most.
Part Two: What happens when you file it (Chapters 6–10)
Black holes are not permanent. They radiate, cool the universe’s patience, and evaporate. A small one does this fast, and faster as it shrinks. This is a law, not a fault, and cannot be appealed.
Information that falls into a black hole poses a serious unresolved problem in physics. It should not, therefore, be used as departmental storage.

Two things that interact can become entangled : correlated so completely that neither has a definite individual value, only a shared one. This transmits nothing faster than light and cannot be used to send a memo.
Correlation leaks. When a system’s alternatives get recorded in its surroundings, interference between them becomes practically unrecoverable. This is decoherence .
Decoherence is why large ordinary objects look definite: the air, the light and the warmth of the world are interacting with them constantly, on nobody’s authority and at no charge.
Consequently, the moon does not require forty-one residents with clipboards. Any officer who has built a billing schedule on the contrary assumption should expect difficulty.
Part Three: What cannot be done (Chapters 8–9, restated for emphasis)
An unknown quantum state cannot be copied. This is the no-cloning theorem , and it is not a procurement problem.
A state may, however, be moved, and a known state may be prepared again. The distinction is the difference between a backup and a crime.

Certain pairs of properties — position and momentum among them — cannot both be sharply defined at once. This is the uncertainty principle . It is a fact about the world, not about the quality of the instruments, and requesting both columns to four decimal places does not overcome it.

Information can nonetheless be protected, by spreading it redundantly across many parts without ever copying it. This is quantum error correction , and it works up to a threshold, beyond which it does not.
Part Four: What the experts do not agree about (Chapters 11–14)
If evolution is smooth and universal, nothing in the mathematics says when a single definite outcome occurs. This is the measurement problem . It is unsolved.
It is unsolved in a specific and embarrassing way: an observer can be inside another observer’s unresolved description. (See Wigner’s friend , and Mr Keinschein’s dietary arrangements.)

Matter has wave properties, with a wavelength set by momentum. Pilot-wave theory takes this seriously: particles have definite positions at all times, guided by a real wave. It is deterministic. It is also explicitly nonlocal.

Bell’s theorem proves that no theory in which distant things have their own separate pre-existing properties can reproduce the correlations we measure. Experiment has confirmed the violation repeatedly and, since 2015, without loopholes.
This rules out local hidden variables. It does not rule out all hidden variables. Pilot-wave theory survives precisely because it never claimed to be local.

String theory and M-theory propose that everything is made of extended objects in more dimensions than are currently invoiced. The mathematics is extraordinary. The experimental confirmation is nil, and should be described as such in all correspondence.

A black hole’s entropy is proportional to the area of its horizon, not to its volume. What a region contains can apparently be accounted for on its boundary. This is the holographic principle , and it is the reason evaporation may constitute disclosure rather than destruction.

Officers are reminded that Copenhagen, many-worlds and pilot-wave are interpretations, not competing products, and that no experiment has yet distinguished between them. The Ministry has no position. The Ministry is not entitled to one.
Part Five: What can be recovered (Chapters 15–16)
Recovery is partial. Below a threshold, loss can be corrected; above it, it cannot. Some things are genuinely gone, and saying so in writing is the whole of professional honesty.
One may act correctly on quantum mechanics without knowing which interpretation is true. This is inconvenient for philosophy and sufficient for work.
The second law stands: total entropy does not decrease. Local order is always paid for by exporting disorder somewhere else.
Living things do not defeat this. They maintain themselves by feeding on order and excreting disorder — Schrödinger’s negentropy — which is a scheme within the accounts, not an exemption from them.

Therefore: any institution promising to make things simpler is proposing to move complexity somewhere you cannot see. Always, and by law. The only honest question is where, and the only crime is refusing to say.

On the longest timescales the stars go out, the remnants cool, the black holes evaporate, and a dark and extremely uneventful era follows. The timetable depends on unsettled physics and should not be entered in the diary.
In the meantime there is an enormous middle, in which order remains to be spent and some arrangements of matter can ask what they are made of.
The universe contains very few places where it is described. These are the scarce resource. Simplicity is not.
There is no moment at which a state is finally settled and may be filed. Correlation continues outward indefinitely.
There is no lid.
Officers unable to retain the foregoing may retain the final two lines, which are the only ones that ever mattered.
Officers who retain nothing at all are directed to the novel, which contains the same information in a more agreeable order.

prosody.emphasis: A Word on Who Is Who

p.prosody: This novel gives away real physicists twice over, by two entirely different methods.

The first is a joke told out loud. Characters in this book say the names of real scientists without the faintest idea who they are. A woman whose crockery has been administratively altered will demand to know who Hawking is, and be told, correctly, that he is a physicist and not a department. That one is free.

The second method is quieter, and if you enjoy working things out before you are told, stop reading this page now and come back when you have finished the book. Nothing here spoils the plot. It does spoil a run of small pleasures.
Still here?

The Ministry, faced with a civic black hole it cannot explain, does what any large institution does: it brings in consultants. The consultants are the greatest physicists of the twentieth century, lightly disguised, mildly inconvenienced, and required to explain themselves to a Third Grade officer with a green notebook. They are not caricatures of the real people and their private lives here are wholly invented — but their physics is theirs.
Here is who is who.

In these pages, Alfred Keinschein — immaculate, courteous, and a vampire who feeds on collapsed and discarded branches — is, in reality, Albert Einstein, made to explain the measurement problem, Wigner’s friend, and why he will not accept the tidy answer.
The Duc de Brévanne, who explains himself very slowly indeed, is Louis de Broglie, made to explain matter waves, pilot-wave theory, and determinism at the cost of locality.
Werner Heitmann, who declines to speculate about anything he cannot measure, is Werner Heisenberg, made to explain operationalism and the Copenhagen position.
Max Tegnér, who cheerfully believes in all of it, all at once, is Max Tegmark, made to explain many worlds and the mathematical universe.
Jack Bellew — deceased, of Belfast, and still the most dangerous man in the room — is John Stewart Bell, made to explain Bell’s theorem, the C H S H inequality, and the end of local hidden variables.
Leonhard von Wittenberg — eleven dimensions and no experimental confirmation whatsoever, and says so — is Edward Witten, made to explain string theory, M-theory, black-hole entropy, and holography.
And Erich Schrottfinger — eighty-nine, and with views about how his cat has been reported — is Erwin Schrödinger, made to explain negentropy, what living things actually do, and the missing lid.

No disrespect is intended to any of them, living or dead. All of them did rather more for human understanding than anyone in this book manages, and not one of them, so far as the author has been able to establish, was ever required to complete a Form four C in triplicate.

prosody.emphasis: Prologue: Before Anything Went Wrong

p.prosody: There was a time when the Ministry of Eventualities was not in trouble.
This was mainly because nobody had yet noticed that it existed.

The Ministry occupied a respectable grey building in Coldharrow, between a Department of Minor Infrastructure and an office responsible for the licensing of ceremonial ladders. Its sign was small. Its corridors were long. Its carpets had the peculiar brown colour adopted by institutions that have survived several changes of government and are now too embarrassed to ask for anything.
Its official purpose was simple: to deal with events that had not happened yet.
This sounded reasonable when written in a memorandum. All was well, obviously. Or was it?
Almost anything did, apparently.

The Ministry had forms for anticipated accidents, projected disputes, future absences, possible administrative consequences, and one particularly unpopular form for things that were almost certainly going to happen but had not yet acquired the courtesy to do so.
Nobody considered this strange.
This was the first mistake.
The second was believing that reality could be made simpler by paperwork.
The third was giving the paperwork a budget.

By the time Lolly Wren arrived at Transit Reconciliation, the Ministry had developed a sophisticated theory of reality. It was not a good theory, but it was laminated, indexed and available in three approved colours.
According to the theory, the universe was fundamentally orderly, provided that nobody looked too closely at it.
There was, unfortunately, a universe. All was not well. Or was it?
And the universe had recently begun behaving like an employee who had discovered that the staff handbook contained no provision for refusing an unreasonable instruction.

People arrived before they had decided to travel. Forms appeared before they had been completed. Objects became difficult to describe. A moon, in one unfortunate district, was placed on administrative hold because its status had become unclear.
Then someone discovered that the Ministry had been quietly moving complexity somewhere else.
Not solving it.
Moving it.
Into a place called four C.
This would have been alarming even without the black hole.
There was, unfortunately, a black hole.

And so, on an otherwise unremarkable morning, Lolly Wren sat down with a cup of tea, a complaint terminal, and the entirely reasonable expectation that the worst thing she would have to deal with that day was a misplaced train.
She was wrong.
Obviously.
She simply did not yet have the paperwork to prove it.

prosody.emphasis: Chapter 1: The Form That Would Not Resolve

p.prosody: There are, in the management of large and failing systems, certain sounds one learns to distrust. The metallic cough of a heating vent in late November, for instance, which means either nothing at all or a catastrophe in the wall. The tiny, clerical thump of an internal memorandum landing in the inbox, which means either lunch has been moved to Wednesday or civilization has. And then there was the particular soft clicking noise made by the complaint terminal on Lolly Wren’s desk when it had decided, in its own limited but vindictive fashion, that the morning was not going to proceed properly. Lolly looked up from her tea. This was unfortunate for two reasons. The first was that she had not yet had enough of it to be tolerant. The second was that the tea itself, purchased in a spirit of optimism from a machine on the fourth floor, had the colour and emotional range of varnished disappointment, and appeared to have taken a personal view of her. The terminal clicked again. Lolly sighed in the manner of a woman who had once trained in theoretical physics and now worked in Transit Reconciliation, which is rather like having spent one’s youth studying celestial harmony only to discover that the stars have all gone into local government.

Her office, if such a term may be generously applied to a room with one window, four filing stacks, and the temperament of a damp envelope, occupied the far end of the Regional Transit Reconciliation Annex.

Gideon Wigglesworth was one of the few people who visited Lolly there voluntarily. He was also one of the few people Lolly trusted to look at an impossible problem without first asking which form was required. Gideon was very clever, painfully clumsy, and so generally agreeable that even the Ministry’s furniture seemed reluctant to injure him. He appeared in the doorway carrying two coffees, caught his shoe on the threshold, recovered with surprising dignity, and handed Lolly one of them.
“Your machine is making the usual noise,” Gideon said.
Lolly glanced at the terminal. “It has only just started.”
“No. The machine has only just admitted it.” Gideon looked at the case file. “What is the order of those fields?”
“Type, subcategory, status, urgency.”
Gideon frowned. “And the status is already saying present before the journey has been resolved.”
Lolly looked at him.
“That may be the mistake,” Gideon said. “You’re assuming the system is recording what happened. What if it is using what it thinks has happened to decide what was supposed to happen?”
He took a sip of coffee, turned to put it down, and walked directly into the doorframe.
Lolly stared at him for a moment. “That,” she said, “was an excellent insight.”
“Thank you.” Gideon rubbed his shoulder. “The door was less impressed.”
The Annex itself had been designed in the late bureaucratic style, meaning that it was thought to promote openness while in fact promoting fluorescent headaches.

People came there to complain about missed connections, duplicate arrivals, incorrect departures, luggage with philosophical objections to ownership, and, increasingly over the last several months, journeys that had happened in the wrong order.
Lolly had processed three of those this week. She did not care for trends in metaphysics.
The terminal emitted a third click, sharper this time, followed by the appearance of a new case file on the screen.
COMPLAINT TYPE: TRANSIT DISCREPANCY SUBCATEGORY: PREMATURE ARRIVAL / INTENT LAG CITIZEN STATUS: PRESENT URGENCY: MODERATE TO EXISTENTIAL
Lolly stared at the final line. Then she took another sip of tea in the vain hope that liquid might alter the meaning of language. It did not.

There came a brisk knock at the open office door, immediately followed by a woman entering without waiting for permission, which in Lolly’s experience generally indicated either authority or age. In this case, it was age wielded with such competence that it had become authority on its own.

She was in her late sixties, perhaps early seventies, with silver hair pinned back in a way that suggested she had no intention of adjusting it for the convenience of reality. She wore a dark coat, sensible shoes, and the expression of a woman who had once accepted the collapse of standards in public life as regrettable but had no intention of accepting the collapse of space-time.
“Ms Wren?” she said.
“Lolly Wren, yes.”
“Good. I’ve been sent from Admissions.”
This was never good. Lolly gestured to the chair opposite her desk. “Please sit down.”

She sat with the composure of someone settling in for a procedure that should have been unnecessary. “Elspeth Chain,” she said. “Mrs Elspeth Chain, technically, though I’ve found that ‘Mrs’ invites a certain tone from public institutions and I’d rather avoid it.”
“That seems wise,” said Lolly.
Mrs Chain nodded once, as if pleased that one civil servant in the building had not entirely wasted her upbringing.
Lolly brought up the file. “You’ve reported a transit discrepancy.”
“I have.” She glanced down. “Premature arrival with intent lag.”
“Yes.” Lolly folded her hands. “I wonder if you might explain what happened in your own words.”

Mrs Chain did not answer immediately. Instead she removed her gloves, placed them side by side in her lap with the care of a woman whose self-command was holding back a very great deal, and said, “I set out this morning to visit my sister in Whitbury-on-Sea.”
Lolly nodded. “I had not,” she continued, “fully decided to go.”
Lolly paused. “I see.”

“No, Ms Wren, that is rather the problem. I had not fully decided to go, but I had advanced sufficiently in the direction of deciding that I put on my coat, found my umbrella, and went to the bus stop in order, so to speak, to think transitively.”
Lolly regarded her. “Transitively.”
“Yes. It often helps.”
“Of course.”
“It was drizzling,” said Mrs Chain.
“Was it?”
“At home, yes. At the bus stop, less so. Halfway through the route it became bright, then windy, then, for one very unpleasant stretch near the old post office, maritime.”
“Maritime.”
“There were gulls.”
Lolly made a note. Mrs Chain went on. “I was still deciding whether I wished to spend the afternoon with my sister when the bus stopped, the doors opened, and I found I had already arrived.”
“That seems, on the face of it, efficient.”

Mrs Chain gave her a look which suggested that if she continued in that vein she might improve her physically. “Ms Wren,” she said, “Whitbury-on-Sea is twelve miles from my house. I had not committed to the journey. I had not, internally speaking, agreed to it. One ought not to arrive anywhere before one has properly consented to the inconvenience.”
“No,” said Lolly quietly. “One oughtn’t.”
“Quite.” She glanced at the screen again.
The file now read: STATUS: APPROVED RESOLUTION: PASSENGER DELIVERED SUCCESSFULLY
Lolly frowned. Then, before her eyes, it changed.
STATUS: MISROUTED RESOLUTION: PASSENGER ARRIVED WITHOUT COMPLETED INTENTION
Then it changed again.
STATUS: CLOSED RESOLUTION: NO TRANSIT EVENT DETECTED
Lolly did not move for several seconds. The file waited, smugly, in the manner of a form certain it would outlive its complainant. Mrs Chain observed her.
“That isn’t encouraging, is it.”
“No,” she said. “Not especially.”
She pressed the refresh key. The screen flickered and returned to the first status. APPROVED. She pressed it again. MISROUTED. Again. CLOSED.

There are moments in office life when one has to decide whether a problem is technical, personal, or metaphysical. The correct answer is often all three, but procedure requires a degree of optimism. Lolly chose technical first.
“I’m sure,” she said, with the restrained falsity of a trained employee, “that this is simply a processing irregularity.”
Mrs Chain looked at the screen. “Is that why it keeps changing its mind?”
“Possibly.”
“And is that common?”
“No.” “Good,” she said. “I dislike being reassured with uncommon things.”

Lolly reached for a pencil. Most officers in Transit Reconciliation used regulation pens because they were permanent, authoritative, and chained to the desk, much like the officers. Lolly preferred pencil. Pencil admitted the possibility of error, which in her view placed it morally above most institutions.
In the margin of the printed complaint slip she wrote: |journey= a|not yet taken+ b|already arrived
She stopped, considered, and added: with a and b being annoyingly nonzero. Mrs Chain leaned slightly forward.
“What’s that?”
Lolly covered the page with professional reflex. “Nothing official.”
“It’s mathematics.”
“It is a private habit.”
“Is it useful?”
“Not always,” said Lolly. “But it occasionally stops me shouting.”
Mrs Chain accepted this at once. “Sensible.”

On the ceiling, the office speaker made a soft ping. A voice of cultivated female neutrality announced, “Attention staff. Due to the implementation of the Simplification Initiative, all departments are reminded that duplicate interpretations of public events create avoidable confusion. Please encourage outcomes to settle promptly. Thank you for supporting a clearer tomorrow.”
Lolly looked up. Mrs Chain looked up. The speaker, having made its contribution to civilization, remained silent.
“Did that seem odd to you?” she asked.
“Very.”
“Good.” “It used the phrase ‘encourage outcomes,’” said Lolly.
“I heard it.”
“You can’t encourage outcomes.”
Mrs Chain gave her a dry look. “Everything in this building appears to encourage outcomes.”
That, Lolly felt, was unpleasantly fair.
She turned back to the terminal and opened the transit record in detail. A route map appeared, though it was not behaving in a route-like manner.

The line representing Mrs Chain’s bus journey seemed to have split in three places and doubled back through a district which, unless Lolly was badly mistaken, had been a municipal duck pond until last February.
She zoomed in. The map reconfigured itself. Whitbury-on-Sea moved three streets inland.
Lolly blinked. Then the little sea icon beside the town name vanished altogether and was replaced with a notation reading COASTAL STATUS: LEGACY.
Mrs Chain was watching her. “What is it now?”
Lolly hesitated. Civil service etiquette discouraged alarming the public before lunch. “How attached,” she asked carefully, “would you say Whitbury is to the sea?”
Mrs Chain stared at her. “It is in the name.”
“Yes.” “Very attached.”
“Quite.” “Why?”
Lolly turned the screen very slightly in her direction. Mrs Chain adjusted her spectacles and read the notation.
There was a small silence. Then she said, in a voice made sharp by disbelief, “What does ‘legacy’ sea mean?”
“I haven’t the faintest idea.”
“Can seas be legacy?”
“They ought not to be.”
“Yes,” she said. “That was my own view.”
Lolly printed the file. This took much longer than it should have, because the printer on her floor had been designed to detect urgency and resent it.
When the sheet finally emerged, it came out warm and faintly humming, which was unusual unless a document was either very recent or very nervous. She flattened it on the desk.

Across the bottom margin, in type too small to have been there a moment earlier, appeared a sentence she was quite certain had not existed in the record before: DESTINATION UPDATED TO NEAREST STABLE VERSION.
Lolly read it twice.
Mrs Chain read it once and said, “That sounds appalling.”
“Yes,” she said. “And what does it mean?”
She chose her words with care. “I believe it means the system considers the place you went to sufficiently similar to the place you intended.”
Mrs Chain drew herself up. “A sister is not sufficiently similar to a seaside town.”
“No.”
“Nor is a town without a sea sufficiently similar to itself.”
“No.” She folded her gloves again. “Well. I’m glad we agree on fundamentals.”
Lolly looked back at the terminal. The file was changing once more. APPROVED. MISROUTED. CLOSED. APPROVED.
The statuses cycled with a kind of clerical impatience, as if the machine itself wished she would stop noticing.

She opened her bottom drawer and took out a thin green notebook labelled, in her own hand, PRIVATE / UNHELPFUL. It contained several pages of equations, four pages of complaints about the new software, and one pressed bus ticket from a journey that had taken place twice but only on alternate Tuesdays.
She wrote: If a citizen may arrive before deciding, then decision and arrival are no longer properly ordered.
Then beneath it: If place may be updated to nearest stable version, then location is no longer being treated as factual.
Then, after a moment: This is going to become a row.
Mrs Chain watched the pencil move. “You’re worried.”
Lolly closed the notebook. “I’m employed.”
“Yes,” she said, “but are you worried?”
She considered the matter honestly. “I wasn’t,” she said, “until the sea became historical.”
Mrs Chain stood. “Excellent.”
“I beg your pardon?”
“I prefer an official who begins worried. It saves time.”
Lolly stood as well, mostly because it seemed rude not to. “Mrs Chain, I’ll need to escalate this.”
“To whom?”

She almost laughed, which would have been unprofessional and also inaccurate, because there was no one in the building to whom one escalated anything with confidence. One merely moved trouble into a higher room and waited.
“I’m not yet sure,” she said.
As if in answer, there came from the corridor the sound of running. This alone was alarming.
People did not run in the Annex unless the kitchen had reopened unexpectedly or the laws of existence were behaving in a manner likely to reflect badly on management.
A figure appeared at the door: a narrow young man from Internal Intake, breathless and carrying a stack of forms with all the dignity of someone trying not to admit the forms were winning.
“Wren,” he said.
Lolly straightened. “Yes?”
“You’ve got the Chain file?”
“Yes.”
“Don’t close it.”
“I hadn’t planned to.”
“Good.” The young man swallowed. “Three more just came in.”
“Three more what?”

“Premature arrivals. One man reached a funeral before the deceased had committed. A woman in Clerken Rise got off the tram and found she’d already had lunch tomorrow. And somebody in East Wexham has reported commuting home to a house listed as an equivalent residence unit.”
Mrs Chain, still by the chair, said very distinctly, “An what.”
The young man looked as if he wished to be elsewhere, preferably in a different branch of causality. “Equivalent residence unit,” he repeated. “It’s on the paperwork.”
Lolly felt something cold settle in the centre of her thoughts. “Who issued the classification?”
The young man held up one of the forms. Across the top, in a new departmental font Lolly already despised, were the words:
SIMPLIFICATION INITIATIVE CIVIC STABILITY THROUGH OUTCOME CONSOLIDATION
Lolly took the paper. For a moment the office seemed to become very still. Even the terminal stopped clicking, which was somehow worse.
Mrs Chain spoke first. “Ms Wren,” she said, “is someone altering the world on purpose?”

Lolly looked from the form to the flickering complaint file, to the private notebook on her desk, to the pale and panting messenger in the doorway, and at last back to Mrs Chain, who had arrived somewhere before deciding to go there and now seemed, quite reasonably, to require a grown woman to explain the universe.
She wished very much that the tea had been better. “I sincerely hope not,” she said.
Then the terminal clicked again. A new line appeared across the screen in bright administrative blue: CASE ESCALATED. PLEASE REPORT TO QUEUE MANAGEMENT.
Lolly stared at it. There are few phrases in government more sinister than Queue Management. Most of them are longer, and available only in landscape format.

Mrs Chain picked up her handbag. “Well,” she said, “that sounds dreadful.” Lolly reached for her coat. “Yes,” she said. “I rather think it does.” Blankly, almost cheerfully, the printer produced a second sheet all by itself. Across the top it read: FOR THE AVOIDANCE OF CONFUSION Lolly shut her eyes. This, she felt, was how serious things generally began. Not with thunder. Not with prophecy. Not with reason. With stationery.

prosody.emphasis: Chapter 2: The Wrong Queue

p.prosody: The difficulty with queues, Lolly Wren had always felt, was not that they were slow.
Slowness, while regrettable, was at least honest. A slow queue made no promises except eventual disappointment, and there was a kind of dignity in that.
No, the real difficulty with queues was that they encouraged hope in manageable portions, which was far more dangerous.

You advanced by inches, watched your fellow citizens undergo minor spiritual decay in front of you, and came at last to the desk only to discover that your existence required Counter Four, a corridor, and a form obtainable exclusively from the place you had just left.
This was the ordinary version. The queue to which Lolly had now been summoned was not the ordinary version.
She and Mrs Elspeth Chain followed the signs down two flights of stairs, along a beige corridor devoted entirely to lowering expectations, and through a pair of glass doors bearing the legend:
QUEUE MANAGEMENT For the Avoidance of Unauthorised Resolution
“That,” said Mrs Chain, reading it once and rejecting it absolutely, “is a revolting sentence.”
“Yes,” said Lolly. “It’s new.”
Inside, the room was larger than it had any right to be. Queue Management occupied what must once have been an atrium, though one that had since been persuaded to regret its openness.
A high ceiling hung above ranks of chrome stanchions and retractable belts arranged into lanes of such subtle cruelty that one suspected professional input.
At the far end stood six service desks beneath softly glowing signs:
INITIAL DETERMINATIONS REVISIONAL DETERMINATIONS POST-DETERMINATE APPEALS PRE-RESOLVED EXCEPTIONS INTENT ALIGNMENT GENERAL ENQUIRIES / NO
Between the doors and the desks stood perhaps fifty people in a queue which immediately, and with appalling confidence, divided into six.
Lolly stopped. Mrs Chain stopped beside her. “I see,” she said after a moment, “that this is idiotic.”
Lolly stared ahead. “Yes.”
“How does one join it?”
“I’m not yet sure it can be joined in any recognisably civic sense.”
At the entrance stood a free-standing pillar dispensing numbered tickets. This, in any civilized institution, would have been reassuring.
Lolly pressed the button. The machine emitted a mild chime and produced three tickets. A17. A17 (provisional). A17/b.
Lolly looked down at them in silence. Mrs Chain took one, adjusted her spectacles, and read it. “What,” she asked, “is a provisional seventeen?”
“I would assume,” said Lolly, “a seventeen that has not committed.”
“And the b?”
“I refuse to speculate.”
Near the pillar a young man in a reflective waistcoat was attempting to provide guidance to the public in the bright, exhausted tone of someone whose training had been both inadequate and recent.

“If you are here regarding an unresolved outcome,” he was saying, “please proceed to the queue most closely aligned with your present state. If uncertain, join the uncertainty lane until a more definite uncertainty becomes available.”
A woman clutching a pram said, “Which one is the uncertainty lane?”
The young man looked around helplessly. “At the moment, madam, all of them.”
Mrs Chain closed her eyes briefly. “Oh, very good. They’ve hired a poet and issued him a lanyard.”
Lolly examined the room. The six lanes were not stable. That was the first problem.
The second was that they were not, in any useful sense, separate. The queue seemed to divide and rejoin itself according to principles more suggestive of philosophy than architecture.
A man in a pinstripe suit stood simultaneously in two adjacent lanes by means of a posture so strained that it deserved a pension.
An elderly couple had somehow entered the Revisional Determinations line and emerged, several yards farther on, in General Enquiries / No.
A student with a rucksack advanced almost to the front of Initial Determinations only to be gently redirected sideways by an apologetic barrier.
Lolly watched for perhaps ten seconds and had the distinct feeling that the room was selecting answers based on the questions people brought into it. She disliked rooms that had opinions.
“Ms Wren?”
She turned. A woman was approaching from Desk Three with a file tucked under one arm and the expression of a person who had once been patient by temperament and had since overcome it.
She was in her forties, perhaps, dressed in dark grey with a badge clipped so exactly to her lapel that it appeared pinned there by moral force alone.
BEATRIX SLOAN Internal Audit
She looked first at Lolly, then at Mrs Chain, then at the three contradictory queue tickets in Lolly’s hand, and seemed not at all surprised. “You’re the Chain case,” she said.
Lolly inclined her head. “Lolly Wren. Transit Reconciliation.”
“I know.” She held out a hand to Mrs Chain. “Sloan. Internal Audit.”
Mrs Chain shook it. “Are you in charge of this?”
“No,” said Beatrix. “Otherwise it would be less decorative.”
She took one of Lolly’s tickets and read it without approval. “They’ve started branching admissions.”
“What does that mean?” asked Lolly.

“It means,” said Beatrix, “that rather than deciding what category a problem belongs in, the department now permits the problem to be processed under several mutually incompatible interpretations until one of them becomes administratively cheaper.”
Mrs Chain considered this. “That sounds immoral.”
Beatrix gave a tiny shrug. “Yes, but efficiently so, which is the current preference.”
She turned and set off toward the lanes without waiting to see if they followed, which they did, because some people generate obedience merely by walking as though corridors owe them truth.
At the mouth of the queue Beatrix stopped and pointed. “Look carefully,” she said.
Lolly did. To an untrained eye, the movement of the lanes might have appeared merely disorderly. But once one attended to the signs, a pattern emerged.
Citizens approaching with misplaced luggage tended to be pulled toward General Enquiries / No. Those with contradictory documents drifted toward Revisional Determinations.
People with the stunned, inward-looking expression of persons whose day had become ontological were drawn, slowly but unmistakably, toward Intent Alignment.
“Is it sorting by complaint type?” Lolly asked.
“Not exactly,” said Beatrix. “It’s sorting by interpretive frame.”
Mrs Chain gave her a sharp look. “In English.”
Beatrix obliged at once. “The room decides what sort of problem you are having, and then forces you to become that sort of problem.”
Lolly felt a small, unpleasant quickening in the back of her mind. “Based on what?”
“On what is observed first,” said Beatrix.
There are sentences which, to a former physicist trapped in public administration, land with the emotional force of a brick through stained glass.

Lolly looked again at the room. A man holding a damp briefcase was being asked, at Desk One, whether his issue concerned delay, duplication, or symbolic displacement. Each answer altered the forms placed before him.

A woman near Desk Five had apparently described her missing husband as both late and increasingly hypothetical, and was now being redirected toward Post-Determinate Appeals with an orange folder marked DOMESTIC AMBIGUITY.
Lolly said quietly, “It’s choosing what kind of complaint it can bear to have.”
Beatrix looked at her. “I beg your pardon?”

“The system,” she said, more quickly now. “It isn’t receiving the complaint. It is deciding, from the first question, what sort of person is permitted to bring it. Delay, identity, route, intent — after that, everything has to fit.”
Mrs Chain folded her arms. “So if I say I took the wrong bus, that’s one problem. And if I say I arrived before deciding, that’s another.”
“Exactly,” said Lolly. “But they are the same thing.”
“Yes.” “That’s monstrous.”
“Yes,” said Beatrix. “But very modern.”
Lolly took out her pencil and, balancing the green notebook against one hand, wrote: First question becomes first answer.
Then below it: The queue does not ask. It assigns.
Mrs Chain peered at the page. “That’s not going to improve matters, is it.”
“No,” said Lolly. “But it may help identify the species of disaster.”

They entered the lane marked INTENT ALIGNMENT. At once the carpet changed colour from apologetic blue to a slightly sterner shade of blue, as if to indicate that uncertainty was tolerated here only under supervision.
The barriers to either side gave a faint electric hum.
Ahead of them stood five citizens in various states of administrative fatigue.
The first was a man in cycling clothes trying to explain that his office had received him before he had left his house, though only emotionally.
The second was a schoolteacher insisting that her afternoon had been reassigned to Thursday without consultation.
The third, a nervous teenager with an oblong parcel, kept muttering that he had only meant to visit his grandmother “in principle.”
As the line advanced, Lolly noticed something even less encouraging. The questions changed people.
A clerk at the front desk, hidden until now by a partition, was speaking in a soothing voice to the cyclist.
“Did you intend,” she asked, “to go to work?”
“Yes, obviously.”
“Fully?”
The cyclist blinked. “What?”
“Would you say your intention was complete, partial, or symbolic?”
“Complete, I suppose.”
The clerk ticked a box. At once the screen beside her updated:
COMMUTER MISSEQUENCING SUBTYPE: PRE-COMMITTED ARRIVAL
The cyclist looked down at the label that had printed for him, and in that instant his whole complaint seemed to shrink.
He began repeating the clerk’s terminology back to her, as though his own experience had already been translated into something smaller and easier to store.
Lolly felt cold.
The teacher stepped up next. Her account of a missing afternoon was reframed, within seconds, as TEMPORAL MISALLOCATION WITH EDUCATIONAL IMPACT.
By the time she left the desk, she seemed almost persuaded that the matter concerned staffing.
Mrs Chain said under her breath, “They file you until you agree.”
“Yes,” said Lolly. Beatrix, ahead of them, nodded once. “That’s the model.”
Then it was Mrs Chain’s turn. The clerk looked up with the professionally laundered smile of a person trained never to acknowledge originality in suffering.
“Good morning. Nature of unresolved intent discrepancy?”
Mrs Chain set her handbag down on the counter with deliberate care. “I went to visit my sister in Whitbury-on-Sea.”
“Certainly.”
“I had not entirely decided to go.” “Yes.”
“And when I arrived, the town seemed to be missing part of its sea.”
The clerk’s fingers paused above the keyboard. “Was the destination emotionally authorized prior to embarkation?”
Mrs Chain stared at her. “It was what?”
“Emotionally authorized.”
“No,” said Mrs Chain. “It was my sister.”
The clerk blinked. “Would you classify your journey as voluntary, reluctant, habitual, or familial?”
Mrs Chain drew herself up. “I would classify it as none of your business.”
Lolly almost admired the speed with which Beatrix stepped in. “Internal Audit,” she said, placing her badge on the counter. “This case is under review.”
The clerk’s face changed by perhaps half a millimetre, which in administrative environments counts as a passionate emotional event. “Of course,” she said.
“Then I’ll need Form IA-9 for diverted interpretive handling.”
“You will not,” said Beatrix. “You will give me the current classification tree and the routing logic for this lane.”
“That material is not available at desk level.”
“Then fetch someone to whom availability has happened.”
The clerk hesitated. There are many people in bureaucracy who wield power, but very few who wield certainty.
Beatrix Sloan wielded certainty in a way that made lesser officials briefly consider confession.
The clerk rose and vanished through a side door. Mrs Chain turned. “I like her.”
“I noticed,” said Lolly. “Does she ever smile?”
“Possibly in private,” she said. “Wasteful.”
While they waited, Lolly examined the counter terminal. On the edge of the screen, where some programmer had assumed no one with curiosity would ever be employed, ran a diagnostic panel:
PRIMARY MEASUREMENT FRAME: INTENT SECONDARY FRAME: ROUTE TERTIARY FRAME: CIVIC STABILITY AUTO-COLLAPSE ENABLED: YES
Lolly’s mouth went dry. She copied it into the notebook.
Auto-collapse. That was not a phrase one used by accident.
She drew a line beneath it and wrote: Ask different first question obtain different world.
A quiet voice at her elbow said, “That’s true more often than people care to admit.”

Lolly turned. The speaker was the thin young man she had noticed only in passing when they entered: dark coat, narrow face, stack of sealed envelopes under one arm, the general air of someone who belonged everywhere on a provisional basis.
He had somehow arrived beside them without ever seeming to cross the intervening space.
“I’m sorry?” said Lolly.
The young man nodded toward the notebook. “Different question, different world. Sensible. Bit gloomy, but sensible.”
Mrs Chain eyed him. “Were you in this queue?”
“Briefly,” he said.
“And now?”
“I’ve improved my position by not belonging to it.”
Beatrix looked over. “Who are you.”
“Jago Flint.”
He produced an identification card so quickly and casually that Lolly entirely missed where it had been kept.
Interdepartmental Courier Service Restricted / Floating Clearance
“Floating clearance?” Lolly asked.
Jago smiled. “Means I’m authorized where things aren’t fully settled.”
“That can’t be an actual credential,” said Lolly.
“Ms Wren,” said Jago pleasantly, “neither, at present, can your sea.”
Before Lolly could reply, the side door reopened and the clerk returned with three forms, a thin man in a mustard tie, and an atmosphere of immediate uselessness.
“This is Deputy Lane Supervisor Pritchard,” she said.
Pritchard had the stooped, hesitant manner of a man who had been promoted specifically because he would not resist language.
He gave them all a smile of deep institutional sadness. “What seems to be the difficulty?”
Beatrix handed him Mrs Chain’s printout, Lolly’s contradictory tickets, and the audit badge in one economical movement.
“The difficulty,” she said, “is that Queue Management is collapsing cases into interpretive states based on intake phrasing.”
Pritchard glanced at the papers. “Ah.”
“Do you deny it?”
“No,” he said. “That is the intended service enhancement.”
Lolly spoke before she could help herself. “Service enhancement?”
“Yes. Citizens were becoming distressed by prolonged ambiguity. The new system ensures each event is processed under a stable descriptive regime at the earliest convenience.”
“But if the description is wrong,” said Lolly, “the outcome is wrong.”
Pritchard offered a smile of almost paternal despair. “Ms Wren, outcomes are more manageable when they are stable.”
“That is not the same thing.”
“No,” said Pritchard. “But it is budgetable.”
There was a brief silence. Somewhere across the room a woman began arguing that her fiancé had split into a weekday version and a weekend version, both of which were disappointing in different ways.
Lolly looked at Pritchard. “Who authorized auto-collapse?”
Pritchard’s expression altered very slightly. “That terminology is internal.”
“So is panic,” said Beatrix, “but here we are.”
Pritchard cleared his throat. “The Simplification Initiative has determined that multiple coexisting interpretations of public events create undue load on systems, staff, and public confidence.”
Mrs Chain said, “Public confidence in what?”

No one answered. Jago, leaning one shoulder against the barrier as though he had always been part of the architecture, said, “That’s usually a bad sign. The fuller answer is probably restricted to senior management.”
Lolly held up the printout. “Whitbury-on-Sea has been updated to its nearest stable version.”
Pritchard nodded sympathetically. “Coastal redundancies are outside my lane.”
“It has a sea in the name.”
“Yes,” said Pritchard, “but names can be legacy features.”
Mrs Chain made a sound that would have done credit to artillery.
Beatrix stepped forward. “I want the routing logic, the collapse parameters, and the policy authorization.”
“I’m afraid I can’t release-”
“Then I’ll seize.”
Pritchard looked at her, then at the badge, then at the growing unease around the room as more people noticed that their complaints were being translated into sanctioned nonsense.
Lolly saw the moment at which the deputy supervisor made his choice.
It was not a noble choice, or even a thoughtful one.
It was the small, bleak calculation of a bureaucrat determining which form of trouble might leave fewer marks.
He reached into his folder and withdrew a pale blue memorandum.
“This,” he said carefully, “was circulated yesterday under restricted headings. I should not, strictly speaking, have brought it to floor level.”
Beatrix took it. Across the top, in a typeface Lolly already despised on moral grounds, were the words:
SIMPLIFICATION INITIATIVE PHASE ONE IMPLEMENTATION NOTES
Below that: To minimize interpretive drift, all citizen-facing anomalies are to be resolved within the first viable measurement frame.
Lolly read the sentence twice. Then a third time.
There are few moments in life when one feels the exact hinge on which a disaster turns.
Lolly felt this one with mathematical clarity.
They were not merely mishandling reality. They were teaching it to answer too soon.
At the bottom of the page, almost as an afterthought, a line in smaller type read: Where persistence of alternate states produces resistance, escalate to Continuity Review.
Jago let out a low whistle.
Mrs Chain said, “What is Continuity Review?”
No one replied at once. Because all four of them, in their different ways, understood that some phrases explain themselves.
Across the room, a printer began to chatter. Then another. Then another.
Sheets emerged at half a dozen desks simultaneously. The clerks read them, and several visibly paled.
Pritchard took one from the nearest tray, glanced down, and closed his eyes.
“What now,” said Beatrix.
He swallowed. “We appear to have an expansion event.”
Lolly felt the skin tighten at the back of her neck. “Meaning?”
Pritchard handed her the notice.
IN RESPONSE TO INCREASED PUBLIC VARIANCE, QUEUE MANAGEMENT WILL NOW OPERATE IN PARALLEL MODES.
As she looked up, the six service signs at the far end of the room flickered.
There was a soft electrical sigh. Then each sign doubled.
Twelve desks. Twelve lanes. Twelve different ways, Lolly thought, for the wrong question to become official.
Beside her, Jago Flint smiled in a way that was either delighted or appalled, and with him one could never be sure that the distinction existed.
“Well,” he said, “that’s new.”
Beatrix snatched the memo from Lolly’s hand. Mrs Chain clutched her handbag like a weapon of last constitutional resort.
Somewhere behind them a child asked whether they were all in the wrong line and was told, with admirable honesty, that no one knew.
Lolly opened the green notebook and wrote only one sentence. The queue is measuring the public.

Then she shut it. Because ahead of them, under a newly lit sign reading PROVISIONAL REALITY ADJUSTMENTS, a door had opened that Lolly was quite certain had not been there before. And from beyond it came the unmistakable sound of someone important approaching with papers.

prosody.emphasis: Chapter 3: A Small Error in Reality

p.prosody: By half past eleven, Lolly Wren had formed the view that there were only so many times one could watch reality subdivide before lunch before it became, in a professional sense, personal.
This was not, strictly speaking, an official category.

Official categories, in Lolly’s experience, tended to involve words like variance, alignment, and public-facing anomaly mitigation, all of which had the remarkable property of making a crisis sound both tedious and deserved.

But as she followed Beatrix Sloan out of Queue Management with Mrs Elspeth Chain at one side and Jago Flint apparently materialising at whichever side was least geometrically defensible, Lolly felt that the morning had crossed some invisible civil-service boundary between inconvenience and insult.
Beatrix walked quickly, which is to say not hurriedly but with the sort of pace that made other people re-evaluate their commitment to blocking corridors.
“We’re not going upstairs?” said Lolly, clutching the pale blue memorandum marked Phase One Implementation Notes.
“No,” said Beatrix.
“To whom, then, are we escalating this?”
“No one.”
Lolly blinked. “That seems institutionally unsound.”
Beatrix pushed through the revolving doors with the crisp violence of a woman who viewed architecture as a minor procedural obstacle. “We are going to the address.”
Mrs Chain nodded. “At last.”
Lolly hesitated on the pavement outside the Annex. “You mean your house.”
“Yes, Ms Wren. That is what an address generally indicates unless one has been promoted.”
Jago, hands in his coat pockets, glanced up at the sky. “Good plan. If the map’s lying, the streets usually start first.”
Lolly turned. “Why are you still here?”
Jago seemed mildly surprised by the question. “Professional curiosity. Also, the courier bag I’m carrying is now addressed to a district that no longer exists, so I feel personally included.”
He produced one of the envelopes and showed it to Lolly.
District Transit Review Office, Lower Whitbury Maritime Fringe
Lolly stared at the words Maritime Fringe. “Was that ever a place?”
“Not with commitment,” said Jago.

They took the bus because Beatrix did not trust Ministry pool cars, taxis were on strike across three adjacent boroughs for reasons no longer entirely causal, and Mrs Chain maintained with some force that she would not pay to revisit her own compromised life.
The bus stop opposite the Annex had changed since morning.
Lolly was certain of this. Not in a dramatic sense. It had not become a cathedral or a crater.

But the timetable case was now mounted three inches farther to the left, the bench had acquired a municipal plaque praising Civic Flow Modernisation, and the route map showed a district called Chain Terrace which Lolly could have sworn had not existed at breakfast.
Mrs Chain leaned in. “It was Elm Grove.”
“Yes,” said Lolly. “Is it still Elm Grove?”
The map, in a spirit of petty hostility, updated while they watched.
CHAIN TERRACE (formerly Elm Grove)
Lolly made a note in the green notebook.
Place names now settling after observation.
That was bad enough.
Then she added:
Or perhaps because of it.
The bus arrived at once, which made everyone on the pavement suspicious.
Public transport is not meant to behave efficiently without a motive, and preferably a consultation period.
The destination display read:
CHAIN TERRACE / STABLE RESIDENTIAL CLUSTER / VIA MOST PROBABLE ROUTE
Mrs Chain looked up at it with the silence of a woman preparing to dislike something professionally. “What,” she said at last, “is a stable residential cluster.”
“An insult,” said Beatrix.
They boarded.
The driver had the hollow, resigned expression of a man who had spent the morning being ordered to carry passengers to places that had become technically adjacent to where they wanted to go.
He took Mrs Chain’s pass, looked at it, looked at her, and said, “This one may take a slightly revised path.”
Mrs Chain replied, “My life appears to be doing much the same.”
Lolly sat by the window and watched the city fail to remain itself.
It did not happen continuously. That would have been easier, in a dreadful sort of way.
Instead the street altered in small, indecent increments.
A barber became an orthodontist. A florist became a closed florist, which is not the same thing.
A narrow Victorian pub called The Patient Meteor blurred at the edges and resolved into a branch office of the Civic Harmony Board with hanging baskets and no moral centre whatsoever.
Jago sat opposite, balanced carelessly on the edge of his seat as if ordinary posture were a kind of local superstition.
Gideon Wigglesworth had joined them by then, having arrived three minutes late, apologised to everyone, and knocked over a sign that had not previously been in danger.
Lolly had asked him to look at the changing street names.
Gideon, after a moment’s thought, pointed at the map. “They are not changing randomly,” he said. “They are settling toward the description that people expect to be true.”
Lolly looked down at her notebook. “Observation changes the record.”
“Or the record is selecting which observation survives.”
Gideon smiled. “Either way, you shouldn’t trust the first version you see.”
Then he stepped backwards, caught his heel on the kerb, and sat down rather abruptly on the pavement.
Mrs Chain looked at him. “Are you all right?”
“Perfectly.”
Gideon looked up at the map. “Apparently.”
“You’re doing the notebook thing again,” he said.
Lolly looked down.
She had, without noticing, already written:
|street= a|remembered+ b|revised
“Private habit,” she said.
“Dangerously sensible, that.”
Beatrix, without looking up from the memorandum, said, “She uses equations to avoid feelings.”
“I use equations,” said Lolly, “to postpone feelings until I’ve identified the problem.”
Mrs Chain nodded. “Exactly right.”
Jago smiled. “I’m outnumbered by the emotionally repressed.”
“No,” said Beatrix. “You’re merely outclassed.”
When they got off at Chain Terrace, the weather had acquired the strained brightness of something that had recently been approved by committee.
The street itself was neat, calm, and appalling.
It had the shape of suburbia but not the conviction.
Semi-detached houses stood in rows behind low hedges and gates of selective memory, each one appearing, at first glance, perfectly acceptable.
Only at second glance did the violations begin to emerge.
House numbers were fractionally out of sequence.
Curtains matched too well.
Three front gardens had identical stone birdbaths, all weathered in precisely the same place.
A cat sat on a wall with the vague, overdetermined air of an animal that had been generated from survey data.
And the clocks were wrong.
Lolly noticed that first. Not the time itself, though that was bad enough.
One house displayed eleven twenty-three in the front room, another eleven nineteen, a third almost noon.
Yet all the clocks possessed the same odd quality, as though they were not inaccurately set but drawn from different but administratively compatible afternoons.
Mrs Chain stopped in the middle of the pavement. “There,” she said, pointing.
On the far side of the street stood a modest cream-coloured house with blue trim and a small front garden bordered by white stones.
Lolly might have called it cheerful had it not looked so distinctly as if someone had described cheerfulness to a machine and accepted the first draft.
Beside the gate, mounted where a brass house number ought to have been, was a plaque.
EQUIVALENT RESIDENCE UNIT 7B
Mrs Chain closed her eyes. “That,” she said, “is not my house.”
Beatrix looked at her. “It’s your address.”
“No,” said Mrs Chain, “it is an impersonation of my address.”
This was so exactly the right distinction that Lolly wrote it down at once.
Address is not home. Similarity is not continuity.
As they approached the gate, Jago glanced along the terrace. “Interesting,” he said.
Lolly looked up. “What is.”
“Every house has one.”
He was right.
Brass plaques gleamed all the way down the row.
Equivalent Residence Unit 7A. Equivalent Residence Unit 7B. Equivalent Residence Unit 7B (Revised). Equivalent Residence Unit 8. Equivalent Residence Unit 8A / Provisional.
Mrs Chain made a soft, offended noise which in another person might have been panic but in her case suggested the prelude to effective retaliation.
“My gate,” she said.
Lolly turned back.
The gate was there, technically. But it had become less a gate than a consensus. The hinges were in the right place, the latch existed, and the general notion of enclosure had clearly been respected.

What had vanished was its individual history: the small dent near the bottom, the flake of blue paint, the slight droop to one side that Mrs Chain had likely resented for years in a deeply domestic manner.
“It’s been averaged,” said Lolly quietly.
“Nothing in my life,” said Mrs Chain, “has earned the right to be averaged.”
Beatrix opened the gate. It gave no sound at all, which was somehow more ominous than a creak.
The front path was lined with potted daffodils.
Mrs Chain stopped again. “I don’t own daffodils.”
“They look official,” said Jago.
“They look synthetic,” said Beatrix.
Lolly bent slightly. The flowers were, indeed, artificial, but in the careful premium manner of a procurement team that had been instructed to provide “warmth.”
Mrs Chain’s voice lowered. “I had geraniums.”
“Perhaps they benchmarked poorly,” said Jago, which was not advice likely to preserve him.
Mrs Chain gave him a look that could have restructured a lesser man.
Inside, the house was immaculate.
This was the first and worst clue.
People really living in a place, Lolly felt, introduced minor frictions into it.
Shoes with opinions. Hall tables burdened by keys of varying utility. A newspaper not quite where it should be. Umbrellas that remembered rain.
This hallway contained an umbrella stand, a narrow mirror, and a bowl for keys, all placed so correctly that none of them had ever once been looked for in irritation.
Mrs Chain stepped in and drew a sharp breath. “My mirror was oval.”
The mirror on the wall was rectangular, tasteful, and entirely wrong.
“And the bowl?”
“Blue,” she said.
“That is teal, which is the sort of colour invented by people who wish to avoid a verdict.”
Lolly looked toward the stairs.
Framed photographs hung along the wall.
She moved closer.
In the first, Mrs Chain stood beside a short man in spectacles whom Lolly assumed had once been her husband.
In the second she stood alone in a garden she did not recognize.
In the third she appeared beside a dark-haired woman and a small white dog.
The trouble was not that the people were implausible. The trouble was that they were almost plausible.
“Is this your sister,” asked Lolly.
Mrs Chain came to her shoulder, looked, and stiffened. “No.”
“But it is you.”
“Yes,” she said. “Or enough of me to be impertinent.”
Beatrix moved toward the sitting room. “Look at the furniture.”
Lolly followed.
It was a good room. Comfortable armchair. Bookshelves. Two lamps. A sideboard. The sort of room one might spend fifteen years improving by tiny, stubborn increments.
Only this one had clearly been assembled in one afternoon by an intelligence that understood comfort as a category but not as a memory.
The armchair was too symmetrical.
The books were arranged by spine colour in blocks of reassuring compliance.
A table by the window held three coasters, each identical, because no real household has ever truly believed in identical coasters.
Mrs Chain walked to the mantelpiece. “My husband hated clocks,” she said. “Said they made the room feel supervised. There is now a clock where his photograph should be.”
Lolly looked. The clock ticked in a faint, officious manner.
“That,” said Mrs Chain, “is not a design choice. That is malice.”
Jago had drifted to the bookshelves. “These aren’t books,” he said.
Lolly joined him.
They were indeed books in the legal and physical sense, but not in the intimate one.
Their titles were subtly wrong.
The Collected Coasts of Sussex. Houseplants of Civic Value. Pleasant Soups Through the Year. A Listener’s Guide to Harp Moderation.
“Has anyone,” Jago asked, “ever voluntarily read a listener’s guide to harp moderation.”
“No,” said Beatrix. “It’s decorative literacy.”
Lolly wrote the phrase down immediately.
Then she crossed to the kitchen, drawn by some instinct of domestic triage.
There, too, things were nearly right and therefore unbearable.
The kettle was stainless steel instead of enamel.
The tea caddy had been labelled HOT BEVERAGE INFUSION MATERIALS in a neat Ministry hand.
Three mugs hung from hooks, each printed with a motivational saying about mornings.
Mrs Chain appeared in the doorway, saw the mugs, and muttered something so compressed and eloquent that Lolly felt it should possibly be preserved for future constitutional use.
She opened the tea caddy.
Inside were sachets.
“Dear God,” she said.
Beatrix leaned in. “What.”
“Bagged herbal alternatives.”
Mrs Chain gripped the counter. “No.”
Jago peered over Lolly’s shoulder. “Lemon serenity.”
Mrs Chain shut her eyes. “Ms Wren, if at any point it becomes necessary to break the law in order to restore my kitchen, I should like you to know in advance that I am philosophically available.”
Lolly was about to reply when the wall clock in the sitting room chimed eleven.
A moment later, the kitchen clock chimed ten forty-eight.
Then, somewhere upstairs, another clock struck noon with irritating confidence.
All four of them froze.
Beatrix said, “That’s not acceptable.”
“No,” said Lolly.
“Why not,” said Jago, “from a strictly theoretical standpoint.”
“Because,” said Lolly, “the house cannot hold its story together.”
There was a brief silence.
Then Beatrix looked at her. “Explain.”

Lolly set the tea caddy down very carefully, as one does with explosive materials and herbal substitutes. “Someone has made it choose a version before its details match,” she said. “It is trying to look finished and failing.”
Mrs Chain folded her arms. “So it’s not my proper house and not a proper replacement either.”
“Yes.”
“It’s botched.”
“Yes.”
Jago nodded appreciatively. “That’s almost comforting.”
Lolly took out the green notebook and wrote:
Premature decision settled house
Then below it:
A forced answer is not necessarily a finished one.
Beatrix was already moving again, opening cupboards, checking drawers, pulling at labels with the brisk resolve of an auditor committed to making the world justify itself.
“In here,” she said.
They joined her in a small room at the back of the hall which Mrs Chain identified, with indignation, as the airing cupboard.
A white sticker had been fixed above the handle.
OPTIONAL LINEN SPACE
Mrs Chain stared at it as if she had finally found the exact point at which civilization had given up. “It is not optional,” she said.
Beatrix held up a folded sheet of paper she had found wedged behind the towels. “It gets worse.”
The sheet was a checklist. At the top, in small unforgivable capitals, it read:
DOMESTIC CONSOLIDATION VISIT - RESIDENTIAL CLUSTER 7
Below were boxes, some ticked, some not:

Remove low-value uniqueness markers. Standardise navigational cues. Replace emotionally dense objects with compliant equivalents. Align photographs to nearest stable kinship model. Ensure clocks converge within tolerated interpretive spread. Install replacement beverage protocol.
Lolly felt something inside her sit down heavily.
Mrs Chain read the line about kinship twice. “Nearest stable what.”
Beatrix turned the page over. On the back someone had written, by hand and in pencil:
Unit 7B resisting final set. Memory adhesion unusually high. Recommend secondary review before identity trimming.
No one spoke. Even Jago, who seemed to consider silence a hobby for other people, looked briefly without charm.
Mrs Chain took the paper from Beatrix. “Identity trimming,” she said.
Lolly nodded once.
She looked at her with a terrible steadiness. “That means me.”
“Yes.”
The house, perhaps sensing that it had been discussed too accurately, made a small sound overhead. Not a creak. More a correction.
Then, from the sitting room, came the flat electronic ding of an arriving message.
They returned to find the rectangular mirror in the hall faintly lit. Words were appearing across its surface in blue.
WELCOME, RESIDENT. YOUR DOMESTIC EXPERIENCE HAS BEEN UPDATED FOR GREATER CONSISTENCY. PLEASE REPORT ANY REMAINING ATTACHMENT TO PREVIOUS LAYOUTS.
Mrs Chain set down the paper and picked up the umbrella from the stand.
Lolly, recognising the posture of a woman about to improve technology by force, said, “Possibly not-”
Too late.
She struck the mirror smartly across the middle.
The text vanished. The mirror cracked in a neat diagonal line and, for the first time all day, something in the house seemed honestly itself.
Jago let out a breath that might almost have been admiration. “That,” he said, “felt clinically significant.”
Beatrix bent to inspect the broken frame. Behind it, fixed to the plaster, was a small grey module no larger than a cigarette case, humming very softly.
Lolly stared. “What is that.”
Beatrix prised it loose. On the back was stamped:
CIVIC STABILITY SUBSTRATE - HOME EDITION Beneath it, in smaller type: Property of the Simplification Initiative
Lolly took the device in both hands. It was warm. Too warm.
“It’s local,” she said. “The revision isn’t only happening in central records. They’re installing reality correction hardware in people’s houses.”
Mrs Chain said, with terrible calm, “Remove it.”
Lolly looked uncertainly at Beatrix. Beatrix said, “Do it.”
Jago stepped back into the doorway. “Before you do, a practical note.”
Lolly glanced up. “What practical note.”
“If this thing is part of a wider correction network, unplugging it may tell someone that Unit 7B has become ideologically restless.”
Mrs Chain tightened her grip on the umbrella. “Excellent.”
Lolly turned the device over. On one edge was a recessed catch.
She pressed it.
The module clicked.
For one instant nothing happened.
Then everything in the room became uncertain. The clock vanished, reappeared, and turned into a photograph of a man with spectacles.
The daffodils in the hall browned into geraniums, then back again, then both at once in a manner Lolly found deeply rude.
The carpet pattern shifted underfoot from stripes to faded blue swirls to bare boards and back.
Somewhere upstairs, a door opened and shut in several incompatible styles.
Mrs Chain grasped the banister.
Lolly felt the air thicken around her, not physically but informationally, as though the house had ceased to know which version of itself it had most recently been ordered to become.
She opened the notebook with one hand and wrote almost blindly:
System disturbed. Underlying states still present. False certainty was holding them down.
Beside her Beatrix said, “Wren.”
She looked up.
At the far end of the hall, where the front door should have shown a small rectangle of afternoon light, there was now a man in a dark coat standing just inside the threshold.
No one had heard the door open. No one had heard him enter.
He held a slim case in one hand and wore the faint, polished smile of someone whose job consisted entirely of describing intolerable things as procedural necessities.
He inclined his head. “Good afternoon,” he said. “Continuity Review.”
Mrs Chain lifted the umbrella a little higher.
The man’s smile remained in place with professional courage. “I’m afraid,” he said, “someone appears to have interrupted an authorized domestic convergence.”

Lolly looked down at the humming module in her hands, at the cracked mirror, at the photograph that was still trying intermittently to become a clock, and then back at the man in the doorway. For the first time that day, the problem seemed almost refreshingly simple.
“Oh,” he said. “Was that yours.”

At the end of the corridor, a door that had been there ten minutes earlier was no longer there. Lolly wrote its number down before she could forget it. When she looked again, the number was still in the notebook. The door was not.
That was the first time she understood that the Ministry was no longer merely recording errors in reality. It was beginning to acquire them.

prosody.emphasis: Chapter 4: Continuity Review

p.prosody: There are several ways in which a stranger may stand in one’s hallway and become immediately unwelcome. He may be damp. He may be cheerful. He may carry a clipboard with the sort of ease that suggests long moral decline. Or, as in the present case, he may incline his head by half an inch and say “Continuity Review” as though this were the sort of phrase a decent person ought to find reassuring.

The man in Mrs Chain’s doorway managed all of these conditions except dampness, which only served to make the rest of him more offensive. He was in a dark coat of almost expensive sobriety, with a narrow tie and a face that looked as though it had once tried charm and settled, after a risk assessment, on procedure. In his right hand he carried a slim case of brushed grey metal. In his left he held a card badge displaying a silver spiral and the words:
MINISTRY OF CIVIC STABILITY CONTINUITY REVIEW Field Resolution
Mrs Elspeth Chain tightened her grip on the umbrella.
“I’m afraid,” said the man pleasantly, “someone appears to have interrupted an authorised domestic convergence.”
Lolly Wren looked down at the warm grey module in her hands, then back at the visitor. “Yes,” she said. “That does seem, in hindsight, to have occurred.”

The man stepped one shoe inside the threshold, then paused as if waiting for the house to endorse him. It did not, exactly, but a lamp in the sitting room brightened by a degree that felt sycophantic.
“My name is Alistair Venn,” he said. “Senior Review Officer, Continuity. If you’d all remain calm, this can be resolved locally.”

Mrs Chain gave a short laugh of such pure disbelief that even the daffodils in the hall seemed to reconsider themselves. “Mr Venn,” she said, “you have entered my house during a metaphysical burglary and used the word locally.”
“I do understand this is a distressing transition.”
“It is not a transition,” said Mrs Chain. “It is vandalism with signage.”

Beatrix Sloan had already moved to one side of the hall, where she stood with her arms folded and the air of an auditor preparing to improve a man’s afternoon beyond recovery. “Show me your authority,” she said.
Venn smiled. “Internal Audit.”
“Yes.”
“How comforting.”
“No,” said Beatrix, “specific.”

Venn set the slim case on the hall table-teal, Lolly noticed with renewed disgust—and removed a folded document stamped with too many approvals to be morally sound. “Phase One continuity authority,” he said. “Regional domestic stabilisation. Sub-clause twelve permits local correction where unresolved identity adhesion threatens public confidence.”
Mrs Chain pointed the umbrella at him. “Public confidence in what.”
Venn’s smile remained in place with admirable institutional training. “In dwellings, among other things.”
Jago Flint, who had taken up a position against the wall in the vague manner of a man unwilling to commit to being fully in one room, said, “That’s not an answer, is it.”
“It is the one currently issued,” said Venn.

Lolly, still holding the detached module, felt the house shifting minutely around her. The cracked mirror in the hall was attempting to decide whether it had always been cracked, and the clock in the sitting room had, for the moment, become a photograph again. One sensed a large number of small possibilities pressing upward through a badly fitted administrative lid.
Venn noticed the module in Lolly’s hand. “If you’d return that to me,” he said, “I can re-establish coherence.”
Lolly did not move. “What exactly does it do.”
“It supports stable domestic identity.”
“By replacing people’s teacups,” said Mrs Chain, “and misfiling their dead.”
Venn gave her a patient look. “By reducing low-value divergence.”
There are phrases which, once spoken aloud, remove any residual doubt as to whether a person deserves tea.
Beatrix said, “Define low-value.”
“Features whose emotional significance exceeds their civic necessity.”
Mrs Chain stared at him. “You ghastly man.”
Venn ignored this with professional ease. “Now then. If we proceed promptly, most residual variance can be contained.”

He opened the slim case. Inside lay a small handheld scanner, three blank forms, a silver pen, and a set of coloured tabs arranged with the sort of order one associates with people who have promoted neatness to an ethical principle.
Lolly felt a tightening at the back of her mind. “What do the tabs do,” she asked.
“Nothing dramatic,” said Venn. “They classify continuity pressure.”
“That is a dramatic sentence,” said Jago.
Venn selected a pale yellow tab and affixed it to the top of one form. “Site unstable,” he murmured. “Occupant resistant. Decorative conflict moderate.”
Mrs Chain made a sound like a kettle about to begin legal proceedings.
Then Venn raised the scanner and pointed it at the mantelpiece. A soft tone sounded. The photograph of the spectacled man flickered and became, for half a second, the clock again.
Lolly stepped forward. “Stop that.”
Venn lowered the device. “Ms-”
“Wren.”

“Ms Wren, your interference is understandable, but not helpful. The property is currently exhibiting unresolved domestic supernumeraries. Until I determine which elements belong to the authorised continuity path, the environment may display minor symbolic agitation.”
“Symbolic agitation,” said Beatrix. “Is that what you call deleting a woman’s life.”
“No,” said Venn. “That would be an escalation.”
The room went still. Even Jago seemed briefly at a loss for an appropriate angle of insolence.
Lolly looked at the scanner. “You’re testing the house object by object.” “Of course.”
“And every test makes it narrower.”
Venn tilted his head. “That is a somewhat theatrical way of putting it.”
“It is an accurate one.”
“Accuracy,” said Venn, “is not always the same thing as usefulness.”
This was, Lolly felt, the sort of remark that ought to disqualify a man from discussing reality.
Venn turned to Mrs Chain. “I’ll need to confirm a few details to reduce remaining branch pressure.”
“No,” said Mrs Chain.
“I’m afraid yes.”
“No,” she repeated, with the sort of clarity one associates with church bells and artillery.
Venn consulted the form as if the form might lend him courage. “Was your late husband,” he asked, “habitually visible in the front room.”
Mrs Chain blinked. “What.”
“On display,” Venn clarified. “Photographic representation, commemorative object, or emotional proxy.”
Lolly shut her eyes briefly.
Beatrix said, “You cannot possibly think that is an admissible question.”
Venn sighed the sigh of a man burdened by other people’s attachment to language. “We have found that unresolved bereavement often creates object density around obsolete personal states.”
Mrs Chain advanced one step. “My husband,” she said, “was not an obsolete personal state.”
Venn made a small note on the form. “High memorial adhesion,” he murmured.
Jago straightened from the wall. “I wouldn’t write that down if I were you.”
Venn, not yet appreciating the counsel, continued. “Now then. Sister present or absent in core domestic narrative?”
Mrs Chain simply looked at him.
Venn tried again. “Would you say your sister is structurally central to your self-model.”
Mrs Chain turned to Lolly. “Ms Wren.”
“Yes.”
“If I strike him, will the paperwork improve.”
“No,” said Lolly honestly. “But I am beginning to see its appeal.”

Venn raised the scanner again, this time toward the bookshelves. The titles shimmered. Pleasant Soups Through the Year became Regional Stews for Quiet Evenings, then Domestic Warmth: A Practical Guide, then settled once more on soup.
Lolly stared.
The scanner was not detecting a stable reality. It was forcing a choice each time it asked.
Question. Narrowing. Selection.
She opened the green notebook and wrote quickly:
Repeated inspection. Narrower answers. The form decides what survives.
Underneath that she added: The house is larger than the form.
She looked up and said, “You’re not restoring anything. You’re compressing it.”
Venn glanced over with mild interest, as one might regard a spaniel that had unexpectedly solved an invoice. “Compression,” he said, “is an inelegant term.”
“It’s exact.”
“It is practical.”
