“It’s theft.” This from Mrs Chain, with such force that even Venn chose not to answer at once.
Then, from upstairs, came a crash.
Everyone looked up.
Venn frowned. “That shouldn’t happen.”
“Good,” said Jago. “I enjoy it when systems lose confidence.”
Another crash followed, then the sound of a drawer opening in what Lolly would have sworn were at least two contradictory bedrooms.
Venn stepped toward the stairs. “Please remain here.”
Beatrix moved at once to block him. “No.”
“Ms Sloan, this is authorised territory.”
“You’ve already revised the kitchen into herbal defeat. You don’t get the upper floor without witnesses.”
Venn considered objecting, thought better of it, and climbed.

They followed in a compact and deeply unwilling procession: Venn first, Beatrix at his shoulder, Lolly with the notebook and the warm module, Mrs Chain gripping the umbrella like the last practical principle in the cosmos, and Jago behind them, carrying no visible authority at all and somehow appearing the least concerned.
Upstairs, the landing had changed again. The stickers remained on the doors, but they no longer agreed with the rooms.
BEDROOM A hung over what was plainly a bathroom. SANITATION UNIT had attached itself to the airing cupboard. OPTIONAL LINEN SPACE now marked the stairs to the loft.
“That,” said Mrs Chain, “is deranged.”
Venn scanned the corridor, and the labels jumped once more, nervously, as though caught gossiping. “Substrate drift,” he muttered.

He opened the first door. Inside, what had been earlier a bedroom now existed in a state of elaborate compromise. Half the wallpaper showed faded blue flowers; the other half had become a tasteful cream stripe. On the bed lay two duvets, one floral, one aggressively neutral, occupying the same territory with visible resentment. A framed photograph on the chest of drawers showed Mrs Chain beside the spectacled man from downstairs; another, half-phased into it, showed her alone on a cruise ship she had almost certainly never taken.
Lolly felt the strange and sudden intellectual terror of recognition. It was not that the room contained random errors. It contained alternatives still trying to survive.
She whispered, almost to herself, “They’re all still here.”
Venn turned. “What.”
“The discarded versions. The house hasn’t lost them. It’s suppressing them.”
Beatrix looked sharply from the room to Lolly. “Meaning.”
“Meaning the imposed version needs constant effort. Every scan and classification keeps pressing the other details out of view.”
Jago nodded as if this were perfectly ordinary conversation to be having beside a bed with contradictory duvets. “So the house is pretending harder than it can manage.”
“Exactly.”
Venn’s expression tightened for the first time. “Ms Wren, you are not qualified to assess continuity architecture.”
“No,” said Lolly. “But I am qualified to notice when a lie requires electricity.”
Venn took a step forward. “Return the substrate module.”
Lolly did not.
There followed one of those brief, lucid silences in which every person present understands that the day has crossed from paperwork into decision.
Then Jago said, “I may be wrong, but is this little grey thing wireless.”
Venn’s gaze flicked toward him. “Restricted information.”
“Excellent,” said Jago. “That means yes.”

He was moving almost before the sentence had ended. One moment he was in the doorway; the next he had crossed the room, lifted the floral duvet, and yanked from beneath the bed a thin cable leading into the skirting board.
“Jago,” said Lolly.
“Trust me.”
“Why would I.”
“No time.”
She pulled. The cable came free with a crack and a shower of plaster.
The effect on the house was immediate. Not catastrophic. Worse. Intimate.

The cream stripes on the wall dissolved into blue flowers. The photograph of the cruise ship vanished and was replaced by one of Mrs Chain and a dark-haired woman laughing over some unseen mishap. The neutral duvet slid to the floor.
From downstairs came a rapid sequence of sounds: the kitchen mugs shattering, the herbal sachets dropping like failed policy, a clock giving up halfway through a chime.
Mrs Chain gripped the bedpost. “My sister,” she said softly.
The woman in the restored photograph was, unmistakably, someone she knew.
Venn swore, and the effect was so startling in a man like him that it briefly improved him.
He lunged toward Lolly for the substrate module.
Beatrix intercepted him with the clean, efficient brutality of a person who had spent years carrying boxes of evidence and had made peace with leverage.
Venn hit the wardrobe, rebounded, and sat down abruptly on the edge of the bed with all the dignity of a policy meeting its evidence.
Jago looked genuinely impressed. “Oh, splendid.”
Beatrix did not look at him. “Wren.”
Lolly, heart thudding in a most administratively inconvenient way, turned the grey module over in her hands.
On its underside, beneath the Ministry stamp, something had been scratched in tiny letters as if by a previous handler unwilling to trust official channels.
If found active in residential field, contact S. Fainrose.
She was right.
Lolly read it twice. Then a third time.
“Beatrix,” she said.
“What.”
She held out the module.
She read the inscription, and for the first time since she had known her, her expression shifted from contemptuous control to something much closer to recognition.
“Bloody hell,” she said quietly.
Mrs Chain looked up. “What is it.”
Beatrix straightened. “A name.”
“Whose.”
She glanced at Lolly. “Someone who may know how bad this actually is.”
Venn, still recovering both breath and authority, said, “You cannot involve external theoretical parties.”
“No,” said Beatrix, tucking the module into her coat. “But we may.”
Downstairs, the house continued rearranging itself in unhappy little surges, as if relieved to be less wrong but not yet sure how to be right.
Lolly looked once more at the half-restored room: at the wallpaper finding its conviction, at the single duvet, at the photograph of the sister returned from administrative extinction.
Then she opened the notebook and wrote:
Too much observation can make the wrong world stick.
And below it: Need Fainrose.

prosody.emphasis: Chapter 5: Dr Fainrose Is Not Reassured

p.prosody: There are, Beatrix Sloan believed, only three proper responses to institutional catastrophe. The first was documentation. The second was containment. The third, reserved for special occasions and senior management, was witness selection.

This was why, forty minutes after the interruption of Mrs Elspeth Chain’s domestic convergence, she found herself in the back of an unlicensed grey car with Lolly Wren, Jago Flint, a confiscated Civic Stability Substrate module, one morally indignant umbrella, and a woman whose house was fluctuating between several unsatisfactory versions of itself.

The car belonged to Jago. Or rather, it belonged to a man in Croydon who believed it was in long-term bonded storage, which was not identical but had, Jago maintained, all the practical advantages of ownership without the correspondence.
Lolly sat in the back holding the grey module in both hands, as if it might otherwise begin revising her.
Mrs Chain sat beside her with the umbrella across her knees like a constitutional amendment awaiting use.
Beatrix occupied the front passenger seat in a state of concentrated disapproval.
Jago drove with one hand and the relaxed fatalism of a man who trusted neither maps nor causality.
“Where exactly,” said Lolly, for the third time, “are we going.”
Beatrix did not turn. “Fainrose.”
“That is not a place.”
“No,” said Jago. “It’s worse. It’s a person.”
Mrs Chain looked up. “The name on the device.”
“Yes,” said Beatrix.
Lolly glanced down at the scratched inscription on the module, though she already knew every stroke of it by heart.
If found active in residential field, contact S. Fainrose.
She was right; she had been trying, without great success, not to dwell on the final sentence.
There is something uniquely disheartening about the discovery that a person one has not yet met has already won an argument with the universe.
“Who is she,” asked Mrs Chain.
Beatrix was silent for a moment, which in her case meant the answer required enough accuracy to be annoying.
“Former Ministry physicist,” she said at last. “Systems architecture. Interpretive dynamics. Early transition modelling.”
“I’m sorry,” said Lolly. “Are those real subjects.”
“They were funded as if they could be made to sit still in a briefing paper.”
Jago turned left through a yellow light with the lightness of conscience that comes from never having truly recognised traffic law as binding philosophy.

“She used to be very fashionable,” he said. “Brilliant, impossible, terrifying in committee. Left after some unpleasantness involving continuity theory and a minister who thought eigenstates were a minority voting bloc.”
Mrs Chain considered this. “And we trust her.”
“No,” said Beatrix. “Good.”
“We require her.” “Better.”
They drove west.
The city thinned gradually, as though suburban planning had once set out to continue and then lost conviction.
Office blocks gave way to terraces, terraces to detached houses, detached houses to stretches of overmanaged green in which municipal trees stood at intervals suggesting budget approval.
The morning had developed into one of those bright English afternoons which seem determined, against all meteorological instinct, to deny the possibility of disaster while helping it along socially.
Lolly watched the route display on the dashboard.
It altered twice.
The first time, their destination changed from Wetherby Lane to Wetherby Approach.
The second time it became Fainrose Cottage / Pending Local Address Reconciliation.
She sighed.
Jago noticed. “You’ve got to stop taking road systems personally.”
“They’ve started first.”
“Fair.”
At length they turned off the main road and followed a narrow lane bordered by hedges, old brick walls, and an atmosphere of concentrated refusal.
A wrought-iron gate appeared where Lolly would have sworn there had been no gate half a second earlier.
It bore, in flaking black paint, a sign reading:
THE INSTITUTE FOR UNHELPFUL CLARITY Visitors by prior argument only No refunds for conclusions
Jago braked.
Mrs Chain leaned forward. “I like her already.”
Beyond the gate stood a long, low brick house with a slate roof, tall narrow windows, and the defensive air of a property that had spent years discouraging governments.
An old dish antenna had been bolted to one chimney.
Three bicycles leaned against a side wall in ways suggesting neither sport nor leisure.

On the lawn stood a brass armillary sphere, two folding chairs, and what appeared at first glance to be a weather vane but, on closer inspection, was almost certainly measuring something less forgivable.
Lolly got out and stared.
“This,” she said, “is where the Ministry’s former continuity architect lives.”
“No,” said Beatrix. “This is where she waits for it to fail.”
Before anyone could knock, the front door opened.
Stephanie Fainrose was not tall, and not young, and had the sort of stillness that makes other people feel physically over-articulated.
She wore a dark cardigan over a pale shirt, narrow trousers, and spectacles that looked less like an accessory than a final administrative judgment upon the human face.
Her hair, cut short and streaked with steel, suggested she had long ago discovered vanity to be one of several forces in the universe that could safely be ignored.
She looked first at Beatrix, then at Lolly, then at the module in Lolly’s hands, and then at Mrs Chain’s umbrella.
“Oh dear,” she said. “You’ve brought evidence and emotion.”
Mrs Chain drew herself up. “I beg your pardon.”
“Not criticism,” said Fainrose. “Classification.”
Her eyes moved to the module again.
“Come in,” she said. “If that thing is active, the hallway is the worst possible place for it unless you happen to dislike your staircase.”
They entered.
The house smelled of paper, tea, solder, and intellectual impatience.

Books lined every wall, not decoratively but in layers of active use. Blackboards leaned against shelves already burdened by journals, manuals, and notebooks labelled in a hand so precise it seemed almost vindictive.
A long table beneath the window held three microscopes, two mugs, several stacked crockery plates, a brass desk lamp, and what Lolly realised with quiet alarm was half of a dismantled detector array.
Mrs Chain looked around. “She lives properly.”
“I make allowances for entropy,” said Fainrose, closing the door.
Beatrix removed the module from Lolly’s hands and placed it on the table.
Fainrose looked at it for perhaps two seconds. Then she said, “Idiots.”
Lolly, who had spent the day surrounded by euphemism, felt an immediate and unreasonable surge of gratitude.
“You know what it is,” she said.

“Yes,” said Fainrose. “A domestic projection stabiliser, third-generation civilian adaptation, vulgar casing, incompetent thermal shielding. I warned them not to deploy these into lived environments without local phase damping. They said I was being precious.”
“Were you.”
“No,” said Fainrose. “I was being exact. Precision merely looks emotional to the incompetent, who prefer it in bullet points.”
Jago wandered toward the bookshelves. “Did you scratch the note.”
“Of course.”
Mrs Chain stepped forward. “My house has been replaced.”
Fainrose looked at her then, properly, and the severity of her face altered by a fraction.
“Not replaced,” she said. “Compressed. There’s a difference.”
“I don’t care for either.”
“No,” said Fainrose. “Most sane people don’t.”
She picked up the module with thumb and forefinger, carried it to a bench at the far end of the room, and placed it inside a wire mesh box connected to several cables.
A screen above the bench lit at once with graphs, matrices, and a pulsing red bar marked LOCAL COERCION FIELD.
Lolly took an involuntary half-step closer.
Fainrose noticed without looking up.
“You studied physics seriously once.”
She blinked. “How do you know that.”
“You’re standing like a woman being insulted by notation.”
“That seems unfairly accurate.”
“Yes,” said Fainrose. “The world rarely improves under scrutiny.”
She tapped several keys.
The red bar lengthened.
Then lengthened again. Then, to Lolly’s mounting discomfort, split into several thinner lines that rose and fell like competing heartbeats.
Fainrose stared at them. “Oh, that’s worse than I expected.”
Beatrix folded her arms. “How worse.”

Fainrose pointed at the screen. “This device is not merely enforcing one stable domestic reading. It’s selecting from multiple possible home-states and driving the property toward whichever one best satisfies central continuity metrics.”
Mrs Chain said, “In English.”
“It is choosing the cheapest version of your life that still looks enough like your life to survive complaint.”
Mrs Chain inhaled once, slowly, in the dangerous manner of a woman considering whether murder may briefly count as tidying.
Lolly said, “But it isn’t settling cleanly. The clocks, photographs, labels-they contradict one another.”
“Of course they do,” said Fainrose. “Because they’ve confused a state with a solution.”

She turned from the screen and looked directly at her. “When a system evolves naturally,” she said, “it doesn’t jump from richness to paperwork. It moves through lawful change. You can dislike the law, but you may not skip it. They’re imposing an end state without understanding the dynamics that produce one.”
Lolly felt the sentence land in her with peculiar force.
“You mean-”
“Yes,” she said. “They’re vandalising the evolution.”
Beatrix frowned. “Evolution of what.”
“Of everything that has not yet become final,” said Fainrose. “Homes. Routes. Identities. Intentions. Any state with multiple live continuations.”
Jago, still scanning titles on the shelves, said, “That sounds broad.”
“It is broad,” said Fainrose. “Which is why one grows tired.”
Lolly had taken out the green notebook without noticing.
Now she wrote:
Not state alone. Need law of change.
Fainrose saw this and gave the smallest of nods. “Good,” she said. “At least one of you is house-trained.”
Mrs Chain looked from one to the other. “What exactly are they doing to my house.”

Fainrose paused, perhaps deciding how much truth a person with an umbrella ought to receive at once. Then she said, “Imagine your home not as a place, but as a cloud of possible details held together by habit, memory, objects, routes through rooms, repeated actions, shared history, emotional residue, and expectation.”
Mrs Chain stared. “That is a surprisingly poetic start.”
“Don’t interrupt. It won’t happen again.”
Jago smiled openly.

Fainrose continued. “Now imagine some administrative imbecile decides this complexity is inefficient. Instead of letting that cloud develop into the version sustained by your actual life, they force it into a reduced pattern selected for stability, compliance, and cost. The trouble is, they don’t understand the equations well enough to know which details support the rest. So they flatten the system before it has finished cohering.”
Mrs Chain considered this. “In other words,” she said, “they have made a bad substitute.”
“Yes.” “Of something they did not understand.” “Yes.” “While being certain.” “Yes.”
Mrs Chain nodded. “Animals.”
Fainrose almost smiled. It was a quick, dangerous thing, gone before it could become sociable.
Beatrix said, “Can it be reversed.”
“Locally, perhaps. Systemically, not by amateurs.”
“We did not come to you because we enjoy amateurs,” said Beatrix.
“No,” said Fainrose. “You came because someone at last noticed the Ministry has confused measurement with authority.”
Lolly looked up. “That’s what the queue was doing.”
“Obviously.”
“It was selecting the interpretive frame first and forcing the case into it.”
“Yes.” “Then the house module does the same thing materially.”
“Yes.” “And the whole Simplification Initiative is-”
“A badly governed experiment in coercive collapse,” said Fainrose. “Congratulations. You’ve almost caught up with your own morning.”
Lolly might have objected to the tone if the content had not been so offensively plausible.
On the screen the cluster of lines shifted again.
One trace detached itself from the others and dropped steadily downward.
Fainrose’s face changed. Not much. Just enough.
Beatrix saw it first. “What.”
Fainrose leaned closer. “That,” she said quietly, “is not domestic.”
Lolly joined her at the bench.
A label had appeared beneath the descending line:
REMOTE ANCHOR LOSS GRAVITATIONAL CIVIC MASS INDEX BELOW TOLERANCE
She read it twice. Then again.
“Gravitational civic mass?” she said.
Fainrose rubbed the bridge of her nose. “There are days,” she said, “when I miss private thought.”
Mrs Chain came round the table. “What does it mean.”

Fainrose did not answer at once. Instead she reached for a second keyboard and called up a satellite map, then a network diagram, then what looked to Lolly like a topological model overlaid with municipal infrastructure and three equations pretending not to be terrified.
At the centre of one regional cluster blinked a small black icon. Next to it, in yellow:
Singularity Asset four C Status: Diminishing
Jago put down the book he had been pretending to browse. “Oh,” he said. “That seems bad.”
Fainrose was very still now. “Yes,” she said. “It does.”
Lolly looked from the screen to her face. “What is Singularity Asset four C.”
She answered without turning. “A black hole.”

No one spoke. This was partly because the statement had arrived with the calm administrative weight of a tea tray and partly because each of them, in different ways, required a moment to resent the universe properly.
Mrs Chain said at last, “Why is there a black hole in a civic cluster.”

Fainrose’s mouth tightened. “Transport curvature, waste density management, long-range compression, several profoundly stupid infrastructure efficiencies from fifteen years ago. The Ministry likes gravity when it can invoice it.”
Beatrix was already back in audit mode. “Why is it diminishing.”
“That,” said Fainrose, “is the question.”
Lolly looked again at the falling line on the screen. “Can black holes diminish.”
Fainrose gave her a sidelong look. “Yes.”
“In a municipal timeframe?”
“That,” she said, “would be unusual enough to ruin my afternoon.”
Jago leaned against the doorframe. “Would it be the sort of thing one ignores until it devours a county.”
“No,” said Fainrose. “Worse.”
He frowned. “Worse than devouring a county.”
“It may be evaporating.”
The room went quite still. Lolly heard the sentence not as sound but as a rearrangement of threat.
“A black hole,” she said carefully, “cannot simply evaporate.”

Fainrose looked at her with almost maternal disappointment. “Oh, Lolly,” she said, and it was the first time she had used her name, which made the correction land harder, “of course it can. The only question is whether someone has been foolish enough to make it do so where the public can object.”
Mrs Chain gripped the umbrella. “I object already,” she said.
“Quite right,” said Fainrose.
She shut down the domestic display and isolated the black-hole trace in a narrow window of its own.

“We will leave Mrs Chain’s house for the moment,” she said. “Not because it is unimportant. Because it is now evidence of a larger stupidity. If they have begun forcing collapse locally and interfering with gravitational anchors centrally, then the system is no longer merely rude. It is unstable.”
Beatrix nodded once. “Next step.”
Fainrose looked at all of them in turn. “Tea,” she said.
Jago brightened. “At last. A response proportionate to the danger.”
“Then,” said Fainrose, “we begin by assuming the worst and trying, with discipline, not to underestimate it.”
Mrs Chain set down the umbrella with ceremony. “At last,” she said, “someone sensible.”
Lolly opened the green notebook and wrote only four words.
Fainrose not reassured.
Then, beneath it: Neither am I.

prosody.emphasis: Chapter 6: The Object Is Not Mislaid

p.prosody: There are few statements less welcome in a country with planning committees than the sentence there is a black hole in regional infrastructure.
There are fewer still which improve on second hearing.

Stephanie Fainrose delivered it while adjusting the flame under a kettle with one hand and isolating a collapsing gravitational trace with the other, and it was characteristic of her that these acts appeared to belong to the same category of domestic competence.
Nobody spoke for several seconds.
Then Jago Flint said, “I don’t wish to seem needlessly difficult, but that sounds like the sort of thing someone ought to have mentioned on a sign.”
Fainrose ignored him.
On the narrow screen above the wire mesh box, the line marked Singularity Asset four C continued its steady descent.
It did not plunge, jitter, or fail theatrically. It diminished with the calm self-possession of a process obeying a law.
Lolly found this more disturbing than panic would have been.
She moved closer to the display. “When you say black hole-”
“I do,” said Fainrose.
“Yes, but in what sense.”
“In the astrophysical one, regrettably.”

Mrs Elspeth Chain, who had accepted over the last day that government could ruin a home, falsify a queue, and rename a sister out of existence, nevertheless seemed to feel that black holes ought to remain above the civil-service grade at which incompetence became infrastructure.
“You cannot possibly mean,” she said, “that the Ministry put an actual cosmic abyss under public administration.”

Fainrose poured water into a teapot. “My dear Mrs Chain,” she said, “the modern state will administer anything it cannot properly understand. Gravity is attractive to them because it looks authoritative from a distance.”
Beatrix Sloan remained by the bench, arms folded. “You said transport curvature and waste density management.”
“Yes.”
“That sounds invented.”
“Almost everything important does at first hearing.”
She brought the tea to the table with the composure of a woman whose threshold for disaster had long ago ceased to be numerical.

“There were experimental civic singularities fifteen years ago,” she said. “Tiny, engineered, heavily contained, used as anchor points for compression arrays, freight deflection, deep storage, and several proposals too idiotic to survive daylight. Most were decommissioned, on paper. A few, I suspect, were transferred into administrative twilight, where oversight goes when ministers require deniability.”
Jago accepted a cup. “And this one.”
“This one,” said Fainrose, “appears to be shrinking.”
Lolly sat down without entirely deciding to. “Black holes can lose mass,” she said slowly. “In principle.”
Fainrose looked at her over the rim of her spectacles. “Yes.”
“But not because someone moved a decimal point.”
“No.”
“Then why is it happening now.”
Fainrose set down her cup and returned to the bench. With quick, exact movements she called up a second plot beside the first: one curve descending, another climbing with glacial patience.
TEMPERATURE ESTIMATE.
“Because,” she said, “the universe is under no obligation to preserve large, gloomy objects merely because institutions have built paperwork around them.”
Lolly stood again. “You think it’s Hawking radiation.”

“I think,” said Fainrose, “that if a black hole loses energy by quantum emission, its mass falls. As its mass falls, its temperature rises. As its temperature rises, it radiates more efficiently. Which means the process does not merely continue. It accelerates.”
Mrs Chain stared. “Who is Hawking.”
There was a silence.
Beatrix closed her eyes briefly.
Jago said, “A physicist, Mrs Chain, not a department.”
“Though his name does have the regrettable competence of one,” said Fainrose.
Lolly was watching the screen. “That line-is that temperature increasing.”
“Yes.”
“And the downward line is mass.”
“Yes.”
“So the smaller it gets, the hotter it becomes.”
“Yes.”
“And eventually-”
“Eventually,” said Fainrose, “the object ceases to be a useful noun, which is rarely a calming development.”
Jago sipped tea. “I dislike it when physics becomes literary.”
“It is a flaw in the subject,” said Fainrose.
Beatrix stepped closer to the display. “How certain.”
“Of the mechanism, moderately. Of the consequences, sufficiently.”
“That is not a percentage.”
“No.”
Fainrose adjusted the scale again. The descending curve sharpened at its lower end, as though modestly reluctant to admit what came next.

“There is a vulgar public explanation,” she said, “involving particle pairs and one escaping from the horizon while the other falls inward. It is not wholly useless, but it encourages exactly the wrong sort of confidence. The cleaner statement is that quantum fields do not remain politely empty in curved spacetime, and black holes therefore emit thermal radiation. Once you accept that, the rest is book-keeping with terrible implications.”
Lolly opened the green notebook. “Thermal,” she said aloud while writing.
“So not random debris. Not leakage. Radiation with a temperature.”
“Quite.”
“And if it radiates, it loses energy.”
“Yes.”
“And since mass and energy-”
“Are old friends,” said Fainrose.
She wrote faster.
Mrs Chain, who had no intention of being excluded merely because the apocalypse had become mathematical, said, “What happens when it’s gone.”
Nobody answered her at once.
Outside, something metallic shifted in the garden. A branch tapped the window with the faint insistence of weather wishing to be kept informed.
At last Fainrose said, “That depends on what the Ministry has attached to it.”
Beatrix’s expression hardened. “Anchors.”
“Yes.”
“Compression fields.”
“Yes.”
“Transport shortcuts.”
“Possibly.”
Mrs Chain set down her cup with care. “In ordinary language.”

Fainrose turned. “If they built civic systems around a singularity,” she said, “then those systems are using extreme gravity as part of their structure. Remove the object, and whatever was leaning on it must either fail, detach, or seek another way to remain possible.”
Jago gave this a moment’s thought. “Roads may become philosophical.”
“Roads are already philosophical,” said Lolly.
“Good,” said Jago. “Then they may begin issuing manifestos at roundabouts.”
Fainrose almost smiled again.
Lolly looked from the plots to the wire-mesh box holding the domestic stabiliser. “The house module found it.”
“Yes.”
“Why.”

“Because the same idiots are involved,” said Fainrose. “Coercive civic simplification requires anchors. If you want to force rich systems into cheaper states, you need somewhere for the surplus possibility to go.”
Mrs Chain blinked. “I’m sorry. The surplus what.”
“Possibility,” said Fainrose. “Ambiguity. Unrealised structure. Contradictory detail. The things bureaucracies call inefficiency when they mean life.”
Lolly stopped writing.

A thought had arrived with the unpleasant smoothness of a blade entering water. “You mean the Ministry hasn’t just been classifying reality,” she said. “It has been removing degrees of freedom and dumping the cost elsewhere.”
Fainrose looked at her directly. “Yes.”
“Into the singularity.”
“Likely.”
Jago set his cup down. “And now the singularity is evaporating.”
“Yes.”
“So all the suppressed nonsense comes back out.”
Fainrose tilted her head. “That is not a scientific phrase.”
“Is it wrong.”
She considered. “No,” she said. “Annoyingly.”
Beatrix spoke at once. “Then we need location, rate, and threshold.”
“I’m getting them.”
“And after that.”
Fainrose’s fingers paused over the keyboard. “After that,” she said, “we determine whether this is merely catastrophic, or historically embarrassing.”
Lolly stared at the temperature curve.
There was a peculiar stillness to the room now, the stillness produced when every person present has understood the same fact but not yet found a shape in which to admit it.

The black hole was not being stolen. It was not being hidden. It was not awaiting approval. It was vanishing because the laws of quantum physics, after years of patient neglect, had at last presented their invoice.
Mrs Chain broke the silence first. “Can it be stopped.”
Fainrose did not answer immediately, which was answer enough to be offensive.
“Perhaps slowed,” she said at last. “Not by people who say leveraging gravitational assets in meetings.”
“Can it be repaired.”
“One does not repair a black hole, Mrs Chain. One regrets having treated it municipally.”
Jago let out a quiet breath. “Marvelous sentence.”
Beatrix ignored him. “How long.”

Fainrose expanded the end of the curve until the graph showed only a steepening tail. “That,” she said, “depends on its actual mass, its present feed rate, and how aggressively they have been using it as a sink for administrative overreach. Large black holes evaporate so slowly as to be practically eternal. Small ones are another matter.”
Lolly looked up. “And this one is small.”
“It was designed to be manageable,” said Fainrose, in a tone making plain that this was among the more reckless adjectives ever attached to a singularity, just ahead of affordable.
The kettle ticked as it cooled. Somewhere in the shelves behind them, a clock chose that moment to resume, giving a single abrupt click as though time itself had remembered an appointment.
Lolly turned another page in the notebook. “If the radiation is thermal,” she said, “then what comes out doesn’t obviously tell you what fell in.”
Fainrose’s face became very still. “No,” she said.
Jago glanced between them. “I don’t care for that tone.”
“You shouldn’t,” said Fainrose.
Beatrix said, “Explain.”

Fainrose rested both hands on the bench. “If a black hole forms from real matter, absorbs structure, and later evaporates into radiation that appears to carry only broad thermodynamic character, then one must ask what became of the original information.”
Mrs Chain said, “Information.”
“Yes.”
“Not matter.”
“Both, if you enjoy losing sleep properly.”
Lolly felt a chill quite unrelated to temperature. “The house,” she said.
Fainrose nodded once. “The house.”
“The queue.”
“Yes.”
“The missing details. The erased alternatives. The parts they compressed.”
“Yes, Lolly.”

She looked at the shrinking curve and understood, with a sensation bordering on nausea, that the Ministry’s project was not merely untidy governance. It was a wager against the recoverability of reality.
Mrs Chain rose from the table. “I knew,” she said, “the moment they altered my crockery that this would end in moral sewage.”
No one contradicted her.

Fainrose typed three final commands. A printer beneath the bench woke, considered its obligations, and began producing a long sheet of dense numbers and clipped warnings. At the top, in red, appeared:
SINGULARITY ASSET four C NET MASS LOSS CONSISTENT WITH HAWKING REGIME ANCHOR INSTABILITY ESCALATING
Beatrix took the page as it emerged. “Good,” she said. “Now we can prove they knew.”
Fainrose removed her spectacles, cleaned them once, and put them back on. “No,” she said. “Now we can prove they should have known. Which, in institutional terms, is often the more fatal category.”
Jago stood up. “I’m beginning to like science. It keeps its vindictive edges properly peer-reviewed.”
Mrs Chain picked up her umbrella. “And what exactly do we do now.”

Fainrose looked toward the window, where the morning had become unnaturally bright in the flat administrative way weather sometimes acquires before events. “We go and see,” she said, “how close the country is to being held together by an evaporating hole and several assumptions.”
Lolly closed the notebook.
On the last line she wrote:
Not vanishing by error. Vanishing by law.
Then, after a moment:
Much worse.

Fainrose looked at the gravitational trace and then at Lolly. “We have a clock,” she said. “A real one. Not a Ministry deadline. The anchor is evaporating, and when it goes, whatever is still inside it stops being recoverable.”
Lolly wrote the time down. She underlined it twice. For once, the paperwork was not the most frightening thing in the room.

prosody.emphasis: Chapter 7: What Remains Correlated

p.prosody: By the time they reached the Regional Compression Annex, the day had acquired the exhausted brightness peculiar to national mistakes.
The building stood behind two fences, one camera mast, and a sign which read:
CIVIC INFRASTRUCTURE HARMONISATION SITE Authorised access only No public gravitation beyond this point
“There,” said Jago Flint, slowing the car, “is a sentence nobody wrote with a clear conscience or a functioning solicitor.”
The annex had once been a distribution hub, though years of government improvement had polished it into the sort of place that no longer admitted to having had a function.
Its walls were pale, windowless, and faintly curved in a way that suggested either modern design or local damage to geometry.
Several service roads led toward it and then, halfway there, seemed to lose confidence and become lay-bys.
Stephanie Fainrose observed all this without visible surprise.
“That’s new,” she said.
“The building?” asked Lolly.
“The curvature suppression.”
She looked again.
Now that she had said it, the air above the concrete yard did seem oddly mannered, as if distances were being encouraged not to express themselves fully.
Beatrix Sloan had already stepped out of the car and was walking toward the gate with the clipped inevitability of an approaching audit.
“Do we have entry authority,” said Lolly.
“No,” said Beatrix.
“Then what exactly is the plan.”
“I am going to ask in a tone that makes refusal sound career-limiting and pension-adjacent.”
Mrs Elspeth Chain emerged from the back seat with her umbrella and looked up at the sign.
“No public gravitation,” she read. “They always phrase wickedness as if it were a leisure rule.”

The gate guard, whose relationship with sleep appeared to have become historical, took one look at Beatrix’s identification, one look at Fainrose’s face, and decided that regulations were excellent in principle but perhaps not in this specific hour.
They were admitted.
Inside, the annex was colder than the day required.
Corridors extended in several directions under long white lights, all of them labelled with the sort of terminology institutions use when trying to make dangerous machinery sound recyclable.
Signs pointed toward VECTOR SANITISATION, METRIC STORAGE, and ANCHOR MANAGEMENT.
One arrow had been hastily covered over, but not so well that Lolly could not still read GRAVITY WELL OBSERVATION beneath the tape.
“Subtle,” said Jago.
“It used to be worse,” said Fainrose.
“You’ve been here.”
“Once. I resigned shortly afterwards.”
This seemed fair.

They passed through two security doors, a control station, and a room full of humming cabinets attended by three technicians who possessed the unmistakable air of people who had obeyed instructions for so long that reality itself now felt above their pay grade.

On the far wall, a large display showed the same descending trace they had seen at Fainrose’s house, only here it was surrounded by status lights, internal bulletins, and an amber warning banner that read:
ANCHOR THERMAL DRIFT WITHIN PROJECTED ENVELOPE No intervention required at this time
Fainrose stopped dead.
“Oh,” she said softly. “Now I’m angry.”
One of the technicians rose. He was young, eager, and had the brittle optimism of a man who believed complex systems were improved by badges.
“This area is restricted,” he began.
Beatrix placed the printed diagnostic from Fainrose’s bench on the console.
“No,” she said, “this area is evidence.”
He looked down at the page, then up at Fainrose, and visibly regretted several earlier life choices.
“We’ve been assured,” he said, “that the anchor is shedding excess load in a controlled manner.”
Fainrose stared at him. “That sentence,” she said, “contains so little understanding I scarcely know where to begin.”
Lolly moved closer to the master display.
Several subsidiary windows were open around the main mass-loss curve.
One showed municipal transport routes blinking in and out like doubtful constellations.
Another listed compression burdens by district.
A third, to her growing unease, contained a stream of domestic reconciliation events, each with timestamps and area codes.
Mrs Chain saw it too. “My house,” she said.
There it was.
CHAIN, E. Residential convergence: incomplete. Residual identity conflict: elevated. Overflow channel: accepted.
Lolly read the last line twice.
Overflow channel.
She turned to Fainrose. “They really are using the singularity as a sink.”
“Yes,” she said. “For unresolved alternatives, unstable classifications, excess correlation, and anything else their system cannot afford to keep locally.”
The young technician tried a professional smile and failed at it midway.
“It’s only metadata.”
“No,” said Fainrose. “That is what foolish people call reality when they are too cowardly to say they have abstracted it.”
Beatrix was already scanning the local logs. “How long have they known about the thermal rise.”
The technician hesitated.
Jago leaned on the console. “I ask this as a friend of institutional collapse: answer quickly.”
“Three months,” said the man.
Beatrix looked up. “Three months.”
“It was judged non-critical.”
Fainrose gave a short laugh devoid of amusement. “Of course it was. Slow disasters are irresistible to committees. They offer so many opportunities for scheduling.”
Lolly was no longer looking at the technicians.
She was watching the transport map.
Each time one route vanished, a line elsewhere brightened. Each time a domestic event entered the overflow channel, the anchor field fluctuated by a tiny amount.
Separately, none of it meant much. Together, it produced a pattern so offensively neat that she felt insulted on behalf of causality.
“These aren’t separate failures,” she said.
“No,” said Fainrose. “The routes, the queue, the houses-”
“No.”
“They’re coupled.”
Fainrose came to stand beside her. “Yes.”
On the lower part of the screen, hidden behind system tabs, was a label she had not noticed before:
CORRELATION BUDGET
Beneath it, a meter was moving steadily toward red.
“What,” said Lolly, “is a correlation budget.”
The room became quiet in the way rooms do when language has at last chosen to become incriminating.
Fainrose folded her arms. “It means,” she said, “that some administrative ghoul decided interconnectedness was too expensive to maintain in full.”
Mrs Chain frowned. “Interconnectedness of what.”
“Lives. records. places. choices. Shared histories. Mutual constraints. Any detail whose meaning depends on something else.”
Jago considered this. “So instead of managing complexity, they’ve been charging it rent, with a late fee for sentiment.”
“Precisely.”
The technician, perhaps sensing a need to defend the dead, said, “The system only suppresses non-essential linkages.”
Mrs Chain turned to him with the calm of a woman who had already passed through outrage and was now travelling under clearer weather. “My sister,” she said, “is not a linkage.”
Nobody improved on this.
Fainrose reached over the console and opened a deeper systems pane.

The diagram that appeared looked less like software than a nervous breakdown rendered in geometry: district nodes, domestic nodes, routing lattices, and at the centre a black disk marked four C, around which thousands of fine lines converged and vanished.
Lolly stared. “They attached everything to it.”
“Not everything,” said Fainrose. “Only everything they meant to simplify.”
“And now it’s evaporating.”
“Yes.”
“So the things tied to it don’t just break. They become uncertain together.”
“Exactly.”
One of the senior technicians entered at that moment, carrying a clipboard and the settled confidence of a man who had survived many meetings by confusing sequence with thought.
“What is going on here.”
Beatrix held up her identification. “Official review.”
“We have no notice of review.”
“You do now.”
He took this badly and looked to the monitors for institutional support.
Instead he found Fainrose.
His face altered. “Dr Fainrose.”
“Mr Voller.”
“I was told you had become private.”
“And I was told you had become harmless. We are both disappointed.”
Voller drew himself up. “The anchor remains within tolerance.”
Fainrose pointed at the red-trending mass curve. “No. The software remains within tolerance. The black hole is evaporating.”
He smiled the smile of a career bureaucrat greeting an inconvenient noun.
“That interpretation is contested.”
“It is thermodynamics,” said Fainrose. “Not a consultation.”
Lolly almost wrote that down and then realised she had already started.
Voller turned to the correlation display. “The coupling lattice is robust.”
Fainrose’s expression became almost kind, which made it much worse. “Yes,” she said. “That is the problem. The more robust the entanglement, the less politely the decoherence spreads.”
Voller blinked. “The what spreads.”
Now Lolly was listening with her whole body.

Fainrose tapped the central black disk. “You tied many local systems to one central quantum-gravitational anchor. That means their states are no longer fully independent. They share structure. Once the anchor becomes noisy, hot, or unstable, the environment starts learning which alternatives are linked to which. Coherence drains away. The system stops behaving like one carefully maintained possibility and starts behaving like a classical mess.”
The technician at the near console said, “That sounds speculative.”
“It sounds,” said Fainrose, “like you were never taught any quantum mechanics.”
Lolly looked back at the diagram.
“Entanglement,” she said slowly, “means you can’t describe the parts independently anymore.”
“Yes.”
“And decoherence means the environment starts carrying away the phase relations.”
“Yes.”
“So once that happens, the lost alternatives don’t recombine cleanly.”
“No.”
“They become records of damage.”
Fainrose glanced at her, and for a moment there was something almost approving in her face. “Very good.”
Mrs Chain surveyed the room, the screens, the men, the language, and the trembling civic skeleton of the thing.
“In plain English,” she said.
Fainrose obliged. “They have connected too many delicate realities to one dying object. Now that object is leaking order.”
“That,” said Mrs Chain, “is plain enough.”
On the main display, the correlation budget crossed into red.
Every monitor in the room flickered once.
Then again.
Across the transport map, three routes vanished simultaneously.
The domestic-events stream began scrolling too fast to read.
Somewhere deeper in the annex, an alarm started and then stopped, as if embarrassed to have noticed reality before management had approved the event.
Voller turned pale. “What did you do.”
Fainrose did not move. “I arrived,” she said. “The universe did the rest.”
Lolly was watching one smaller pane on the right-hand side of the screen.
It listed overflow returns.
Items that had been channelled into the anchor were beginning, for want of a better term, to come back.
Not whole.
Fragments. Alternative street names. Contradictory birth records. old queue tokens. ownership disputes. duplicate memorial photographs. rejected room layouts. mislaid correspondences.
A hundred small amputations of the ordinary, all pressing at once against the weakened civic membrane.
“They’re coming out,” she said.
“They were never gone,” said Fainrose. “They were only stored somewhere obscene.”
Beatrix had already moved to the emergency controls. “Can we isolate districts.”
“Not without making choices,” said Fainrose.
“What choices.”
“Which correlations to save.”
Nobody enjoyed that sentence.
Jago looked at the map and whistled softly. “Well,” he said, “we seem at last to have found the national character: underfunded entanglement with a modest contingency reserve.”
Voller was shouting into a desk phone now, demanding senior clearance from people who were almost certainly already practising distance.
The screens flashed again.
This time, Lolly felt it.
Not physically, exactly. More as a brief rearrangement in the logic of nearby things, as if every object in the room had been forced to remember what else it depended on.
She saw Mrs Chain grip the umbrella, saw Beatrix brace one hand on the console, saw Jago step back from a monitor that had begun listing addresses in two different counties at once.
And then, on the central display, a new warning appeared:
ANCHOR COHERENCE LOSS CASCADING LOCAL RECOVERY NO LONGER COMMUTATIVE
Lolly stared at the last word.
Fainrose saw it too. “Oh, excellent,” she said without enthusiasm. “Order now matters.”
Mrs Chain said, “I beg your pardon.”

“It means,” said Lolly, before she could stop herself, “that you can’t fix everything in any sequence you like. If two repairs don’t commute, doing A then B gives a different result from doing B then A.”
Fainrose looked at her. “Yes,” she said. “And now you see why I never sleep.”
Beatrix turned from the controls. “Can we still stop the cascade.”
Fainrose’s answer was immediate. “No.”
The room held that.
Then she added, “But we may still choose its shape.”
That was the point, Lolly realised, at which disaster ceased to be theoretical and became administration again, though of a more honest and terrible sort.
Beatrix straightened. “Right,” she said. “Then we prioritise.”
Mrs Chain lifted her umbrella. “At last,” she said, “a meeting with a moral centre.”

Fainrose began issuing instructions so quickly that even panic had to become organised in order to keep up. “Freeze new convergence events. Cut overflow routing. Detach non-essential transport couplings. Preserve hospitals, archives, and power lattices. Anything sentimental with structural dependency goes above policy threshold.”
Voller stared. “Sentimental.”
“Yes,” snapped Fainrose. “That is where people keep the irreplaceable pieces, Mr Voller. We have been over this as a civilisation.”
Lolly opened her notebook to a clean page and wrote:
Entangled systems fail together. Decohered systems do not forgive sequence.
Then, beneath it: The country is attached to a dying argument with physics.

prosody.emphasis: Chapter 8: The Backup That Could Not Exist

p.prosody: There is a particular species of official calm that arrives only after the situation has become unsalvageable.
It is not courage. It is not competence.

It is the calm of a man who has just realised that the thing he is standing in will shortly be described in a report, and who has begun, quietly and with great professional discipline, to consider his own paragraph.
Mr Voller had reached this stage by twenty past four.
“There is a restoration protocol,” he said.
The Regional Compression Annex had by then acquired the atmosphere of a hospital in which the patient had begun offering opinions.
Two of the wall displays were showing districts that did not currently agree on their own boundaries.
A printer in the corner had produced eleven copies of a form that had never been designed.

Somewhere below them, in the deeper part of the building where the anchor housing sat behind three doors and a good deal of optimism, something was making a sound not unlike a cathedral clearing its throat.
Stephanie Fainrose did not look up from the console.
“Say that again,” she said.
Voller straightened his cuffs, which is what such men do instead of praying, having long ago misfiled the latter as an external dependency.
“There is a restoration protocol,” he repeated. “Full-state civic reconstruction. We hold a reference copy.”
Beatrix Sloan turned very slowly. “You hold what.”

“A reference copy,” said Voller. “Of the pre-simplification configuration. Homes, records, routes, identity linkages. Everything the Initiative touched was mirrored before adjustment. It was a condition of approval. I signed the assurance myself.”
Lolly Wren, who had spent the last hour watching reality itemise its own injuries, felt a brief and treacherous flare of hope.
It lasted approximately as long as it took her to look at Fainrose’s face.
She had gone quite still.
“Mr Voller,” she said, and her voice had lost all its edges, which was infinitely worse than when it had them, “where is this copy.”
“Cold vault. Sub-level two. Independent substrate, isolated field, no live coupling.”
He permitted himself the smallest recovery of dignity. “Precisely so that it could not be affected by anything occurring above.”
“And what,” said Fainrose, “is in it.”
Voller blinked. “The state. The prior state.”
“Which prior state.”
“The correct one.”
Fainrose closed her eyes for a moment. “Lolly,” she said. “Come here.”
She went.
She pulled a fresh pane onto the display and typed a short command.

The vault manifest opened: page after page of entries, each one a district, a street, a dwelling, a person, a linkage, all neatly indexed, all timestamped, all marked with a small green tick indicating successful capture.
It was, Lolly thought, one of the most reassuring documents she had ever seen, and she understood at once that this was the problem with it.
“Look at the fidelity column,” said Fainrose.
She looked.
STATE CAPTURE: COMPLETE CLASSICAL REPRESENTATION: VERIFIED PHASE RECORD: NOT APPLICABLE
She read the last line three times, in the manner of a woman hoping that words might be persuaded.
“Not applicable,” she said.
“Not applicable,” said Fainrose. “They didn’t record the phase relations.”
“They could not record the phase relations.”
“Then this isn’t a copy.”
“No,” said Fainrose. “It is a photograph of a conversation, with all the inconvenient replies removed.”
Mrs Elspeth Chain had come to the console with her umbrella in the crook of her arm and the expression of a woman determined to be present at the moment when the men admitted it.
“Explain,” she said.

Fainrose turned to her, and something in her manner changed. She spoke to Mrs Chain, always, as though Mrs Chain were the only person in the room whose understanding actually mattered - which, Lolly had begun to suspect, was a fairly accurate assessment.
“When they measured your house,” said Fainrose, “in order to save it, they had to ask it questions.”
“They asked a great many.”
“Yes. And each question returned an answer. Blue wallpaper. One duvet. Husband present. Sister absent. All perfectly recordable. All faithfully written down.” She tapped the manifest.
“That is what is in the vault. Answers.”
“And that is not the house.”

“That is not the house. The house was also the relations between the answers. The way the sister depended on the kitchen, and the kitchen on the route to the shops, and the route on forty years of walking it. Those relations were not answers to any question they knew how to ask. To write them down, they would have had to ask a different question - and asking it would have destroyed the answers they had already taken.”
Mrs Chain considered this for some time. “So they could have one or the other,” she said.
“Yes.”
“But not both.”
“Not both. Never both. Not by incompetence - by law.”
Fainrose’s mouth tightened. “And so, being administrators, they took the one that fitted the form.”
Jago Flint, from his position against the doorframe, said, “Forgive me. Could they not simply have made a second house and asked it the other question.”
“No,” said Fainrose.
“Why not.”
“Because you cannot copy it, Mr Flint. That is not a difficulty. That is a theorem.”
Voller made a small noise of protest. “We back up systems constantly. Every department-”

“You back up records,” said Fainrose. “You have never once backed up a state. Nobody has. Nobody will. If a general quantum state could be duplicated, you could measure the copy without disturbing the original, and the entire structure of physics would come apart in your hands like wet cardboard. It cannot be done. It has been known that it cannot be done for a very long time. It is in the literature. It is not obscure.”
She looked at him. “You signed an assurance that you had done an impossible thing, and nobody in the approval chain knew enough to laugh.”
The silence that followed had a specific quality.
It was the silence of five people all doing the same arithmetic and arriving at the same figure.
Lolly broke it. “Then the vault is worthless.”

“No,” said Fainrose. “Worthless would be a mercy. The vault is plausible. Which means that at some point in the next several hours, a senior person will be told that a full restoration is available, and that person will authorise it, and the system will overwrite what remains of the real configuration with a flattened cartoon of it, and it will report success in green letters.”
Beatrix had already moved. “Then we lock the vault.”
“Yes.”
“On what authority.”
“Mine,” said Beatrix, “retroactively.”
Voller found his voice. “You cannot seal a national restoration asset on a theoretical objection.”

Beatrix looked at him with the particular patience of an auditor who has been waiting eleven years for exactly this sentence. “Mr Voller,” she said, “I have sealed a hospital laundry contract over a missing signature. You have no idea what I am capable of when the physics is on my side. It is an unusually well-documented side.”
She began typing.

Fainrose, meanwhile, had turned back to the anchor traces, and Lolly - who had learned over the past day to read her shoulders the way sailors read weather - saw that she had stopped being angry, which meant she had started being useful.
“If we cannot restore it,” she said, “what can we do.”
“Something better,” said Fainrose. “Something the vault people never understood, because they were thinking about storage instead of structure.”
She pulled up the correlation lattice again: the great trembling web of district nodes, domestic nodes, routing lines, all of it still convergent on the black disk marked four C.
“Look at it properly, Lolly. Not as a map. As a code.”

She looked. “There’s redundancy,” she said slowly. “The same information appears in more than one place. Mrs Chain’s sister isn’t only in Mrs Chain’s house. She’s in the ownership record, and the queue token, and the memorial photograph, and the route to the shops, and the two contradictory birth entries-”
“Go on.”
“-and no single one of those is sufficient. But together they overdetermine her.”
She felt the shape of it arrive. “You don’t need the copy. The information isn’t in any one place. It’s in the pattern across all of them.”
Fainrose permitted herself, at last, the full smile. It was brief, and slightly frightening, and Lolly understood that she had just passed an examination she had not known she was sitting.

“That,” she said, “is how one protects a delicate thing without ever holding it. You do not keep a copy. You spread it out so thin that no local damage can find enough of it to destroy. Any single node may be lost, corrupted, misfiled, or run over by a lorry, and the whole may still be recovered from what remains - provided you know which correlations to trust, and provided you repair them in the right order.”
Jago said, “And do we know the right order.”
“No.”
“Ah.”
“But we know it exists,” said Fainrose, “which is more than the Ministry has known about anything since Tuesday.”
Beatrix finished typing and stood back.
On the main display, the words

RESTORATION ASSET: SEALED PENDING REVIEW appeared, followed almost immediately by three separate priority queries from three separate departments, all of which she ignored with the serenity of a woman who had already decided which hill this was.
“How long to work out the order,” she said.

Fainrose was already assembling something on the second console - a syndrome table, Lolly realised, watching the columns fill: not a list of what was broken, but a list of which combinations of breakages could be told apart from one another.
“That depends,” she said, “on whether we can measure the damage without measuring the thing.”
Lolly stared at her. “Is that possible.”

“It is the only thing that is possible,” said Fainrose. “You do not ask the patient how they are. You ask whether their left hand and right hand still agree. The answer tells you where the injury is and nothing whatever about who they are - which is precisely why it does not hurt them.”
She glanced up. “It is the one form of inspection this Ministry never learned, because it requires wanting to know something other than an answer.”
Below them, in the anchor housing, the cathedral cleared its throat again.
Mrs Chain looked at the ceiling, then at the floor, then at Fainrose.
“Dr Fainrose.”
“Mrs Chain.”
“When you have finished,” said Mrs Chain, “will my sister be my sister.”
Fainrose did not soften it, and Lolly thought better of her for it.
“She will be recoverable,” she said. “That is not the same as unharmed. But it is the difference between a person and a form, and I intend to spend the rest of the evening defending it.”
Mrs Chain nodded once. “Then I shall make the tea,” she said, “and you will all stop apologising and start working.”
Lolly opened the green notebook.
She wrote:
No copy exists. No copy can exist.
Then, below it:
But it is written everywhere at once, faintly, and that is stronger than a copy - provided one repairs it in the right order.
And then, after a moment, in smaller letters:
They built a vault. They should have built a code.

prosody.emphasis: Chapter 9: The Two Columns

p.prosody: The order came down at six minutes past nine the following morning, on paper, which was itself a bad sign.
Ministries that intend to be reasonable send email. Email can be amended, forwarded, or quietly forgotten. Paper is sent when someone senior wishes there to be an object later.
Beatrix Sloan read it twice at the annex reception desk, then carried it to the long table in the observation room and put it down in front of Stephanie Fainrose without comment.
Fainrose read it. Then she laughed: one short, unlovely sound, like a chair leg on tile.
“Oh, they’ve done it,” she said. “They’ve actually legislated it.”
Lolly Wren leaned over. The document ran to a page and a half and had passed through at least four hands, each of which had made it worse.
DIRECTIVE 11-C: CIVIC RECOVERY ASSURANCE
In order that public confidence be maintained during the current period of adjustment, all recovery operations shall be conducted so as to satisfy both of the following conditions simultaneously:

The precise present configuration of each affected dwelling, record, and person shall be established and certified to district level, such that no citizen enquiry may receive an indeterminate response.

The precise rate and direction of ongoing change in each affected dwelling, record, and person shall be established and certified to district level, such that all future states may be projected and no citizen enquiry may receive an unforecastable response.
Recovery may not proceed until both certificates are held.
Signed, on behalf of the Board, C. Vale
Lolly read it again.
“Both,” she said.
“Both,” said Fainrose. “To arbitrary precision. Simultaneously. With certificates.”
“That’s—”
“Yes.”
“That’s not a difficult instruction.”

“No,” said Fainrose. “A difficult instruction is one you fail. This is an instruction you cannot begin.” She set the paper down very precisely, squaring it with the edge of the table, which Lolly had learned was what she did instead of throwing things. “Somebody has looked at physics, disliked the terms, and issued a rebuttal.”

Jago Flint, who had spent the night in a chair and looked entirely unaffected by it in a way Lolly found personally offensive, said, “Is it truly impossible, or merely very hard? I ask because I have made a living in the distinction.”
“There is no distinction.”
“There is always a distinction.”

“Not here.” Fainrose pulled a blackboard on castors round from the wall. Something in the room’s temperature changed; even Voller, hovering by the door, stopped pretending to consult his clipboard. “Mr Flint. If I insist on knowing exactly where a thing is, what have I done?”
Jago considered. “Pinned it.”
“Yes. And if I ask, with equal insistence, exactly where it is going?”
“You have asked for a different sort of answer.”

“One which the first answer has made worse.” She put down the chalk. “They are not two independent facts that a sufficiently determined civil servant can requisition. The more tightly one is fixed, the less honestly the other can be certified. There is no apparatus, budget, or signature that alters the bargain.”
Mrs Elspeth Chain, who had appointed herself to the tea and to the moral summary, said, “And they have ordered both.”
“To district level.”
“With certificates.”
“With certificates.”
Mrs Chain set down the pot. “Then they have ordered the tide.”
“Considerably worse,” said Fainrose. “The tide would refuse and continue being the tide. A civil service does not refuse. It complies.”
Lolly felt the floor of the argument give slightly beneath her.
“What does compliance look like,” she said, “when the thing is impossible?”
Fainrose looked at her for a long moment.
“That,” she said, “is the only question in the directive.”

The answer arrived at ten forty in the form of a young woman from Certification named Miss Adaeze Pike, who had a laptop, a lanyard, and the specific brightness of a person doing well within a system she had not yet examined.
She was, Lolly thought, entirely blameless, and she disliked what was about to happen to her.
“We’ve had 11-C too,” she said cheerfully, setting up at the end of the table. “Field Certification. We’ve been running since seven.”
Beatrix’s head came up. “Running what?”
“Both columns.” Miss Pike turned the laptop so that they could see. “Column A is present configuration. Column B is rate of change. Every affected address gets a line.”

The spreadsheet was beautiful. Lolly had spent long enough in electronics to recognise a well-built sheet: conditional formatting, locked headers, validation on every field. Somebody had cared about this.
Every single row was filled.
“How,” said Fainrose.
Miss Pike blinked. “How what, sorry?”
“How did you fill Column B?”

“Oh—from the survey,” said Miss Pike. “The Continuity Review data. We take the certified present configuration, compare it to the previous certified present configuration, divide by the interval. That gives rate of change.” She smiled, pleased with the tidiness of it. “It’s rather elegant, actually. The same measurement serves both columns.”
There was a pause of perhaps three seconds.
Then Fainrose said, very gently, “Miss Pike, would you sit down?”
Miss Pike sat down, because that was the sort of voice it had been.
“When you certified the present configuration,” said Fainrose, “what did the surveyor do to the dwelling?”
“Scanned it. Object by object. It’s a full-resolution pass, so every element is fixed to certified state. That’s what makes Column A reliable.”
“Fixed.”
“Yes.”
“And then you scanned it again a week later, compared the results, divided the difference by seven days, and called the result the rate of change of the house.”
“Exactly.”
“Miss Pike,” said Fainrose, “you have not measured the rate of change of the house. You have measured the rate at which your own instrument disturbed it.”
Miss Pike’s expression did not change immediately. Lolly watched it fail to change, and then watched it change.
“No,” she said. “No, because the disturbance is calibrated out. There’s a correction factor. Annex Four.”
“Show me Annex Four.”
She showed her. Fainrose read it in about eleven seconds, and Lolly, who had developed a reasonable ear for her silences, understood that the eleven seconds were courtesy.
“This factor,” said Fainrose, “was derived by comparing scan results against a reference configuration.”
“Yes.”
“Held in the cold vault.”
Miss Pike’s fingers stopped on the trackpad.
“The vault’s been sealed since last night,” she said. “There’s a note. I assumed it was procedural.”
“It was me,” said Beatrix.
“Why?”
“Because it is a photograph of a conversation,” said Beatrix, “and I did not intend to let anyone restore the country from it.”

Miss Pike looked at the spreadsheet. She looked at it for rather a long time. Lolly did not have forty years of watching people discover that the ground was not where the drawing said it was; she had a physics degree, which covered the same material considerably faster. She recognised every stage of it and could not think of a single kindness to offer.
“Then Column B is—” She stopped and started again, and got it out properly the second time, which she respected. “Then Column B is the instrument looking at itself.”
“Yes,” said Fainrose.
“Nine thousand rows.”
“Yes.”
“And Column A is real.”
“Column A is an answer,” said Fainrose. “It is real in the way a verdict is real. It became true when you asked.”
Miss Pike put both hands flat on the table.
“So the more precisely we certified where things were,” she said slowly, “the more nonsense we generated about where they were going.”
“Yes.”
“And the directive requires both.”
“Yes.”
“So the harder we comply, the worse it gets.”
“Now,” said Fainrose, “you have understood 11-C better than the man who signed it.”
It was Mrs Chain who asked the question that mattered, because it was always Mrs Chain who asked the question that mattered.
“What has it done to the people?”
Nobody answered.
“Dr Fainrose. Nine thousand rows. They are addresses. Somebody lives at each of them.” She folded her hands. “What has it done to them?”
Fainrose crossed to the main display, pulled up the domestic event stream, and filtered it. Lolly saw her hesitate before she let it render: the first time she had seen her flinch from her own data.
The pattern was unmistakable once you knew to look for it.

Every dwelling certified to the highest precision in Column A showed, in the days following, the wildest instability in every other respect. Routes to the shops changed on alternate mornings. Correspondence arrived addressed to residents who were and were not the residents. Two households’ front doors had, for eleven hours, both opened onto the same hallway, an incident logged as shared vestibule, low priority. A man in Sub-District 9 had been certified so exactly that his own employment record could no longer predict where he would be at nine in the morning, and had accordingly been marked unreliable.
“They pinned them,” said Lolly.

“They pinned them,” said Fainrose, “and then wrote down that they were erratic. The more certain the pin, the more erratic the record; the more erratic the record, the stronger the case for a further pin.” She turned. “It is a machine for manufacturing exactly the instability it was built to remove, and it will run as long as it is funded, because every cycle produces evidence that it is needed.”
Jago exhaled. “That is the most administratively perfect thing I have ever heard.”

“It is not a flaw in the Initiative,” said Fainrose. “It is the Initiative. Vale does not need reality to be simple. He needs it to be reportably simple. Those are different projects. Only one is achievable, and it is achieved by insisting on two certificates that cannot both be honest.”
Beatrix had gone very quiet, which in her case meant she had stopped being furious and started constructing.
“Miss Pike,” she said.
Miss Pike looked up.
“Column B is fabricated.”
“Not deliberately—”
“I did not say fraudulently. I said fabricated. Do you dispute it?”
A long pause. Then, to her lasting credit: “No. I don’t.”
“Will you say so in writing?”

Miss Pike looked at the spreadsheet—nine thousand rows, locked headers, conditional formatting, four weeks of good work in service of an impossibility—and Lolly watched her decide. Whatever else came of this appalling week, she thought, that decision had been worth witnessing.
“Yes,” she said.

“Then we have him,” said Beatrix. “Not for the black hole. Not for the houses. Nobody is ever hanged for a black hole.” She picked up the directive and held it out. “For requiring, in writing, over signature, a certification that cannot exist, and then acting on it. That is not a scientific dispute. That is a false instrument in a live system.”
Fainrose looked at the paper with something like respect.
“He wrote it down,” she said.
“He wrote it down,” said Beatrix.
Mrs Chain refilled the pot.
“Men like that always do,” she said. “They cannot bear a thing to be true unless it has been copied twice and misfiled once.”
Lolly opened the green notebook marked PRIVATE/UNHELPFUL.
She wrote:
You may know where it is. You may know where it is going. You may not have both, and the shortfall is not a shortage of effort.
Then, below:
They demanded both. So the second column had to be invented. And then they punished people for failing to match the invention.
And at the bottom, smaller:
The cruelty is not the uncertainty. The cruelty is the certificate.

The two columns were meant to be reassuring. One recorded the state the Ministry had certified. The other recorded the state it intended to certify next. Lolly stared at them until she understood the trap: the system had no column for we don’t know. It had only two kinds of certainty, and both were now being fed back into the thing they were supposed to describe.
“How long?” she asked.
Fainrose looked at the clock. “Until it becomes self-consistent.”
“And if it does?”
She did not answer.

prosody.emphasis: Chapter 10: The Moon That Was Pending

p.prosody: The complaint came in from Outer Fenwick at half past seven in the evening, which was itself unusual, because Outer Fenwick did not officially exist until the moon came up, and the moon did not officially come up until enough people had filled in the form saying they had seen it.
Lolly Wren read the complaint three times before she accepted that she had read it correctly.

“Ratepayer states,” she said aloud, “that on the night of the fourteenth, insufficient observation returns were logged by nine p.m., and the moon”—she checked the wording again—“‘did not come up properly, and hung about at the edge looking unconvincing until gone eleven, at which point enough of the Fecloses had done their forms and it committed.’”
Beatrix Sloan did not look up from her boxes. “Committed to what?”
“Being a moon, I think.”
“That is not how moons work, Ms Wren.”
“I am aware of that, Ms Sloan. I am reading you the complaint.”

Stephanie Fainrose, who had not slept in a describable way for two days and had reached the particular plateau of tiredness at which she became lucid about everything except her own coat, which she had put on inside out, took the sheet from her.
She read it once. She did not read it a second time, which Lolly had learned to find ominous.
“Outer Fenwick,” she said. “Get the car.”

The road out to Outer Fenwick ran along the ridge above Sub-District 6. At a quarter to nine, with the sky doing something tentative and unfinished in the east, Lolly first understood the shape of what they were driving towards. People sat on their front steps. Not many—eleven, perhaps fourteen, scattered along half a mile of terraced housing—each with a folding chair, a flask, and a clipboard, all facing the same direction with the settled patience of racegoers told that the principal attraction was running late.
“What are they doing?” she said.
“Observing,” said Fainrose. “Or preparing to. Look at the forms.”

She looked. Each clipboard held a single sheet headed OUTER FENWICK NOCTURNAL AMENITY — CONFIRMATION OF SIGHTING, with boxes for name, address, and time, and a tick beside the words I confirm that I have observed the lunar body described in Schedule 4 and consider it to be present.
“Schedule 4.”
“Don’t,” said Fainrose, in the tone of a woman reserving strength for worse news later.

Jago Flint, driving, took the last bend onto the ridge somewhat faster than the road recommended and said, without turning round, “I’ve heard of this. Didn’t credit it. There’s a district over Coldharrow way that does the same with its high-street lamp—the one by the butcher’s. Goes out on cloudy nights if nobody’s looked at it by six. Everyone assumed the wiring was at fault.”
“It is not a fault in the wiring,” said Fainrose.

They parked outside a house with a hand-lettered sign in the window—FENWICK RESIDENTS’ MOON WATCH, EST. FOURTEEN MONTHS AGO—and a woman of about sixty came out to meet them before they had properly got out of the car. She wiped her hands on an apron which suggested that she had left something on a stove from sheer bureaucratic duty.
“You’ll be from the Ministry,” she said, without much enthusiasm. “I’m Mrs Prosser. I do the rota.”
“The rota for what, precisely?” said Fainrose.

“The moon.” Mrs Prosser said it as one might say the bins: a fact of civic life requiring management rather than wonder. “It came in with the Continuity Review, love. Fourteen months back. Somebody at the Ministry decided Outer Fenwick’s night sky was an ‘unresolved amenity pending classical adequacy determination’—those are the exact words; I kept the letter—and until it was resolved, resolving it required sufficient corroborated observation from the resident population. So. Rota.”
Lolly had the green notebook marked PRIVATE/UNHELPFUL out already. “How many observers constitute sufficient?”

“Forty-one,” said Mrs Prosser, with the flat authority of a woman who had fought this battle with a spreadsheet and won. “It was thirty-eight for the first six months. Then they moved the district boundary, picked up three more houses, and never revised the number back down. I have written to them nine times about it, and I would like it on record that I have written to them nine times.”
Lolly wrote forty-one in the green notebook and underlined it, then found she wanted a number that mattered more. “How many nights has the rota run, in total?”

Mrs Prosser didn’t have to work it out. “Four hundred and twenty-six,” she said. “I’ve done my turn on three hundred and ninety of them, near enough, because you can’t ask people to stand out in the cold on a promise, so someone has to be reliable, and reliable turned out to be me.” She said it without self-pity, the way she’d have reported a bus timetable. “I missed my granddaughter’s first steps for it. Not because anyone made me choose. Because it was a Tuesday, and Tuesdays are mine, and I’d told the street I’d be there, and I was.”
Nobody said anything for a moment that Lolly felt entitled to interrupt.
“They sent a very nice card,” Mrs Prosser added, “when I mentioned it in complaint eight. I didn’t keep that one.”
“And on the night it dips below forty-one?”

“It gets vague,” said Mrs Prosser. “Not gone. Vague. You get a sort of grey smudge where it ought to be, like a photograph somebody’s thumb was over half of. Cats won’t sit by the window, and my Reginald says his knee plays up, though Reginald’s knee plays up regardless and I don’t put that one on the Ministry. I have standards.”
Fainrose had gone very still, in the specific way Lolly now recognised as her thinking so hard that stillness was the only way to contain it.
“Mrs Prosser,” she said. “On the night the complaint describes, talk me through it minute by minute.”

Mrs Prosser was, it turned out, exactly the witness a desperate physicist could have ordered from a catalogue. She had logged everything. At 8:52 there had been thirty-four confirmed observation returns: people on steps, forms ticked, the usual quorum falling short by the usual margin, which normally resolved itself by nine as the last few latecomers emerged with tea. But on the fourteenth, seven regular observers had been at the church hall for the whist drive, and the moon—Mrs Prosser used the word with the weary precision of someone who had stopped finding it strange—had “sort of dithered.” It was visible from some houses and not from others. One household reported a crescent; the house two doors along, looking at the identical patch of sky, reported nothing at all, “which caused words, because the Hendersons have form for exaggerating and everyone said so to their faces.”

“And then,” said Mrs Prosser, “gone eleven, the whist drive let out, and everybody came home and had cocoa and looked up out of habit more than hope, and there it was. Properly there. Committed, like the letter said.”
“Like the complaint said,” Lolly corrected gently.
“Same thing round here,” said Mrs Prosser.

Fainrose walked to the pavement’s edge and looked up at the sky. It was presently offering a perfectly ordinary, extremely convincing gibbous moon, hanging in high cloud with the smug indifference of an object that had never once been asked to complete a declaration about itself.

“It is not that observation makes it real,” she said, half to herself and half to Lolly. She had learned that this half-address was the closest thing to a lecture she was going to get, and had trained herself to write quickly. “That is the vulgar version, and it is wrong, and it is exactly the version this Ministry has legislated into a rota.”
“Then what is happening?”
Fainrose looked at the moon for another moment. “A moon does not require forty-one people with clipboards. The world is already in contact with it. That is enough to keep it ordinary.”
“Then why did it dither?”

“Because someone built a filter,” said Fainrose. Now she turned to look at him, and there was something close to fury in it, banked low. “Somewhere in that Continuity Review paperwork is a device—probably a receiver mast, something modest and municipal, put up ‘to improve local signal’—coupled to the observation quorum. It is interfering with the local conditions that keep the moon settled, then letting them return only when the paperwork says the humans have earned a definite sky.”
Lolly looked from her to Mrs Prosser to the moon and felt the particular vertigo she had come, over the past week, to recognise as understanding arriving slightly ahead of comfort.
“They’re not making it real by looking,” she said slowly. “They have broken the thing that lets it be real without looking, and then charged the residents to fix it. With a rota.”
“With a rota,” Fainrose agreed, “and quorum thresholds, and presumably a line item.”
“Why?”
