“Because a moon requiring forty-one confirmed observations to commit is a moon the district can be billed for,” said Beatrix Sloan, who had got out of the car at some point during this and had already found, unerringly, the one sentence in the whole business that was actually about money. “Ongoing amenity-resolution services. I should like to see the invoice.”
Mrs Prosser brightened for the first time since they had arrived. “There is an invoice,” she said. “I kept that too.”

It took the annex’s engineers four days to narrow the search to Outer Fenwick Memorial Hall, and rather less time than that for Fainrose to announce that she had no intention of taking anyone’s word for a thing shaped like a bird.

The ladder belonged to the Hall’s caretaker, who lent it with the resigned generosity of a man who had long ago stopped asking the Ministry what it wanted with his roof. Jago went up first, on the grounds that he was, in his own estimation, “constitutionally difficult to surprise.” Lolly went second, notebook wedged in her coat pocket and both hands on the rungs. Fainrose stayed at the bottom and directed operations with the crisp, unhurried authority of a woman who had decided some time ago that gravity was somebody else’s problem.

The weathercock turned out to be a perfectly ordinary weathercock, black-painted, mounted on a spindle, doing a passable impression of a cockerel that had seen better centuries. It was only when Jago worked a gloved thumb under the base plate that the impression came apart: beneath the bird, bolted flush to the roof tile and painted the same weatherproof black so that from any angle that mattered it simply vanished, sat a slim aerial no longer than a rolling pin, humming very faintly to itself.
“Well,” said Jago, peering at it with the frank professional interest of a man who owed money to at least one department that might have built it. “That’s not a weathercock.”

“It was never meant to be interesting,” Fainrose called up. “That’s rather the point of it. Anyone glancing at a roof sees a bird, files it under ornament, and stops looking. It’s not hidden. It’s simply beneath anyone’s notice, which the Ministry has apparently learned is a good deal cheaper than hiding something properly.”

Lolly crouched by the mast and found, screwed to its underside where nobody looking up would ever see it, a small brass plate: PROPERTY OF THE MINISTRY OF EVENTUALITIES. UNAUTHORISED REMOVAL AN OFFENCE. She read it twice, mostly to be sure she wasn’t inventing the second sentence out of spite.
“It’s signed,” she called down.
“Everything they’re ashamed of is signed,” said Fainrose. “That’s how you know it started as a memo.”

It took rather longer than that to establish, to Fainrose’s evident disgust, that the mast had never been installed to interfere with anything on purpose. It was meant to improve mobile reception; it had an unrelated and entirely accidental resonance with local atmospheric scattering, and the Ministry had discovered the side effect, found it useful for enforcing quorum, and built an entire billing schedule on top of an engineering fault nobody had the nerve to report.
“That,” said Fainrose when the report came through, “is the most purely bureaucratic sentence I have heard all week, and I have heard Voller explain the vault.”

They switched the mast off on Thursday. Outer Fenwick’s moon came up that night at the ordinary time, to nobody’s particular attention, and stayed up regardless of the whist drive. Mrs Prosser wrote in for the tenth time, saying that the rota could be stood down. Three weeks later she received a reply thanking her for her feedback and enclosing a revised quorum threshold of thirty-nine.
“They’ve reduced it,” said Jago.
“They have,” said Mrs Prosser. “It is encouraging to see government respond to evidence.”
Lolly opened the green notebook on the drive back.
She wrote:
Nobody has to look at the moon for it to stay a moon. The air is looking at it constantly, on nobody’s authority, and that is a mercy, not a technicality.
Then, underneath:
They found a machine that quietened the mercy, called the silence a shortfall, and billed the street to fix what they had broken.
And at the bottom, in the smaller hand she used for the sentences she did not entirely want to admit to writing:
The moon does not need forty-one witnesses. It needs the sky to be allowed to keep noticing it. Most things do.

prosody.emphasis: Chapter 11: An Uninvited Reflection

p.prosody: The Phase Two papers arrived at two, in eleven boxes, and Beatrix Sloan had read four of them by half past five with the expression of a woman conducting a post-mortem on someone she had known.
Lolly Wren had been given box seven, which contained the consent architecture, and it was in box seven that she found the thing that made her go and stand outside for a while.
“It’s the invitation,” she said when she came back in.
Fainrose looked up. “Say that again.”

“Phase Two doesn’t take memories.” She put the folder on the table and opened it at the tab she had turned down. “It can’t. Not directly. There’s an entire volume here on why not—some poor devil in Legal wrote it in 2019 and nobody read it. A memory cannot be read out by external survey. It only becomes definite when the person is asked.”
Beatrix said, “So they ask.”

“So they ask,” said Lolly. “And the asking is the whole mechanism. The Ministry cannot reach in. But if a citizen fills in a form, describes the memory, selects from options, signs the declaration—then the memory becomes whatever the form says, because the form was the measurement.” She turned the folder round. “Look at the title of the volume.”
Fainrose read it aloud. “Voluntary Recollection Assurance: Establishing Lawful Access Through Citizen-Initiated Enquiry.”
“It cannot come in,” said Lolly, “unless you invite it.”
Jago Flint, who had been asleep in the chair again and had apparently been listening through it, said without opening his eyes, “Oh, that’s an old shape.”
“What is?”
“That.” He sat up. “Cannot cross the threshold uninvited. Very old. Doesn’t usually turn up in policy documents.”
At that point the lamps dimmed by one degree, in a manner Lolly had last seen in Mrs Chain’s hallway and had learned to distrust profoundly.
“Ah,” said a voice from the doorway. “Forgive me. I did knock, but the door was in two minds.”
The man standing there was extremely old and radiantly untidy.

He had a great disorganised nimbus of white hair, a moustache of magnificent indifference, a cardigan that had clearly outlived several arguments, and no shoes. His face was one that everyone in the room had seen a hundred times on posters, mugs, motivational calendars, and the walls of secondary-school physics laboratories. The resemblance was so complete, so unembarrassed, that it produced not recognition but a sort of vertigo.
He beamed at them.
“Alfred Keinschein,” he said. “Please don’t.”
“Don’t what?” said Lolly.

“Say it. Everybody says it. I have had eleven decades of it and it was tiresome by 1931.” He came in without hurrying, and Lolly noticed that the doorframe appeared to accommodate him rather than the reverse. “No relation. Well. Not in the sense you mean by relation.”
Fainrose had risen from her chair.
“Dr Fainrose,” said Keinschein warmly. “I have read you. The correlation paper. Beautiful. Wrong in one place, which we shall come to, but beautiful.”
“Where wrong?”

“Later. You will enjoy it more when you are frightened.” He looked round the room with enormous, benevolent interest. “Ms Sloan. Mr Flint. Mrs Chain—my condolences on your sister and my congratulations on your umbrella. Ms Wren.” He stopped. “Ms Wren, you have found the invitation clause.”
“About ten minutes ago.”
“Yes,” said Keinschein. “That is when I could come.”
Nobody moved.
Mrs Elspeth Chain, who had developed a settled policy of addressing the impossible directly and letting it explain itself, said, “Who are you?”
Keinschein considered the question with visible relish, like a man choosing from a good cellar.
“I am the oldest consequence,” he said. “There is no better phrase. Some have tried. The Babylonians had one, but it does not translate.”
Beatrix said, “That is not an answer.”
“No. Try this.” He crossed to the long window. The late sun came through it and lay on the floor in a rhombus. He stepped into the middle of the rhombus and stood there.
He cast no shadow.

Lolly looked at the floor for a considerable time. The chairs had shadows. The table had a shadow. The old man in the cardigan stood in full, unmediated August light, and the floor beneath him was as bright as the floor beside him.
“There,” said Keinschein comfortably. “That usually does it.”
Jago said, “You’ll want the mirror as well.”

“You are a quick young man, and I shall try to keep you alive.” Keinschein turned to the glass-fronted cabinet on the far wall, in which every one of them was reflected: the sunlight, the doorway, and the eleven boxes.
He was not.
Mrs Chain took a firm hold of the back of a chair.
“You are a vampire,” she said.

“That is the local word and I have stopped resisting it,” said Keinschein. “It is roughly as accurate as calling the sun a lamp. But yes. Approximately. Functionally. For our purposes this afternoon: yes.”
“Then what do you drink?”
Keinschein’s beam faded—not into menace, but into something worse, which was seriousness.
“Ah,” he said. “You go straight to it. Good. I do so dislike the ones who ask about bats.”
He came away from the window and sat, uninvited, in the chair Jago had vacated.

“I do not drink blood, Mrs Chain. Blood is a courier. It carries the thing but it is not the thing.” He laced his old, spotted hands together. “When a question is put to the world, and the world, which had been holding several answers at once quite comfortably, is obliged to produce one, the other answers are not filed. They cease, and in ceasing they release something.” He shrugged, almost apologetically. “I take that. I have taken it since the first measurement, which was much longer ago than your people think and was not performed by anybody.”
Lolly felt the room tilt.
“You feed on collapse.”
“On the discarded branch, yes. The road not taken, as your poet had it—though he was sentimental and I am a diner.”
“Then—” Lolly’s voice came out wrong, and she started again. “Then the Simplification Initiative—”
“Is the finest thing that has happened to me since agriculture,” said Alfred Keinschein.
The silence that followed had a physical weight.

“Nine thousand dwellings,” he said, “each one forced from a rich state into a thin one, tens of thousands of alternatives extinguished per address, per week, at public expense, with certificates. Do you understand what that is, from where I sit? It is not a meal. A meal is a woman deciding at last which of two men she loved and letting the other life go. Sweet. Small. I have lived on such things for aeons and been perfectly content.” He spread his hands. “This is industry. This is a national programme with a budget line.”
Fainrose said, very carefully, “And the anchor. four C.”
Keinschein’s expression changed for the first time.

“No,” he said. “That is not mine, and I want it understood. I did not ask them to build a sink and I did not ask them to hang a county from an evaporating hole. That is not appetite, Dr Fainrose; that is waste, and it will end with the pantry on fire.” He sat forward. “This is why I have come. Not to gloat. I could have gloated from Vienna.”
“Then why?”
“Because Phase Two is a mistake even by my standards,” said Keinschein, “and because I appear to be, in this room, the only person old enough to be genuinely conservative about reality.”
He picked up box seven’s folder and turned it over with distaste.

“Houses I can dine on for a century. But memory is not a house. A memory is the record of which branch was taken. It is how the universe keeps its accounts.” He tapped the cover. “If you begin collapsing memory by questionnaire, you are not merely extinguishing alternatives. You are falsifying the ledger of which alternatives were extinguished. Then nobody can tell what happened, including me, including the thing that comes after me, including—and this should worry you most—the system that is currently trying to repair itself.”
Lolly said slowly, “The error correction.”

“Yes,” said Keinschein, and looked at her with real approval. “Yes, the girl has it. Your Dr Fainrose is quite right that the country can be recovered from its correlations rather than from a copy. But a correlation is a statement about what agrees with what. If you go through the population asking leading questions about what they remember, and each answer becomes true as it is given, then the agreements will be manufactured, and the syndrome will be clean, and the code will report itself intact, and it will be intact—around nothing.”
Beatrix said, “It would look like a successful recovery.”

“It would be a successful recovery,” said Keinschein. “Of the wrong state. Certified. Permanently. With no residue for anyone to appeal to, and no residue for anyone to eat.” He sat back. “I have been dining on your species’ abandoned lives since before you had knees worth mentioning, and I have never once had to explain to a government that a thing can be irrecoverable. You have made me pedagogical. I resent it.”
Mrs Chain, who had not sat down, said, “You want us to stop them.”
“I want the ledger to survive. Yes.”
“For your own reasons.”

“Entirely for my own reasons,” said Keinschein. “Mrs Chain, I am eleven thousand times your age and I have never once acted from virtue. But my reasons and yours are, this month, pointing in the same direction, and you are in no position to be choosy about your allies.” He glanced at the boxes. “Also, I am the only one of you who has read Phase Two, because I was invited into it at approximately half past ten this morning by a Deputy Under-Secretary who filled in a form about his mother.”
Fainrose said, “You said my paper was wrong in one place.”
“I did.”
“Where?”
Alfred Keinschein smiled. It was not a comfortable smile, and Lolly understood that they had arrived at the thing the old man had actually come to say.

“You write,” said Keinschein, “as though a measurement were an event: a thing that happens at a time, after which there is one answer.” He shook his great white head gently. “That is the working assumption of every laboratory on this planet. It has served you admirably. It is not true. When your Mr Venn scanned Mrs Chain’s mantelpiece, what became definite for Mr Venn did not become definite for the mantelpiece, or the county, or me. There is no single moment at which the universe decides. There is only a widening region of agreement, spreading out at the speed of gossip, and no fact of the matter about the parts it has not reached.”
Lolly felt the hair on her arms rise.
“Then when Vale froze Sub-District 6—”

“He froze it for the grid,” said Keinschein. “Not for the woman remembering her sister. She was inside. Different question. Different answer. She could feel the shape of the name, could she not? She told them so, and they marked it no action required.” He rose from the chair with an old man’s effort and an entirely different creature’s economy. “There is no view from nowhere, Ms Wren. Your Ministry believes it is standing outside the room. It is not. There is no outside. When it finally asks its great national question about what everybody remembers, it will not be reading the answer.”
He went to the door, paused, and looked back at the five of them with something that, in a warmer species, might have been affection.
“It will be writing it,” said Alfred Keinschein. “And it will be inside the sentence when it does. Good evening. Do not invite me anywhere without meaning it.”
He left.
The lamps came back up by one degree.
Jago sat down heavily in the chair the old man had used and then, after a moment’s reflection, stood up again and chose another.
Beatrix said, to nobody, “We have an ally who eats the thing we are trying to save.”

“He eats the offcuts of the thing we are trying to save,” said Fainrose. “Which is worse, because it means he is telling the truth about wanting the rest intact.” She was staring at the cabinet where his reflection had not been. “And he is right about the paper.”
Mrs Chain finally sat.
“He cast no shadow,” she said, “and he did not lie to us once. I have met the opposite arrangement all week, and I know which I find more frightening.”
Lolly opened the green notebook marked PRIVATE/UNHELPFUL.
She wrote:
He cannot enter unless asked. Neither can the measurement. They have built a national programme of asking.
Then:
There is no moment when the universe decides. There is only agreement, spreading. No one is outside the room.
And at the bottom, after a long pause:
Phase Two does not read memory. It writes it, and signs it, and the signature is inside the fact.
Lolly closed the consent form. “If the invitation is the measurement, then every signature is an intervention.”
Beatrix went very still. “How many signatures?”
Lolly looked at the box. “Nine thousand, if the rollout goes national.”
Nobody made a joke. That frightened her more than the vampire had.

prosody.emphasis: Chapter 12: The Duc de Brévanne Explains Himself Slowly

p.prosody: Phase Two went live at seven the next morning in four sub-districts, because Vale had been suspended at midnight and the Board had discovered, on reading his file, that they preferred the version of him that had signed things.

By eight, Beatrix Sloan had established that the suspension had been proposed by a committee none of whose members would consent to be named. By nine she had stopped shouting at telephones and started drafting, which Lolly Wren had learned to recognise as the more dangerous phase.
By ten she was no use to anybody.

This was not modesty. She had checked. Fainrose was working on the syndrome tables and required silence and a person who understood stabiliser algebra, which she did not. Beatrix was assembling a case and required a lawyer, which she was not. Jago had gone to Croydon on an errand described only as unlikely to be relevant but almost certainly interesting. Mrs Chain had gone to Sub-District 6 to sit with the woman who had remembered her sister’s name, on the grounds that somebody ought to, and had taken the umbrella.
Lolly had a green notebook marked PRIVATE/UNHELPFUL containing forty pages of observations, every one of which had turned out, on arrival, to be something a professional had known since 1935.
She went out to sit on the wall by the annex car park, which was where the Duc found her.
“You are the one who writes things down,” said a voice.
Lolly looked up.

The man standing over her was slight, elderly, and dressed with an exactness that had gone out of fashion so long ago that it had returned as a moral position: a dark suit of beautiful cut and considerable age, a stiff collar, a narrow grey tie, and gloves. He held a hat. He gave the impression of a person who had been standing there for some time, waiting to be noticed, and who considered impatience a failure of breeding.

“I am sorry to intrude,” he said. His English was slow, exact, and unhurried in a way that made Lolly realise how quickly everybody else had been speaking for three days. “May I present myself? Louis-Raymond-Victor, Duc de Brévanne.”
Lolly got up. She was not entirely sure why, except that one did.
“Lolly Wren.”
“Yes. Transit Reconciliation.” De Brévanne inclined his head very slightly. “I have read your notebook.”
“You have not.”

“Not the object. The shape of it. Dr Fainrose quoted four of your lines to me on the telephone this morning in order to complain about them, which is the highest form of French compliment and, I understand, common enough in English also.” He looked at the wall. “May I sit? It is a long time since I have sat on a wall and I should like to know whether it is still possible.”
They sat on the wall.
“You are not with the Ministry,” said Lolly.
“Certainly not.”
“Are you with him? The old man. Keinschein.”
De Brévanne’s face did something complicated and courteous.

“I have known Alfred Keinschein,” he said, “for ninety-one years, and I have never once forgiven him. I would trust him with my life and nothing smaller. He telephoned me last night. He said: Louis, they have a clerk who has understood four things by herself, and she is about to stop.” He turned his head. “He was correct?”
Lolly looked at the car park.

“I had a PhD in physics,” she said. “I wrote about quantum electrodynamics. Then I realised I could calculate quantum mechanics without understanding it, which was rather more troubling than failing an exam. I left physics, worked in an organic grocery shop, allegedly, and then Feynman reminded me that anyone who says they understand quantum mechanics has probably misunderstood the question. So I came back. Three days ago I started noticing things in a notebook, and every single thing I have noticed turns out to be a standard result with somebody’s name on it.” She heard how it sounded and did not much care. “Fainrose is doing stabiliser codes upstairs. Keinschein has been alive since before agriculture. I write down that the house is larger than the form and feel clever for eight minutes until somebody tells me it is called state reduction and was settled before I was born.”
De Brévanne listened with grave attention, as though it were a technical report.
Then he said, “May I tell you what I was, in 1911?”
“All right.”

“I was twenty-two years of age. I had taken my degree in history.” He said it without emphasis. “Medieval history. My family had been soldiers and diplomats for six hundred years and I was, by inclination, an archivist. I intended to spend my life on charters and legal instruments of the fourteenth century. My brother was the physicist. I was the one who read.”
Lolly turned to look at him.

“In 1911 my brother served as secretary to a congress of physicists,” said de Brévanne, “and brought home the papers. I read them because I read everything. I did not understand them, and I could not stop.” He turned the hat over in his gloved hands. “You must understand my position. I had no laboratory. I had no mathematics beyond the ordinary. I had no standing whatever. What I had was the habit of a historian, which is this: when two authorities disagree, one does not choose. One looks for the document they have both misread.”
“And what were the two authorities?”

“Light,” said de Brévanne, “which everybody knew was a wave, and which Einstein had shown behaved in some circumstances as though it were a great number of small hard things.” He shrugged very slightly. “The physicists were embarrassed by this. They spoke of it as a difficulty to be managed. I was not embarrassed, because I was not a physicist, and so I did the thing that only an ignorant man would do, which was to take it seriously in both directions at once.”
“Meaning?”

“Everyone was asking how a wave could be a particle.” He looked at Lolly. “Nobody was asking whether a particle might be a wave. It is the same question turned round, Ms Wren. Turning a question round is not a discovery; it is a manner. It required no apparatus and no genius. It required only somebody outside the room, with the wrong training, who did not know which of the two facts he was supposed to find awkward.”
“And you were right.”

“I was right,” said de Brévanne, “and it took four years to say it properly. When I said it, my examiners did not believe it, and my thesis was sent to Einstein because nobody else was willing to have an opinion. He wrote back that I had lifted a corner of the great veil.” A pause. “He also said, privately, that if I were wrong it was a very handsome error. He was always careful to leave himself the exit.”
Lolly said nothing for a while.
“You are telling me the outsider sometimes gets it.”

“No.” De Brévanne’s voice was suddenly quite firm. “That is a comforting story and I dislike it. The outsider usually gets nothing and dies unpublished, and there is no justice in the distribution. I am telling you something narrower and more useful.” He set the hat down on the wall. “Ms Wren, you have said that every observation in your notebook has turned out to have a name already. Tell me: which of them did you write down before you were told the name?”
“All of them. That’s rather my point.”

“No,” said de Brévanne. “That is my point. You are treating the pre-existence of the name as evidence that the observation was worthless. It is evidence that the observation was correct.” He let that sit. “There are two ways to hold a piece of physics. One may receive it, in which case one possesses a fact and may repeat it. Or one may arrive at it, in which case one possesses the reason and may go on from there to the next thing, which has no name yet. The second is the only kind that is any use in a crisis, and it is the only kind you have. You are sitting on a wall in a car park despising yourself for it.”
Lolly found that her throat had gone rather tight, which was inconvenient.
“Fainrose does both,” she said.

“Dr Fainrose is formidable and will save perhaps nine thousand houses this week,” said de Brévanne. “But she cannot hear the question she was trained out of hearing. That is not a criticism. It is what training is for. It is expensive and necessary, and it costs precisely one thing.” He picked up the hat again. “Now. Keinschein told you last night that there is no view from nowhere, and that nothing is definite until agreement has spread. It frightened you.”
“Yes.”

“Good. It should. It is also not the only available account, and he did not tell you that because he is an old snob who enjoys the vertigo.” De Brévanne looked out at the car park, at the pale curve of the annex wall, at the air above the concrete that still did not quite admit to its own distances. “May I show you the other one? It is mine, unfashionable, and I have been out of favour for eighty years, which gives a man leisure to be sure.”
“Please.”
“Then tell me. When Mr Flint pulled the cable from beneath Mrs Chain’s bed, and the wallpaper became flowers again—where had the flowers been?”
Lolly opened her mouth and stopped.
She remembered writing it down, standing in a bedroom with two duvets and feeling the strange intellectual terror of recognition.
“They were still there,” she said. “Underneath. Suppressed, not deleted. It was being held in place by continuous intervention.”

“Yes,” said de Brévanne quietly. “On Keinschein’s account, that is loose talk. On his account there was no fact about the flowers until agreement reached them, and what you felt in that room was a metaphor.” He turned. “But you did not write down a metaphor, Ms Wren. You wrote down a mechanism. You said the lie required electricity.”
“I did say that.”
“It is the best sentence in your notebook, and you have not understood it yet.”
Lolly said slowly, “Go on.”

“Suppose the house always had one definite configuration. One actual wallpaper. Not a haze of possibilities: an actual state, at every moment, as common sense insists and as your Ministry pretends to believe.” De Brévanne raised one gloved finger. “And suppose, in addition, there exists a wave: a real physical wave, not a bookkeeping device, spread out over every configuration the house might have had, including the ones it did not have. Suppose the actual configuration is guided by that wave. Steered. Never anywhere but somewhere, yet always told where to go next by a thing that fills the whole space of alternatives.”
Lolly sat very still.
“Then the unrealised versions are real,” she said. “Even though they never happened.”

“Real, and empty, and effective,” said de Brévanne. “That is the whole of it. The branch nobody took is not a ghost and not an accounting error. It is part of the object that decides where you go. Interference is what it feels like when an empty possibility pushes.”
“So when Venn scanned the mantelpiece—”

“He did not create a fact. There was already a fact.” De Brévanne’s voice sharpened for the first time. “He deformed the guidance. He put his apparatus into the space of alternatives and altered the shape of the wave steering a hundred years of that woman’s household. The actual configuration went where the deformed wave sent it, which was somewhere thin. When Mr Flint tore the cable out, the deformation ceased, and the guidance relaxed towards what it had always been. The flowers came back, not because they had been in storage, but because the wave that had always contained them was permitted, briefly, to matter again.”
The air over the car park did something. Lolly chose to disbelieve it.
“That’s a different crime,” she said.

“It is an entirely different crime,” said de Brévanne, “and this is my lesson, and the only thing I came to say.” He turned to face her fully. “Ms Sloan is upstairs building a case that the Ministry falsified records. That is true and it is small. Dr Fainrose is building a case that they interfered with lawful evolution. That is truer and larger. But if what I have described is so, then every single thing they have done—the queue, the scanner, the certificates, the continuous assurance, and now the memories—was not an intrusion into knowledge.”
“It was an intrusion into what steers.”
“Yes.”
“They have been standing in the wave.”
“They have been standing in the wave,” said the Duc de Brévanne, “with clipboards, for fifteen years, charging rent.”
Lolly was already writing. She was aware that her hand was not entirely steady and did not much care about that either.
“Keinschein said you cannot record the phase,” she said, still writing. “That the vault was worthless because there is no phase record.”
“He is right.”

“But if the wave is real—if it is a physical thing out there in configuration space—then it is not information anybody has to store. It is not a bookkeeping quantity that got lost.” He looked up. “It is still there. Deformed, but there. You would not restore the country from a copy. You would restore it by taking your apparatus out of the wave and letting the guidance relax.”
De Brévanne did not answer at once.
When he did, his voice had changed, and Lolly realised with a small shock that the old man had not, until that moment, been certain of her.
“Ms Wren,” he said. “Nobody told you that.”
“No.”
“It does not have a name.”
“Doesn’t it?”

“There are people who would recognise the shape of it,” said de Brévanne. “There is no one who has said it about a country.” He rose, set his hat on his head, and adjusted it. “You will now go upstairs and say it to Dr Fainrose. She will tell you it is unfalsifiable metaphysics and a hundred years out of fashion. She will be quite right on both counts. Then she will be unable to sleep, because it also happens to specify a procedure, and hers does not.”
Lolly stood. “And is it true?”

“I have believed it for eighty years without being able to prove it,” said the Duc de Brévanne, “which I am told is called faith, though I maintain it is merely patience.” He put out a gloved hand. Lolly shook it. It was quite cold. “One last thing, since you asked me nothing and I shall tell you anyway.”
“Yes.”

“You said you were a physicist for eleven minutes as a working physicist.” He was already turning away. “I was a historian until I was twenty-two, and a physicist for sixty years afterward, and I was never once both. That is why I could not see what your bureaucracy was doing to those houses and you could.” He paused. “You have spent your whole working life on things that must actually work, and three days on paperwork that must actually be filed. You are therefore the only person in that building who knows what an institution is as well as what a wave is. Do not stand on a wall about it. It is not a small combination. It is simply not a fashionable one.”
He walked off across the car park. The sunlight fell on him properly, and he cast a completely ordinary shadow, for which Lolly was obscurely grateful.
Upstairs, Fainrose did not look up.
“If that was the Duc,” she said, “he is a mystic and I love him and he is eighty years out of date.”
“Probably,” said Lolly. She put the notebook on the console, open. “Read it anyway.”
She read it.
Then she stopped working, which she had not done in nineteen hours.
“Lolly,” she said.
“Yes.”
“Where exactly,” said Stephanie Fainrose, “did you get the idea that you were the assistant?”

prosody.emphasis: Chapter 13: The Panel of Experts

p.prosody: The Board of Inquiry sat at eleven in the annex conference room, and its first act was to establish that it did not intend to decide anything.

“We are not here to adjudicate physics,” said the chair, a Mr Pilbeam, who had been brought in from Transport on the grounds that he had once managed a bridge, although the bridge had not supplied a reference. “We are here to determine whether a recommendation exists. If the expert panel is unanimous, we may act. If it is divided, the matter is unresolved and current arrangements continue.”
Beatrix Sloan, at the side table with eleven boxes and a fountain pen, wrote a single word on her pad.
Lolly leaned over and read it.
Divided.
“They’ve designed it so that disagreement means Phase Two proceeds,” she said.
“They have designed it,” said Beatrix, “so that nothing is ever anybody’s fault. It is the same instrument every time. Convene the ones who cannot agree and call the noise a lack of evidence.”
Fainrose said, “Who did they convene.”
Beatrix turned her pad round.
Three names.
Fainrose read them and put her face in her hands, briefly, which Lolly had not seen before.
“Oh, that’s marvellous,” she said. “That’s genuinely inspired. They’ve picked three men who have spent their entire lives disagreeing about exactly this, and one of them is dead.”
“Which one is dead.”
“It has not noticeably impeded his work.”
They came in at ten past.
The first was tall, hollow-cheeked, immaculately grey, with the posture of a man who had spent decades being the cleverest person in rooms that were themselves dangerous.
He carried nothing at all - no papers, no case - and sat down at the far end with his hands folded, and Lolly noticed that she chose the seat furthest from the window.
“Professor Werner Heitmann,” said Pilbeam. “Foundations.”
“Formalism,” said Heitmann. “Not foundations. There is a difference and it is the entire difference.”
The second arrived talking.

He was younger by decades, sandy-haired, in a jacket over a T-shirt, and he came in mid-sentence with a tablet in one hand and a coffee in the other and an air of enormous delight at being alive in a universe that had turned out to be so interesting.

“-which is the thing nobody wants to say out loud, that if the equations are the ontology then this whole crisis is a bookkeeping dispute - sorry, hello, Max Tegnér, cosmology, I’ve read the Fainrose paper four times, Dr Fainrose it’s an honour, your syndrome table is gorgeous, I think it’s solving a problem that doesn’t exist but it’s gorgeous.”
Fainrose said, “Sit down, Professor Tegnér.”
“Absolutely.”
The third came in last and quietly, and the room’s temperature dropped about it.

He was a smallish man with a red beard going white, in a jumper, with the specific bright unblinking gaze of somebody who has spent thirty years being polite to people he considers to have been sloppy.
He had a Belfast voice, unhurried and precise, and he sat down without shaking hands with anyone.
“Dr Jack Bellew,” said Pilbeam.
“Aye,” said Bellew.
“Dr Bellew, forgive me, our records indicate-”
“They do,” said Bellew. “Shall we get on.”
Nobody pursued it.

Pilbeam distributed the question. It had been drafted by a committee and ran to a paragraph, but stripped of its clothing it asked this: does the Ministry’s programme of civic simplification cause damage to physical reality that is not captured by the loss of records?
Heitmann answered first, and answered fast.
“No,” he said. “And the question is malformed.”
Pilbeam looked up hopefully. “You find no damage?”
“I find no meaning.”

Heitmann’s hands stayed folded. “You are asking about damage to something you call physical reality, over and above the records. But the formalism of quantum mechanics does not describe a reality behind the records. It relates preparations to observations. It tells you, with unrivalled precision, what your instruments will report. It says nothing whatever about what the electron is doing when nobody asks, because that question generates no numbers.”

He turned his head slightly. “Your survey teams asked; they received answers; the answers were correct. If you wish to complain that the answers were unkind, that is politics. If you wish to complain that they misdescribed a hidden state of the house, you are complaining about a fiction.”
Lolly said, before she could stop herself, “The woman couldn’t finish her sister’s name.”
Heitmann looked at her with no unkindness at all, which was worse.

“Then she was harmed,” he said. “I do not dispute the harm. I dispute the ontology of the harm. She was harmed as a citizen, by a procedure, and you should prosecute the procedure. Do not ask me to certify that a wave function was injured. I have spent my life declining to say what the wave function is and I decline again this morning.”

Tegnér had his hand half up like a schoolboy. “See, this is where I get off the bus,” he said. “Werner - may I - this is the thing. You say the question generates no numbers. But the equation generates numbers, and the equation has a mathematical structure, and my position, and I’ll be totally clear that it’s a minority position, is that the mathematical structure isn’t a description of reality, it is the reality. There’s nothing else. The universe is a mathematical object and we’re self-aware substructures inside it.”
Pilbeam wrote this down, visibly hoping relevance might emerge if given enough ruled paper.
“And so?” said Fainrose.
“And so nothing was destroyed,” said Tegnér.
The room went very quiet.
“Say that again,” said Beatrix.
“Nothing was destroyed.”
He said it gently, and Lolly understood with a sinking sensation that the man was neither stupid nor cruel and that this was going to be much worse than if she had been.

“Look - if the equation never stops running, and there’s no collapse, then when the surveyor scanned Mrs Chain’s mantelpiece the universe didn’t pick one answer and delete the rest. It branched. There’s a branch where the photograph is a photograph and a branch where it’s a clock. Both are physically real. Both contain a Mrs Chain. Neither is more real than the other.”

He spread his hands, and he was, Lolly realised, trying to offer comfort. “The alternatives weren’t extinguished. They were decohered from. Every single thing this Ministry allegedly destroyed still exists. It’s just not here.”
Mrs Elspeth Chain had come in at some point during this, with the umbrella, and had been standing at the back by the door.
She said, “Then where is my sister.”
Tegnér turned, and to his credit he did not flinch. “She’s in the branches where the record wasn’t overwritten,” he said.
“Which is most of them, statistically-”
“Where is she here.”
“…Here, she’s gone. Yes.”
“Then do not tell me nothing was destroyed,” said Mrs Chain, “because I am here, and I am the one who noticed.”
There was a silence of some length.
“That’s fair,” said Max Tegnér quietly. “That’s actually a fair objection and it’s the one I’ve never had a good answer to.”
Beatrix Sloan was already writing, fast.
“Chair,” she said. “I want it minuted that a member of the expert panel has advanced a position under which no act of the Ministry can constitute destruction of anything.”
Pilbeam brightened. “Well, that would be-”

“That would be the defence,” said Beatrix. “That is what they convened him for. Not to disagree with Professor Heitmann. To supply Vale’s successors with a physics under which the harm is relocated rather than caused. You will see it in the Board’s response within a fortnight and it will say: no alternative is ever lost, and therefore no citizen has suffered a loss, and therefore Phase Two may proceed as a matter of record-keeping.”
Tegnér put his coffee down. “I’d hate that,” he said. “For the record - I’d hate that. It’s a real misuse. The multiverse doesn’t make cruelty free. My branch still has the crying person in it-”
“It does not matter what you would hate,” said Beatrix. “It matters what you have said in a minuted proceeding.”
“Yeah,” said Tegnér. “Yeah, I know. That’s - yeah.”
And it was into this that Jack Bellew spoke for the second time. “Now that,” he said, “is the whole disease, and the two of you have just performed it for me, so I’m obliged.”
Everyone looked at him.

Bellew had not moved. He sat with his forearms on the table and his bright pale eyes going from Heitmann to Tegnér and back. “Werner says the question has no meaning. Max says the question has too many answers, all of them real. And between the pair of you there’s not one single thing a Board of Inquiry could go and check.”

He tapped the table once, softly. “You’ve both got theories in which nobody can ever be wrong. I’ve spent my career objecting to that, and I’ll object to it in a car park in a suspended county if the room-booking requires it.”
Heitmann said, “The formalism is confirmed to twelve decimal places.”
“The formalism is grand,” said Bellew. “The formalism is the best thing our species has done. I’m not talking about the formalism, I’m talking about the word.”

He looked round the table. “Measurement. You’ve all been saying it all morning. The Ministry’s directives say it four hundred times. It’s in the legislation. And it is the most disastrous word in the vocabulary of physics, because it makes it sound as though there’s a special class of event, involving a professional and an apparatus, that the rest of nature is exempt from. There isn’t. A surveyor is a physical system. A form is a physical system. There is no magic in a clipboard.”
Lolly said, “Then what did happen in Mrs Chain’s house.”
And Bellew turned to her, and Lolly had the disconcerting experience of being properly looked at by somebody who had died before she had finished caring about this.
“You’re the fella with the notebook.”
“Yes.”
“The Duc’s been at you.”
“Yesterday.”
“Aye, he does that.”
Something almost like affection crossed Bellew’s face and left again. “Right. Here’s your answer, and it’s the only part of this morning worth putting in the minutes.”

He held up two fingers. “There are two things a reasonable person wants to believe. One: things have properties whether or not anybody’s asking - the wallpaper is some colour when the room’s empty. Call that realism. Two: what you do here cannot instantly affect what’s true over there - no influence outrunning light. Call that locality.”

He lowered the fingers. “Every sensible person in this room wants both. Werner avoids the problem by giving up the first. Max keeps both by multiplying the worlds until the question dissolves. And in 1964 I sat down and did a small piece of arithmetic, and the arithmetic said: you cannot have both. Not as a matter of taste. As a matter of measurable numbers.”
Pilbeam said, “Measurable.”
“That’s the point of it, Mr Chairman. That’s the whole point of it.”

Bellew leaned forward. “If both things were true - properties in advance, no influence at a distance - then certain correlations between distant events have a ceiling. A definite number. You can work it out with school algebra in an afternoon. And if nature ever exceeds that ceiling, then one of your two comfortable beliefs is finished, and no amount of interpretation gets it back.”
“And has it been done,” said Beatrix.

“It’s been done for sixty years,” said Bellew, “in Berkeley and Orsay and Innsbruck and Delft and Vienna, tighter and tighter, and every hole anybody found in it has been plugged - the detectors, the timing, the choice of what to measure, all of it - and they gave a Nobel Prize for it in 2022, and the answer is the same every time and it isn’t close.”

He sat back. “The ceiling is violated. Nature is not locally real. That is not philosophy and it is not fashion and it does not depend on which interpretation you take home at night. It is an experimental fact and it is the only weapon in this building.”
Fainrose had gone extremely still.
“Say the last part again,” she said.

“You’ve been trying to argue in front of committees,” said Bellew, “that the country is held together by relations rather than by objects, and they’ve told you it’s metaphysics, and they’ve told the young man there that his guiding wave is unfalsifiable, and both of those dismissals are true and both are beside the point.”

He nodded toward Lolly. “Because you don’t need to win the interpretation. You need to establish one thing in front of Mr Pilbeam here, and it happens to be the one thing that has been tested to death: that a change made in one place can alter what is true in another place, with no signal passing between them.”
Lolly felt the whole architecture of three days slide into position with an almost audible click.
“The overflow channel,” she said.
“Go on.”
“They tied nine thousand dwellings to one anchor. Fainrose’s correlation lattice.”

He was standing now, without having decided to. “The Board’s position is that each dwelling was surveyed separately, so each certificate is separately defensible. Local decisions. Local harms. Nine thousand small administrative matters, each too small to be worth an inquiry.”
“And?”

“And if the correlations exceed Bellew’s ceiling,” said Lolly, “then they weren’t separate. It’s not an interpretation that they weren’t separate. It’s a number. You can go and measure it in Sub-District 6 this afternoon and get a figure that no committee can call metaphysics, because the arithmetic doesn’t mention wave functions or branches or guidance at all. It just says: if these were independent systems being independently surveyed, this correlation is impossible.”
Bellew smiled for the first time, and it was not a warm expression, it was the smile of a man watching a tool being picked up by the correct end.
“There you are,” he said. “Now you’ve got a case.”
Heitmann said, quietly, “The inequality does not tell you what is real.”

“It does not,” Bellew agreed. “It tells you what is not permitted. That’s a smaller claim and it’s the reason it can’t be argued with. Werner, you spent your life saying we should confine ourselves to what can be checked. I took you at your word and went and checked something, and you’ve never forgiven me for it.”
“I have forgiven you,” said Heitmann. “I have never agreed with you.”
A pause. “There is a difference, and after everything, it is the only distinction I have left that I am still entitled to.”

Something passed across the old man’s face - Lolly could not read it, and later, when Beatrix showed her what was in box eleven about Heitmann’s employment between 1939 and 1945, she thought perhaps she could - and Heitmann folded his hands again and said nothing further for the remainder of the proceeding.
Tegnér said, “Jack. If they measure it and it violates, my picture survives that.”
“It does,” said Bellew. “Your picture survives everything, Max. In a less robust theory that would be an administrative concern.”

“No,” said Tegnér, with real cheerfulness, “but I’ll take it. And for what it’s worth-” he turned to Mrs Chain, and did it properly, and looked at her while he said it - “you were right and I was glib. Nothing being destroyed globally doesn’t buy anybody anything locally. Somebody in this branch lost her sister. I’ll put that in the minutes.”
“Thank you,” said Mrs Chain.
Pilbeam, who had understood perhaps a third of the last twenty minutes but had grasped with the unerring instinct of his species that a decision was forming, said, “So is the panel unanimous?”
“No,” said all three of them.
Pilbeam sagged.

“But we’re agreed on a measurement,” said Bellew. “Which is worth ten unanimous opinions and you may minute that too. Werner will accept it because it’s an instrument reading and that’s all he ever accepts. Max will accept it because his branch has instruments in it. I’ll accept it because I designed it. And whatever number comes back, none of the three of us can wriggle.”

Beatrix laid down her pen. “Chair,” she said. “The panel proposes a test with a pre-agreed threshold and three incompatible experts bound in advance to accept the result. Refusing that is not caution. It is obstruction, and I will write it up as obstruction, and I will name the committee that would not give its members’ names.”
Pilbeam looked round the table for somebody to save him and found nobody.
“Very well,” he said. “Minute it.”
Afterwards, in the corridor, Bellew stopped Lolly with two fingers on her sleeve.
“A word.”
“Yes.”
“Your Duc’s account and Max’s account and Werner’s silence - you’ll be tempted to pick one, because you’ve a tidy mind and you think in circuit diagrams and you want to know what the circuit is.”

The pale eyes were unblinking. “Don’t pick yet. Pick when something forces you. Until then hold all three, and use whichever one tells you where to put the probe. That’s not cowardice, that’s method.”
“And if none of them tells me?”
“Then you’ve found the good part,” said Jack Bellew, “and you’d better write it down.”
He walked off down the corridor and Lolly did not watch him go, on the grounds that she was not entirely certain she would see it.
She opened the notebook instead.
She wrote:
Properties in advance, or no influence at a distance. Choose one.
Nature has already chosen, and it is measurable.
Then:
I do not have to win the interpretation. I have to produce a number the committee cannot call philosophy.
And beneath that:
They surveyed nine thousand houses separately. If the correlations exceed the ceiling, then there were never nine thousand cases. There was one.

prosody.emphasis: Chapter 14: Eleven Dimensions and a Whisper

p.prosody: They went into Sub-District 6 on the Thursday with two vans, a portable timing rack, four hired photodetectors, and a great deal of paperwork Beatrix Sloan had signed in a hand that dared anyone to query it.
The measurement would take two days to set up.
Fainrose was in the primary school hall running cable with the concentration of a woman defusing something.
Jago Flint had gone to acquire a fifth detector on terms nobody had asked about.

And Lolly Wren, who had been sent out to find somewhere to work because she had apparently exceeded her permitted quota of useful questions, had ended up in the reading room of the branch library on Coldharrow Street, at a table by the window, with the green notebook and eleven photocopied pages from box seven.
There was one other person in the reading room.

He had been there when Lolly arrived and gave every impression of having been there for some years: a slight man in his seventies, entirely bald, in a plain shirt and unremarkable trousers, surrounded by an arrangement of papers so extensive and so orderly that it had colonised two additional tables, as though the furniture had signed a memorandum.
He wrote in pencil. He wrote continuously.
Every twenty minutes or so he stopped, looked out of the window at the car park of a shut-down carpet showroom, and then wrote some more.

At about four o’clock he said, without turning round, in a voice so quiet that Lolly was not initially certain it had been aimed at her: “You are the person doing the Bell test on the housing lattice.”
Lolly put down her pen. “How do you know that.”
“Dr Bellew mentioned it.”

The man turned. He had a pleasant, unemphatic, slightly abstracted face and the mildest possible manner, and he spoke so softly that Lolly found herself leaning forward before the sentence was finished.
“I think it is an excellent idea. It is the correct instinct - to find the one claim that does not depend on taste. Forgive me. Leonhard von Wittenberg.”
“Lolly Wren.”
“Yes.”
Von Wittenberg gathered three sheets of paper together, apparently at random, and came and sat down opposite her. “May I ask you something before you ask me anything?”
“Of course.”
“When you say the country is held together by correlations” - he said it gently, as though it might be fragile - “what do you imagine the correlations are between?”
Lolly thought about it. “Houses,” she said. “Records. Routes. Districts. People. The nodes on Fainrose’s lattice.”
“Yes. And what are those made of.”
“Bricks. Paper. Copper. People are made of cells.”
He heard where this was going. “Cells are made of molecules, molecules of atoms, atoms of nuclei and electrons, nuclei of quarks.”
“And quarks?”
“Are made of nothing. They’re fundamental. Points.”

Von Wittenberg smiled very slightly and looked out at the carpet showroom. “That is the standard answer and it is the best-tested answer in the history of thought,” he said. “It is also, I believe, wrong, and I have believed it for about fifty years and been unable to prove it, which is a condition your Duc de Brévanne has described to you rather well, I understand.”
Lolly sat back. “You’re going to tell me they’re strings.”
“I am going to tell you something a little worse than that,” said Leonhard von Wittenberg apologetically. “May I use your notebook? I shall use a clean page.”
He drew, very small, a dot. “A point particle,” he said.

“It has no size and no internal structure and no way of being anything other than what it is. If you wish to explain why there are so many different particles, you must simply list them, and we have listed them, and the list is seventeen items long and nobody knows why it is that list rather than another.”

Beneath the dot he drew a tiny closed loop. “Now suppose instead that the fundamental object is not a point but a small loop, of a length so short that every experiment ever performed sees it as a point. A loop can do something a point cannot.” He looked up. “It can vibrate.”
“Different vibrations, different particles,” said Lolly.
“Different vibrations, different particles. Not seventeen unrelated facts. One object, seventeen notes.” She said it without any drama whatever, which somehow made it land harder.
“A violin string is not seventeen instruments. It is one string, played differently.”
Lolly looked at the loop for a while. “And the electron and the quark and the photon-”
“Notes.”
“And gravity?”

“Ah,” said von Wittenberg, and for the first time something in his face brightened. “That is the part that persuaded me. You must understand - for fifty years the great scandal of physics was that our theory of the very small and our theory of gravity would not sit in the same room. Put them together and the answers came out infinite. Not large. Infinite, which is nature’s way of saying that the question was malformed. Every attempt failed.”

He tapped the little loop. “But if the objects are loops rather than points, the infinities do not arise. And more than that - among the notes the loop can play, one of them, unavoidably, is a massless spin-two particle.”
“Which is?”
“The graviton,” said von Wittenberg. “You do not put gravity in. You cannot keep it out. It is simply one of the things the string does.”
He paused. “I have never got over that. I am seventy-four and I have not got over it.”
Lolly realised she had stopped taking notes and started again. “Where’s the catch.”
“There are three, and I shall not hide them.”

Von Wittenberg counted them off on his fingers, mildly. “First: the strings are so small that no accelerator we could build on this planet or in this solar system could see one directly, and so the theory has never been tested. Not once. Dr Fainrose is entirely right to say so and she says it to me every time we meet.”
“Second?”
“The mathematics does not work in four dimensions. It requires ten.” He said this the way another man might mention that a recipe requires buttermilk.

“Nine of space, one of time. And since we plainly experience three of space, the other six must be curled up small - at every point in what you think of as empty room there are six additional directions, wound so tightly that nothing you or I can do will ever push anything along them.”
Lolly looked out of the window at the carpet showroom. “That is a great deal to ask of a car park,” she said.
“It is, yes.” Von Wittenberg looked pleased.

“And the third catch is the one that mattered most, and it is the reason I am in a library in Sub-District 6 rather than at home. For a long time there were five different string theories. All consistent. All beautiful. All slightly different. Which was, you understand, an embarrassment - one had set out to explain why there is only one world and had produced five candidates and a great deal of silence.”
“So what happened.”
“In 1995,” said Leonhard von Wittenberg, “I gave a talk.”
He said this with the caution of a man aware that institutions have been damaged by less. He said it so quietly and so flatly that Lolly nearly missed the size of it.

“The five theories were not five theories,” said von Wittenberg. “They were five descriptions. Each one was a different limited view of a single underlying structure - and one could pass between them by a set of relations we call dualities. Take one theory and turn a certain quantity up very high, and it becomes, exactly and provably, a different theory with that quantity turned very low. They are the same thing seen from different sides. And when one assembled all five together properly, they did not fit in ten dimensions. They fitted in eleven, and the fundamental objects were not only strings but also membranes - surfaces, sheets, extended things of various dimensions.”
“And that’s the theory.”
“That is the theory, and it has no proper formulation yet, and so it has no proper name. I called it M-theory.”
“What does the M stand for.”
“Membrane,” said von Wittenberg. “Or mystery. Or magic. According to taste. I have never settled it, and I have come to think the vagueness was accidentally honest.”

Lolly put her pen down. “Professor von Wittenberg,” she said. “I have to say this. In three days I have been told by an extremely old vampire that nothing is definite until agreement spreads. I have been told by a French duke that everything is definite and steered by a wave over all the alternatives. I have been told by a Swede that every alternative actually happens somewhere. I have been told by a dead man from Belfast to stop picking and go and measure something. And you have now told me that everything is made of eleven-dimensional membranes that nobody can see and no experiment can reach.”
She looked at the little loop on the page. “I have a woman in this district who was stopped in the middle of remembering her sister’s name. What am I supposed to do with strings?”
Von Wittenberg did not take offence. He seemed, if anything, to have been waiting for it. “That is the right question and I shall answer it in the correct order,” he said.

“First: nothing. You are supposed to do nothing with strings. The Bell measurement is what matters this week and I would not have you divert a single cable from it. Anyone who tells you that eleven dimensions will help you get an injunction is lying to you.”
“All right.”

“Second: I did not come here to tell you what everything is made of. Dr Bellew would rightly say that I cannot demonstrate it, and I cannot.” He shifted the three sheets of paper he had brought and turned one round. “I came because of your black hole.”
Lolly looked down at the sheet. It was covered in an extremely dense and entirely orderly hand, and among the symbols she could make out almost nothing, but at the top, underlined once, was written:
four C - HORIZON ENTROPY - WHERE IS THE LEDGER
Her mouth went dry. “Keinschein,” she said.
“Alfred telephoned me on Tuesday and shouted at me for eleven minutes, which at his age is a considerable investment and, I think, a form of affection.” Von Wittenberg’s mouth twitched.

“His concern, as I understand it, is that your Ministry has used a small engineered black hole as a disposal channel for suppressed alternatives, and that the object is now evaporating, and that when it has gone there will be no record of what was destroyed. He calls this the falsification of the ledger. He is frightened. I have known him ninety years and I have not heard him frightened before.”
“And you can tell him it’s all right?”
“No,” said von Wittenberg. “But I can tell you why he may be wrong, and it is the one thing my subject has actually achieved.” He turned the sheet over.

“A black hole has an entropy,” he said. “Bekenstein saw it and Hawking made it precise: the entropy is proportional to the area of the horizon. Not to the volume inside. To the area of the surface.” He let that sit for a moment.

“That was extremely strange, and for twenty years nobody could say what it was counting. Entropy counts states. Which states? Of what? The black hole was supposed to have almost no properties at all.”
“And?”

“In 1996 two colleagues took a particular class of black hole in string theory, built it out of membranes and strings, counted the possible configurations of those objects - an ordinary counting problem, tedious but honest - and found that the number of states gave exactly the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy. Exactly. With the correct factor. No adjustment.” He said it very quietly indeed.
“That is the only occasion on which anyone has ever counted the microscopic states of a black hole and got the right answer, and it came out of strings, and I do not think it was luck.”
Lolly said slowly, “So there are states. It isn’t featureless.”
“It is not featureless. It has an enormous number of internal configurations, and the horizon area measures how many.”
“Then when it evaporates-”

“Then the question becomes whether the radiation carries them out,” said von Wittenberg, “and here is the deeper thing, and it is why I asked you what the correlations were between.” He turned the sheet again.

“The area law suggests something outrageous, which we now half understand. It suggests that everything happening inside a region can be encoded on its boundary. That the interior is not the fundamental description at all - that the true account is written one dimension lower, on the surface, and that what we call the inside is a kind of projection of it. There is a precise mathematical version of this in which a theory of gravity in a certain space is exactly equivalent to a theory without gravity living on its edge. Two descriptions. Same physics. Neither one more real.”
Lolly sat completely still. “Then the ledger isn’t inside it,” she said.
“That is what I came to say.”
“The record of what fell in - of what they dumped - isn’t in the interior waiting to be annihilated when the interior stops existing. It’s on the horizon. It’s in the surface.”
She was writing now, fast and badly. “And the horizon is exactly what the radiation comes out of.”

“Yes,” said Leonhard von Wittenberg. “And so the current view - not proven, not settled, but the view - is that evaporation does not destroy the information. It is scrambled almost beyond recovery, it emerges in correlations so subtle that no practical measurement could unpick them, but it is not annihilated. Unitarity survives. The books balance.”
He put the sheet down. “Tell Alfred that the ledger is not kept in the vault. It is kept on the wall.”
Lolly looked up. “Do you believe it?”

“I believe it in the way de Brévanne believes his wave,” said von Wittenberg. “Which is to say: I have thought about it for decades, the mathematics is far too good to be an accident, and I cannot show it to you. Dr Bellew would give me no credit at all and he would be right to.”

He gathered his papers. “This is the difficulty with being in my line of work. We have produced, I think, the most beautiful structure in the history of physics, and we have not produced a single number a committee could check. Your Bell test will produce one in two days. I am aware which of us is more useful this week.”
He stood, and paused. “May I say one more thing. It is not physics.”
“Please.”
“You told Dr Bellew you were a physicist for eleven minutes as a working physicist.”

Von Wittenberg looked faintly embarrassed. “I was a history major. I intended to be a journalist. I worked on a political campaign. I came to physics late and by an unusual road, as did de Brévanne, as did - in his fashion - Alfred, who came by no road at all.”

He picked up his pencil. “I mention it only because I notice that everybody who has come to talk to you this week arrived from somewhere else, and I do not think that is a coincidence, and I do not think it is a compliment either. It is simply that the people who ask what a thing is are usually people who were not trained to take it for granted.”
He went back to his table, and to his papers, and did not speak again for the rest of the afternoon.

At half past six Lolly walked back to the school hall through streets that were still visibly deciding things, and found Fainrose sitting on a crate eating a sandwich beside a rack of timing electronics.
“You’ve been with von Wittenberg,” she said. “You’ve got the expression. Everyone gets the expression.”
“He says everything is eleven-dimensional membranes.”
“Yes.”
“And that the record of everything the Ministry dumped into four C is written on the horizon rather than inside it, so it can’t be destroyed by evaporation.”
Fainrose stopped chewing. “Say that again,” she said.
Lolly opened the notebook and showed her the page. She read it, twice, and then said something Lolly had not expected at all.
“That’s not a defence,” she said. “That’s a deadline, which is the one thing this building can be relied upon to understand.”
“How?”
“Because if the information is on the horizon, then it comes out in the radiation, in the correlations, over the entire remaining lifetime of the object.” She was already up, sandwich abandoned.

“Which means there is a window. And the window closes when four C does. And the smaller it gets, the hotter and faster it goes.” She looked at her. “Lolly. How long have we been treating the evaporation as the catastrophe?”
“Three days.”

“It isn’t the catastrophe,” said Stephanie Fainrose. “It’s the disclosure. The thing is telling us everything they put into it, in the most scrambled possible handwriting, and it will stop when it has finished burning.”
Lolly sat down slowly on the crate.
Then she opened the notebook and wrote: One object. Many notes. Five theories that were one theory seen from five sides.
Then: The entropy goes as the area, not the volume. The account is kept on the surface.
And beneath it, underlined twice: The evaporation is not the destruction of the record. It is the reading of it, aloud, once, at increasing speed, and nobody has been listening.
The first detector clicked.
Then the second.
Then all four together.
Fainrose stopped writing. “That’s not a signal.”
“What is it?” Lolly asked.
She looked at the timing trace. “It’s the apparatus measuring itself.”

prosody.emphasis: Chapter 15: Final State Pending

p.prosody: Beatrix Sloan won the injunction application on the Monday morning and lost the argument about what to do with it by lunchtime, because the Board, faced with an order it could not ignore, did what boards do when cornered: it asked for a plan, in writing, by four o’clock, confident that no plan could possibly exist and that confidence, once minuted, would constitute a defence.
“They think we’re bluffing,” said Beatrix, setting down the telephone with the particular gentleness of a woman who would have preferred to throw it.
“We are not bluffing,” said Fainrose. “We simply do not yet have a plan.”
“That is the same thing to a Board, for four hours and two biscuits.”

Lolly Wren, who had spent the walk back from the courthouse turning something over in the green notebook that she could not yet make into sentences, said, “We have three plans. We have never had fewer than three.”
Everyone looked at her.

“Keinschein says nothing is definite until agreement spreads, so the fix is to spread better agreement - his word, not mine, though I notice he never once told us how.” She turned a page. “De Brévanne says nothing was ever lost, only steered wrong, and the fix is to take the apparatus out of the wave and let the guidance relax. Fainrose says the fix is error correction: don’t restore a copy, repair from the correlations that survive, in the right order. And von Wittenberg says the record isn’t inside four C at all, it’s on the horizon, coming out in the radiation, and the fix is to listen faster than it burns.”
“Those are four different physics,” said Fainrose, “held by four people who have never once agreed on anything else.”

“Yes,” said Lolly. “And Bellew told me not to pick until something forced me to, and to use whichever one told me where to put the probe.” She closed the notebook. “Nothing has forced me to pick. So I’m not going to. I’m going to use all four, because none of them actually contradicts what we do on a Tuesday afternoon with a cable and a timing rack. They only contradict each other about what it means. Nobody has ever asked us to certify what it means. The injunction asks us to fix nine thousand houses in eleven weeks.”
Fainrose was quiet for a moment, in the stillness that Lolly now knew to wait out rather than fill.
“Say the plan,” she said. “Slowly. I want to write it down exactly once.”
She said the plan slowly.

Von Wittenberg’s people would go to the horizon and listen - not to solve anything, but to recover, from the scrambled radiation, whatever fragments of the four hundred and eleven suppressed states could still be pulled out before the anchor finished evaporating, on the working assumption that the record was written on the surface and not lost inside it. That was the deadline, and it was fixed, and nothing anyone did elsewhere would move it.

Meanwhile, Fainrose’s team would treat the correlation lattice exactly as error-correcting code, exactly as she had described to Voller in the cold vault: not restoring any single node, but repairing the pattern across all of them, in the order the syndrome tables specified, measuring damage without measuring the citizens who carried it.

And the apparatus - the survey scanners, the certification passes, the entire industrial machinery of asking - would be switched off first, before any repair began, on de Brévanne’s theory rather than Fainrose’s, because if he was right that the apparatus itself was what had been deforming the guidance all along, then the single most useful thing anyone could do, before attempting a single clever repair, was to stop actively making it worse.
“That’s not physics,” said Fainrose. “That’s just turning it off.”
“It is the least fashionable intervention available,” said Lolly.

“That’s what turning it off is, when you’ve spent fifteen years arguing about the theory instead,” said Lolly. “De Brévanne didn’t give me a new machine. He gave me permission to stop running the old one before we’d agreed why it was broken.”

Beatrix wrote this down in the flattened, unpoetic language a court could not misread, and delivered it at four o’clock precisely, and the Board - who had wanted a plan mainly in order to have something to reject - discovered with some irritation that they had been handed one they could not credibly call absent, and were obliged, for the first time in the Initiative’s history, to fund something rather than merely surviving a review of it.

It was in the eighth week, with the scanners silent, the lattice repairing itself in the patient, unglamorous order the syndrome tables specified, and von Wittenberg’s rented industrial unit outside Sub-District 6 producing its first usable fragments of scrambled record, that Mrs Elspeth Chain came to the annex on a Wednesday and asked to see Fainrose alone, which she had not done before.

Lolly was not present for the conversation. She learned what mattered from Fainrose afterward, on the crate by the timing rack, with two mugs of the tea Mrs Chain no longer made for them because she had stopped coming in every day, which everyone had noticed and nobody had said anything about.

“She asked me for a number,” said Fainrose. “How much of her sister we would get back. A percentage. She wanted it before the injunction ran out, not after, because she said she had spent her whole life being told good news arrived on time and had never once seen it happen and did not intend to be surprised twice.”
“And you gave her one.”

“I told her the truth, which is that I did not know, and that anybody who told her a number this week was lying to her for the same reason Voller lied to himself about the vault - because a number is comforting and a distribution is not, and she deserved the distribution.” Fainrose turned the mug in her hands. “She said that was the first honest answer anybody in this building had given her, and that she would come back when there was one worth hearing, and she left, and she did not shout, which frightened me considerably more than if she had.”

Lolly thought about the photograph on the mantelpiece, restored by a man pulling a cable out of a skirting board without permission, and about the two duvets, and about a woman standing in a doorway in her own house asking a government to explain itself.
“What do we actually owe her,” she said. “Not the district. Her.”
Fainrose did not answer immediately, which she had learned to recognise as the shape of an answer arriving.

“I used to think the job was restoration,” she said at last. “Put it back. That’s what I trained for, that’s what the vault was supposed to do badly, that’s what I have spent eight weeks doing carefully instead. But de Brévanne asked me a question in the corridor last month that I have not been able to put down. He asked whether a fully restored district - every node repaired, every correlation exact, every citizen certified back to their prior configuration - would in fact be a country, or merely a very good forgery of the country that would have existed if nobody had touched it. And I did not have an answer, and I am unused to that, and I have decided I dislike it less than I expected.”
“What’s the alternative to restoration.”

“Not a cartoon. Not a copy. Not a photograph of a conversation.” Fainrose looked at her. “Something that is allowed to have come through this. A district that remembers, imperfectly and honestly, that a Ministry once stood in its wave with a clipboard - rather than one so perfectly repaired that the crime leaves no mark and therefore, eventually, no lesson. Mrs Chain does not want her sister back exactly as she was. She has told me so, in those words, twice. She wants her sister back as someone who is recoverable, not someone who is undamaged. She told you that in week one and none of us were listening properly.”

Lolly opened the green notebook and found the page - eight weeks old now, ink slightly faded, Mrs Chain’s own words, taken down almost as an aside: She will be recoverable. That is not the same as unharmed.

“Then that’s the plan,” she said slowly. “Not full-state reconstruction. Not the vault’s dream of exactness. A negotiated settlement between what was and what can honestly be recovered - published, itemised, with the gaps named rather than papered over. Von Wittenberg’s list, when it comes. Whatever fraction it turns out to be.”
“A country that admits its own scar tissue,” said Fainrose, “rather than one that pretends to have been born without a wound.”
“Will the Board accept that.”

“The Board,” said Fainrose, “will accept whatever a court orders it to accept, and courts, it turns out, have a great deal of respect for an itemised list of gaps and no respect whatever for a certificate of perfection. Beatrix explained this to me on the second day and I did not believe her and I believe her now.”
They sat for a while without talking, which by that stage of the year had become one of the more comfortable things either of them did.
“I keep thinking about the moon,” said Lolly eventually.
“Outer Fenwick.”

“It didn’t need forty-one people to stay a moon. It needed the air to be let alone to keep noticing it.” She turned the notebook to a blank page. “I think that’s what we’re actually trying to give Mrs Chain back. Not a certificate. Not a copy. Just - permission for her ordinary life to go on being noticed by everything around it, undisturbed, so it can stay itself without anyone standing over it with a form.”

“That is either the plainest sentence you have said all year,” said Fainrose, “or the most sentimental, and I find I am too tired to tell which, which may itself be the first reliable instrument reading we have had all week.”
She wrote it down anyway.

The final settlement, when Beatrix filed it in the ninth week, ran to one hundred and forty pages and itemised, district by district, exactly what had been recovered, what had been reconstructed by inference and flagged as such, and what remained - honestly, permanently, unsoftened - missing. It did not satisfy the Board, which had wanted an ending, or Voller, who had wanted a vault to be right about something, or, entirely, Mrs Chain, who read it twice at her own kitchen table and said only that it was the first document the Ministry had ever given her that she believed.

It was not a resolution. Lolly had stopped expecting one of those. It was, she wrote in the green notebook that evening, a state - honestly reported, imperfectly repaired, still and forever in the process of becoming whatever it was going to become next, which she had come, over four months, to understand was the only kind of ending the universe had ever actually offered anybody.
She wrote:
We did not restore the district. We admitted what could be recovered, and named what could not, and called both of them true.
Then, underneath:
A perfect copy would have been a forgery wearing the country’s face. An honest gap is not a failure of the repair. It is the repair.
And at the bottom, in the smallest hand of all:
Final state: pending. It will always say pending. That was never the fault in the filing.

The deadline was no longer an administrative fiction. At four C, the anchor had begun to lose mass. Every hour they spent arguing about interpretation was an hour in which information could become physically unrecoverable.
Gideon looked at the clock. “We should probably stop debating whether we’re ready.”
Beatrix looked at him. “Why?”
“Because the universe doesn’t appear to have asked whether we are.”

prosody.emphasis: Chapter 16: The Decision

p.prosody: The injunction was granted on the Tuesday by a judge who understood none of the physics and all of the paperwork, which turned out to be sufficient.
Beatrix Sloan had not argued that reality had been damaged. She had learned, by then, that courts do not adjudicate ontology.

She had argued instead that the Ministry had certified nine thousand separate local determinations while holding, in its own filing system, a measurement establishing that they were one act - and that a body which certifies nine thousand times what it knows to be one thing has not made an error of physics but a false instrument in a live system. Which is a thing the law has known how to dislike since the fourteenth century, as the Duc de Brévanne observed with some satisfaction from the public gallery.
They got eleven weeks. It was not enough, and nobody had prepared a form in which enough was an available option.
