Von Wittenberg’s people listened to the horizon for nine of them, from a rented industrial unit outside Sub-District 6, with equipment that cost more than the district’s entire housing stock and had, for that reason, a more generous maintenance schedule, and that Fainrose described, in her only published remark on the matter, as “an ear held against a burning wall.”
Of the four hundred and eleven P nine states, they recovered three hundred and eight. It was not a triumph and Fainrose refused, in every interview afterwards, to let it be described as one.

Three hundred and eight pending human states were unscrambled from the radiation and returned to the districts they had come out of: a child’s route to school, a marriage in the middle of being decided, an apprenticeship, two reconciliations, a great many small unfinished intentions of no civic significance whatever.

One hundred and three were not recovered, and their names were published, because Beatrix insisted, and because Miss Dorothy Kell wrote to the inquiry to say that a list of the unrecovered was the only memorial such things could have.
They cut the coupling on the fourteenth of November at six oh four, which was Jago Flint’s idea and which nobody objected to.
S across the paired dwellings of Sub-District 6 came up to two point seven nine within forty minutes.

The districts resolved over the following month, badly and thinly and in the wrong order, and it looked on every screen exactly like collapse, and Crispin Vale - who by then had testified for eleven days and had stopped bringing biscuits, a loss the inquiry did not minute—was blamed for the noise he had permitted rather than credited for the paralysis he had ended, precisely as Fainrose had told him he would be.
Mrs Elspeth Chain’s sister was settled record. She was in the seventy-eight per cent.
She did not come back.

But the photograph was on the mantelpiece at Twenty-Two Coldharrow Rise the following spring - the one of the two of them laughing at some unseen mishap, restored by a man pulling a cable out of a skirting board without permission - and Mrs Chain took the view, expressed at the inquiry and quoted rather widely afterwards, that a photograph a burglar had returned was worth more than a certificate a government had signed.
Alfred Keinschein left in December, without ceremony, having eaten nothing for six weeks.

“They have stopped asking on an industrial scale,” he said, on the annex steps, with his coat over his arm and no shadow on the concrete. “It is a famine and I have brought it on myself and I find I do not mind as much as I expected. There will be other centuries.”

He shook Lolly’s hand with his cold one. “Ms Wren. You will want to know whether I was right or whether the Duc was, and I shall tell you honestly that I have had eleven thousand years and I do not know. Ask the fellow with the box. He has been waiting since 1935 and nobody has had the courtesy.”
Lolly said, “Which fellow with the box.”
But Keinschein had already gone, in the manner of a thing that had not, strictly, been present.
Max Tegnér testified for the prosecution, at his own request, on the specific question of whether a multiverse makes cruelty free. His answer ran to four hours and can be fairly summarised as no.
Werner Heitmann sent a letter.
It was two lines long.
It said:
The measurement was correctly performed and the inference is sound. I have never in my life been able to say more than that and I have never been able to say less.
Fainrose kept it in the front of the syndrome file for the rest of her career.
Jack Bellew did not appear again, which Lolly chose to interpret as approval.

In February, Stephanie Fainrose was appointed to chair the reconstituted oversight body, on terms she dictated in writing and which included the phrase no certificate may require the simultaneous determination of conjugate quantities,

and she offered Lolly Wren the post of Principal Officer, Relational Integrity, which was a job title she had invented late on a Thursday and defended for eight months with the ferocity of a constitutional principle.
She asked what the work was.
“Noticing,” said Fainrose. “Professionally. With a budget.”
“I’m not qualified.”
“Lolly,” she said, “we have been over this in a car park.”
She took it, and kept the green notebook, which by then had four hundred pages and had begun a second volume, and which is quoted in the schedule to the Act.

And on a Friday in March, in the reading room of the branch library on Coldharrow Street, at the table by the window overlooking the shut-down carpet showroom, she found a very old Austrian gentleman waiting for her with a wooden box on the table and two cups of coffee already going cold.
Prologue

“Sit,” said the old man. “I have ordered you a coffee and it is already unpleasant, which is the most reliable thing in this building. Erich Schrottfinger. You have been sent to me by a dead Irishman, a French duke, and a vampire, which is a referral pattern I have not had since 1953.”
He was very old and very Viennese, in a bow tie that had been tied by somebody who cared, with a great deal of white hair and an air of enormous and slightly disreputable charm.
There was a wooden box on the table between them, about the size of a hatbox, with air holes.
Lolly looked at the box.

“Don’t,” said Schrottfinger. “It is empty. It has always been empty. It was always a joke, Ms Wren, that is the thing nobody will accept - I invented it to be ridiculous, to show my colleagues that their position led somewhere absurd, and within twenty years it was on the side of coffee mugs. You cannot win. You make one sarcastic remark about a cat and it outlives your equation.”
“Then why bring it.”
“Because people sit down faster.”

Schrottfinger pushed it aside. “Now. You have written four hundred pages and you have finished a thing, and you have come to a library on a Friday because you want somebody to tell you what it was all for, and Fainrose cannot tell you because she is a working physicist and von Wittenberg cannot tell you because he will start on the eleven dimensions. So it falls to me, who am not respectable.”
“Keinschein said you’d been waiting since 1935.”
“For someone to ask what the cat was about, yes. Nobody asks. They ask whether it is alive.”
Schrottfinger drank some of the terrible coffee.
“Very well. I shall give you what you came for, and then you will go home. And I shall call it a Prologue, and you will object, and I shall explain.”
He put down the cup.
“Here is the outlook, since you want the outlook.”

Your Ministry believed it was managing a country. It was in fact interfering, in a small and provincial way, with something that is not finished. And I do not mean the paperwork is not finished. I mean the universe is not finished, and it is not nearly finished, and everything you have lived through this year took place in what future arrangements of matter will regard as the opening seconds.

“The stars are the first thing to understand. There are stars now. This is not the normal condition. Star formation peaked long ago and is declining, and the gas will run down, and in something of the order of a hundred trillion years the last star will form and the sky will begin to go out - not dramatically, one by one, the small red ones outliving all the rest with the patience of the parsimonious. And then there will be a very long time in which the galaxy is a place of embers: white dwarfs cooling, neutron stars cooling, brown dwarfs occasionally colliding and briefly lighting. That era is longer, Ms Wren, than the era of starlight by a factor you cannot usefully imagine. Almost all of history is afterwards.”

Then, if the protons are not eternal - and we do not know, we have looked very hard and seen nothing, which only pushes the number out - then even the embers dissolve, and matter itself is a phase that ends.

“And then it is the age of the black holes, and they are the last structures, and they do exactly what your four C did in a car park in Surrey: they evaporate. Slowly. Then less slowly. Then, at the very end, in a final bright indignity. The largest will take on the order of ten to the power of one hundred years, which is not a length of time so much as an insult to the concept. But they go. Everything that ever consolidated, goes.”
He glanced at the two cups of coffee between them, both now stone cold. “Rather like the coffee. Only slower, and with fewer complaints.”
After that: a very thin, very cold, very dark space with a little radiation in it, expanding, and nothing in it that could be called an event.
“That is the outlook. You asked for it. That is what is next in the galaxy and in the universe, on the current evidence, and I have not exaggerated in either direction.”
He let it sit for a moment, in the reading room, over the cold coffee.
“Now,” said Erich Schrottfinger. “The interesting part, which is why I did not simply post it to you.”

Every physicist my age was taught that the universe runs down. Order becomes disorder; the coffee goes cold; the sun exhausts itself. Perfectly true. And when I was a younger man I looked at a living thing and thought: how does that happen. Because a living thing does the opposite. It maintains itself. It holds a pattern against the current for eighty years.

“And the answer is not that life defies the law. The answer is that a living thing survives by feeding on order - by taking in structure and excreting disorder, by paying the universe’s bill locally and passing the cost outward. It does not violate the accounts. It runs a very good scheme within them. A living thing is a place where order is temporarily concentrated because it has arranged to be paid for elsewhere.”

He allowed himself a small, particular smile. “The cat, I will have you know, was rather better at this than any of the physicists who built a career on it. It kept itself going for as long as anyone let it, and it never once wrote a paper.”
You see it, of course. You have spent a year on it.

“Your Ministry, Ms Wren, was doing the same thing, badly, and without knowing it. It wished a district to be simple - that is, low in complexity, low in ambiguity, cheap to describe. And it discovered what every living system discovers, which is that you cannot simply have that. You must pay for it, and the payment is that the disorder goes somewhere else. So they built a hole and put it in there. That was not a bureaucratic peculiarity. That was thermodynamics, conducted by people who had not been told they were doing thermodynamics, and the reason it ended in a fire is that they never asked where the bill was going.”

“Every institution that promises to make things simple is proposing to move complexity somewhere you cannot see. Every single one. Not sometimes. Always, and by law. That is the sentence I should like you to take away, and you may put it in your notebook, and you need not attribute it to me because Boltzmann said it first and less politely.”
Lolly was writing.
“And so - the outlook,” said Schrottfinger. “Yes. In the long run: the embers, the holes, the dark. I shall not soften it and I dislike people who do.”

But consider what is between now and that. Consider the enormous middle. There is going to be an extremely long period in which there is still order left to be spent, and in which anything that can arrange to be paid for elsewhere may persist, and think, and ask questions. Life did not have to happen. Having happened, it has a very long time to work with, and the sort of thing it may become in a hundred million years does not bear guessing at and would probably not recognise us as ancestors so much as weather.
“And here is what I think, and I am eighty-nine and entitled to think it.”

The universe does not contain many places where it is described. Almost everywhere, things simply proceed. But wherever something has assembled itself into an arrangement that can hold a model of the rest - a bird, a mathematician, a green notebook - the universe acquires, locally and temporarily, an account of itself. That is not nothing. That may be the rarest thing in it. It is certainly rarer than gravity.

“Your Ministry was engaged in reducing the number of such accounts, and calling it efficiency, and the reason that was a crime and not merely a mistake is that the accounts are the scarce commodity and the simplicity was not. Anyone can have simplicity. You can have all the simplicity you want at the end of time, and it will be perfect, and there will be nobody in it.”

“So: what is next in the universe. More of this, for a very long while, and then less, and then none. And in the meantime, an unreasonably interesting middle, in which the correct posture is neither optimism nor despair but attention - which is your job title, I understand, and which somebody has finally thought to fund.”
He picked up the empty box and put it on his lap.
“Now. Why a Prologue.”
“Because you want an ending, Ms Wren, and I will not give you one, and my reason is technical rather than sentimental.”

He tapped the lid. “The whole trouble with my cat was that everybody read it as a story about a box. It is not. It is a story about the lid. The absurdity I was pointing at is the belief that there exists a moment at which the matter is settled - that reality performs a closing act, once, cleanly, and then the fact is a fact and may be filed.”

There is no such moment. Your friend Keinschein was right about that much and it is the only thing he and I agree on. There is only the widening business of things becoming correlated with other things, indefinitely, forever, at the speed of gossip, and a state that has not yet finished resolving is not a mystery awaiting a verdict. It is the ordinary condition of everything.

“Three hundred and eight of your recovered items were pending. Not memories. Things that had not finished happening. You gave them back to people, and they are still not finished, and they will go on not being finished, which is what it means to be alive rather than certified.”

“So this is not the end of your book. It is the front matter of what those three hundred and eight are going to do. It is a Prologue, and it is at the back, and if that offends the printers they may take it up with the second law.”
He stood, and tucked the box under his arm, and drained the appalling coffee with the enthusiasm of a man who had survived worse.
“One last thing, since you have been polite and have not once mentioned the cat’s welfare.”

“You will be tempted, in your new post, to find out which of them was right. De Brévanne and his wave, Keinschein and his agreement, Tegnér and his branches, von Wittenberg and his strings. You will want the answer, because you spent years learning to make theories survive contact with reality, and you want to know what the circuit is.”

Schrottfinger put on his hat. “You will not get it. Not from me, not this century, possibly not ever. And you must not let that stop you from noticing things, because the noticing is the part that turned out to matter and the interpretation was never what saved the district.”
What saved the district was a clerk who wrote down that a lie required electricity. “Keep the notebook, Ms Wren. It is the only apparatus that has never once been wrong about what it saw.”
He went out through the reading room, past the local history shelves, and cast a completely ordinary shadow, and did not look back.

Lolly sat by the window for a while with the cold coffee and the noise of Coldharrow Street coming through the glass - a district in the middle of resolving, badly and slowly and in the wrong order, and not finished.
Then she took out the notebook, and turned to a clean page, and wrote at the top:
PROLOGUE
And underneath:
Order is not free. Simplicity is always paid for somewhere else, and any institution that will not say where is lying or ignorant, and it does not matter which.
The universe is mostly not yet. Almost everything is still pending. That is not a fault in the filing.
Then, last, in the ordinary handwriting of a woman who had somewhere to be:
There is no lid.
THE END which is to say, the beginning of the part that has not been written down.

prosody.emphasis: Epilogue: The Ministry Has Learned Nothing

p.prosody: Three weeks after the incident, the Ministry issued a statement.
It was signed by Q E D, whose full name was Quentin Edmund Darling, allegedly.
It was seventeen pages long.
The first sixteen pages explained that nothing unusual had happened.
The seventeenth explained that the unusual thing which had not happened had nevertheless been handled in accordance with procedure.
Nobody was entirely sure which procedure.
“So everything is fine.”
“Is it?”
“Allegedly.”
“Obviously.”
Mrs Chain was promoted. She accepted on the understanding that it did not involve more meetings. Human Resources disagreed, which was unfortunate for Human Resources.

One former Ministry official was listed as dead. Allegedly. He was, presumably, pushing up daisies, obviously, although the Ministry had not yet completed the form confirming that he had stopped being alive.
Jago Flint put a sign on his door: REALITY UNDER REVIEW. PLEASE DO NOT ASSIST.
Stephanie Fainrose resumed her work in quantum foundations and made the mistake of saying that the Ministry’s explanation of the measurement problem was not entirely stupid.
This was taken as a compliment.
It was not.

Alistair Venn produced a report so long that the report itself became an event requiring a report. Mr Voller was asked to summarise it. He submitted a blank page. This was the clearest summary the Ministry had received all year.

Gideon Wigglesworth turned up on the Friday with two coffees. He caught his shoe on the doorframe on the way in. This was, by now, a tradition, possibly a load-bearing one. He announced that he had been promoted to Interdepartmental Liaison, a position that appeared to exist chiefly to explain his whereabouts for the last several chapters. Nobody asked where, exactly, those had been. He did not volunteer it. He put the second coffee on Lolly’s desk, said something warm and mostly unintelligible about the window, and left — catching his shoe on the doorframe again on the way out, for symmetry.

Lolly Wren was given a new desk, a new title — her second in as many months — and the same notebook. The title was Officer for Eventual Coherence. This replaced Principal Officer, Relational Integrity, which she had held for less time than it took to get the nameplate spelled correctly. The desk had a window. The notebook remained suspicious.
Then the complaint terminal clicked.
COMPLAINT TYPE: FUTURE DISCREPANCY SUBCATEGORY: EVENT HAS OCCURRED BUT IS NOT YET SCHEDULED URGENCY: MODERATE TO EXISTENTIAL
Lolly looked at her tea. Then at the notebook. Then she wrote:
Obviously, this is someone else’s problem.
The terminal clicked again.
It printed a form.
The form was dated tomorrow.
Somewhere in the building, a filing cabinet opened by itself and accepted a document that had not yet been written.
Somewhere else, a physicist would eventually explain why.
Probably.
Allegedly. Apparently. Or, as the Ministry preferred to put it, all is well. Or is it?
And in the basement, beneath several floors of perfectly respectable bureaucracy, the Ministry continued to simplify reality by making it someone else’s problem.
Which was, after all, what it had been designed to do.
THE END.
Obviously.

prosody.emphasis: Appendix: The Physics Lecture

p.prosody: The complete physics course, gathered here as a single lecture after the damage has been done.

The novel is the story. This Appendix is the explanation. Each section takes the quantum-mechanical idea dramatized in its corresponding chapter and explains it from the ground up in plain English. The deeper mathematics is clearly marked as optional.

The sixteen sections that follow are narrated, throughout, by Lothar Feynmann — a lecturer who is not a character in the novel you have just heard, has no opinions about the Ministry, and was engaged for this Appendix alone, on the reasonable theory that physics explained once is improved by being explained a second time in a different voice.

If the surname sounds familiar, that is not an accident, though it is also not a claim. A remark of the real Feynman's — that anyone who says they understand quantum mechanics has probably misunderstood the question — is the reason Lolly went back into physics in the first place, several chapters ago now. Mr Feynmann heard about this use of his near-namesake, considered it at some length, and asked only for a fair hearing and a decent microphone. Both are provided below.
He will not appear again after this Appendix. He was not in the meetings. He is, by his own account, entirely on your side.

prosody.emphasis: Chapter 1: Physics Notes: Superposition

p.prosody: In one breath. A quantum thing is described by its state: the best complete account physics can give of what results different measurements may produce. A measurement is a physical interaction that asks one particular question and produces a result; before that interaction, a state can combine alternatives without already carrying one hidden, definite answer to that question.

Start here. Think of a recipe card still being written, with two genuinely possible dinners pencilled in: soup if the weather stays cold, salad if it clears. Until someone makes the deciding trip to the shops, neither dinner is the one being cooked. The image helps with one point: sometimes it is wrong to imagine that one settled answer has merely been concealed from us.

The idea, step by step. 1. A state is a compact description of a system that lets physics predict the results of possible measurements. 2. A measurement is a physical interaction between the system and an apparatus, such as a detector, which leaves a record of a particular result. 3. For one chosen property, a quantum state can be a superposition: a combination of alternatives rather than a system secretly assigned to just one of them. 4. If the apparatus measures that property, it produces one allowed result, with probabilities set by the state. 5. Before such a measurement, the alternatives can interfere, reinforcing or cancelling one another; this is why a superposition is more than ordinary ignorance.

What this chapter was actually showing you. Lolly’s complaint file does not merely hide one correct status behind a faulty screen: APPROVED, MISROUTED, and CLOSED keep presenting incompatible descriptions. Mrs Chain is likewise caught between not having committed to the journey and already having arrived. Her bus, the terminal, and Whitbury-on-Sea are comic enlargements, not literal quantum systems, but they give a useful first picture of a state that has not yet yielded one answer to a particular question. The Simplification Initiative wants the file to settle promptly because it finds unresolved alternatives administratively inconvenient. The story’s problem is therefore not that the Ministry has misunderstood a hidden answer. It has begun acting as though one must exist before the measurement that would make it definite.

Where the popular version goes wrong. You will often hear that superposition means a particle is simply “in two places at once”. That slogan can be useful for getting someone to put down their tea, but it is not the full idea. Superposition is a state with no definite value for the property being measured in that basis, and its alternatives can interfere. Nor does a conscious person make it collapse by looking. What matters is a physical interaction that records or can spread information about the relevant alternative.

Going deeper (skip freely). This block is optional. In the standard notation, a state with two alternatives can be written as a weighted combination; the weights are called probability amplitudes, and their squared magnitudes give the probabilities when that property is measured:

The amplitudes can be complex numbers, which is why they can interfere before probabilities are calculated. Max Born gave this probability rule its standard interpretation in 1926. Interference of single photons, electrons, atoms, and larger molecules is observed in carefully isolated experiments; it is a testable feature of quantum states, not a metaphor about indecision.

What the reader learns. - A state is physics’ description of what results a system can give in specified measurements. - A measurement is a physical interaction with a recording apparatus, not an act of human attention. - A superposition is not merely an unknown pre-existing answer. - Interference is the observable clue that the alternatives form one coherent quantum state.
One-line summary. Before a measurement forces one answer, a quantum state may be more than a list of answers waiting in a drawer.

prosody.emphasis: Chapter 2: Physics Notes: Measurement Basis and Forced Collapse

p.prosody: In one breath. A measurement can answer only the particular kind of question its apparatus is built to ask; that choice is its measurement basis. For incompatible quantum questions, there is no basis-independent set of sharp “true values” waiting to be read off, and the first measurement can change what a later one is able to find.

Start here. Take two pairs of polarising sunglasses. Hold one lens flat and rotate the second in front of it until the pair is crossed at right angles, and the view through both goes black: the first lens lets through light waving only one way, the second only the opposite way. Slide a third lens between them, tilted at forty-five degrees, and the light comes back — a satisfying trick to perform at a bus stop, though it does nothing for one’s reputation. The middle lens has not opened a gap in the other two; it has forced the light to answer its question first, and answering that question has reset what the light can tell the lenses either side of it. (Ordinary light manages this through wave optics; the identical trick run one photon at a time is what turns it from a party trick into a lesson about quantum measurement.) The image keeps faith with the point that matters here: this is not a case of an answer hiding behind a screen. It is a case of one question changing what a later, different question can find.

The idea, step by step. 1. A measurement basis is the set of distinct alternatives a particular apparatus is able to distinguish. 2. A measurement of one basis gives one result and leaves the system in the state associated with that result; this idealised update is called state reduction. 3. Some bases are incompatible, meaning that preparing a definite result in one does not in general prepare a definite result in the other. 4. Measuring the second basis is therefore an intervention, not a neutral relabelling of a value that was already sharp in both bases. 5. The order of two incompatible measurements can change the later results, because the first physical interaction has prepared a new state.

What this chapter was actually showing you. Queue Management forces Mrs Chain’s one experience into an intake frame: intent, route, or civic stability. When the clerk asks whether her destination was “emotionally authorized”, that question does not simply uncover a pre-existing official category; it starts reducing her account to the distinctions the queue permits. Lolly spots the diagnostic line “PRIMARY MEASUREMENT FRAME: INTENT” and understands the danger. The queue is measuring the public by insisting that its first question determines what sort of problem the citizen may become.

Where the popular version goes wrong. It is tempting to say that a measurement basis is just a different way of looking at one fully specified object. That is false for incompatible quantum properties. The theory does not say that a particle carries a little card listing sharp answers to every possible basis and that our apparatus merely reads one line. A measurement is a physical interaction, never a matter of conscious attention, and the apparatus determines which distinction can leave a record. This does not mean that every everyday question creates its own reality; it is a precise claim about quantum observables and their experimental arrangements.

Going deeper (skip freely). This block is optional. For a two-outcome measurement, the apparatus has states such as |u⟩ and |d⟩ as its basis. A state can be expanded in that basis, and an ideal measurement gives one result with the corresponding squared amplitude before preparing that outcome state:
|ψ⟩ = c u |u⟩ + c d |d⟩, P (u) = | c u | 2.

Two observables are incompatible when their operators do not commute, written AB ≠ BA. The Stern–Gerlach experiment by Otto Stern and Walther Gerlach in 1922 showed discrete angular-momentum outcomes; sequences of differently oriented Stern–Gerlach magnets make the dependence on the chosen axis visible. The word “collapse” is useful textbook shorthand for the ideal state-update rule, while fuller accounts model the measuring apparatus and its physical entanglement with the system.

What the reader learns. - A measurement basis specifies which alternatives an apparatus can distinguish. - The question built into a quantum measurement helps determine the kind of answer obtainable. - Incompatible properties cannot generally all have simultaneous sharp, basis-independent values. - Measurement is a physical state-changing interaction, not a passive glance.
One-line summary. Ask reality through the wrong sorting frame, and the answer may be the only part of it your apparatus has left standing.

prosody.emphasis: Chapter 3: Physics Notes: Premature Collapse

p.prosody: In one breath. Measurement does not merely uncover a completed quantum story: it physically couples a system to something that can record an outcome, changing the state in the process. If that interaction happens before the alternatives have had time to evolve or interfere in the way an experiment requires, the lost coherence cannot simply be recovered by calling the result settled.

Start here. Imagine trying to watch the colours blend in wet paint by pressing a clean sheet of paper onto it every few seconds. Each press leaves a mark, but it also interrupts and spoils the pattern you wished to see. The record and the disturbance come together. The comparison is imperfect, but it shares the crucial feature that obtaining a record involves contact, not passive surveillance.

The idea, step by step. 1. A quantum state can evolve so that its alternatives acquire relationships that later produce interference. 2. A measurement couples the system to an apparatus that records one of the alternatives. 3. In the ideal textbook description, this produces state reduction to the recorded outcome. 4. Uncontrolled interactions with the surroundings can also spread information outward; this is decoherence. 5. When usable information about an alternative is left in a detector or environment, the interference that required keeping alternatives coherent is generally lost. 6. “Premature collapse” is not a standard technical term: here it means intervening before the evolution or interference one cares about has had a chance to develop.

What this chapter was actually showing you. Mrs Chain’s Equivalent Residence Unit 7B has been forced too soon into a narrow approved version of her home. The teal bowl, artificial daffodils, incorrect photographs, and competing clocks show a bureaucratic attempt to make one description stick before the details agree. When Lolly removes the Civic Stability Substrate from behind the cracked mirror, suppressed versions of the house reappear: geraniums, the photograph of Mrs Chain’s husband, and conflicting furnishings. The novel’s house is not quantum-scale physics, but it makes the right point about the Ministry’s intervention: labelling and monitoring are doing the damage, not neutrally reading a finished reality.

Where the popular version goes wrong. The familiar claim that “observation makes it real” is misleading. Quantum experiments do not require a mind, an eye, or a person with a clipboard. They require physical interactions capable of producing records. In a two-slit experiment, for example, a detector that obtains reliable which-path information changes the experimental situation and removes the interference pattern. Decoherence explains why interference becomes inaccessible in practice, but by itself it does not settle the deeper question of why one particular outcome is experienced.
Going deeper (skip freely). This block is optional. For two paths, an unmeasured state may combine two amplitudes; the probability at a screen includes an interference term:

A reliable path record correlates the paths with different detector states. When those record states are distinguishable, the cross-term responsible for the interference disappears from the observed pattern. The relation between available which-path information and reduced interference was analysed quantitatively by Berthold-Georg Englert in 1996. This is an experimentally routine feature of quantum setups, not a rule about a scientist’s thoughts.

What the reader learns. - Measurement creates a physical record by interacting with the system. - That interaction can remove the coherence required for interference. - Decoherence is environment-spread information, not a complete solution to the measurement problem. - A forced outcome can discard correlations and alternatives rather than reveal a fully formed truth.
One-line summary. A measurement gets its answer by touching the system, which is why asking too soon can spoil what the system might otherwise have shown.

prosody.emphasis: Chapter 4: Physics Notes: State Reduction via Repeated Measurement

p.prosody: In one breath. A measurement prepares as well as reports a state, so an immediate repeat of the same ideal measurement gives the same result. Under carefully specified conditions, very frequent physical checks can inhibit a quantum system’s normal change; this real and experimentally observed effect is called the quantum Zeno effect.

Start here. Picture a spinning office chair that is allowed to turn freely only between inspections. If someone stops it, lines it up with a strip of tape, and repeats that intervention again and again, the chair is kept near its starting direction. The chair is only an everyday comparison, but it gives the honest intuition: the repeated checks are not harmless looks; they are actions that help hold the chair near its starting direction.

The idea, step by step. 1. An ideal measurement of a chosen property produces one outcome and prepares the associated state. 2. If the same property is measured again immediately, with no relevant evolution in between, the prepared state gives the same outcome. 3. Left alone, a quantum system can normally evolve away from that prepared state. 4. Very frequent physical measurements that repeatedly test whether it is still in the initial state can interrupt this departure. 5. In the appropriate short-time regime, increasing the rate of those checks can suppress the change; this is the quantum Zeno effect. 6. The effect depends on the system, timing, and measurement protocol, so it is not a magical rule that any amount of watching freezes anything.

What this chapter was actually showing you. Alistair Venn scans Mrs Chain’s house object by object, asking whether a photograph, a book, or her sister belongs to the Ministry’s “authorised continuity path”. Lolly sees the sequence clearly: question, narrowing, selection. Continuity Review treats each inspection as a harmless check, yet every scan presses the household towards a smaller approved version and keeps other details suppressed. The cable Jago pulls and the module Beatrix takes away interrupt that ongoing intervention, allowing the blue wallpaper, the single duvet, and the photograph of Mrs Chain with her sister to return. It is an allegory, not household quantum mechanics, but it is a good one for the physical lesson that repeated measurement can pin behaviour.

Where the popular version goes wrong. “A watched pot never boils” is not quantum theory, and no human attention freezes a system. The quantum Zeno effect concerns repeated physical interactions or measurements, designed to test a particular state on the right time scale. Nor does it mean repeated measurements always freeze change. Other protocols can speed change, an effect known as the anti-Zeno effect, and real environments complicate both. Venn’s scanner is therefore a moral analogy for invasive monitoring, not a literal Zeno machine.

Going deeper (skip freely). This block is optional. Immediately after preparation, quantum theory predicts that the probability of remaining in the initial state falls quadratically for a sufficiently short interval, rather than at a fixed constant rate:
P survival ( t ) ≈ 1 − (Δ H ) 2 t 2 / ℏ 2.

Repeated ideal checks spaced within that regime can repeatedly re-prepare the state and inhibit its transition. Baidyanath Misra and E. C. George Sudarshan named the quantum Zeno effect in 1977. A celebrated experimental demonstration by Wayne Itano, David Heinzen, James Bollinger, and David Wineland was published in 1990 using trapped ions; many later experiments have observed related measurement-induced inhibition. Modern accounts stress that a “measurement” is a physical coupling and that the outcome depends on the complete protocol and environment.

What the reader learns. - An ideal measurement prepares the state corresponding to its recorded result. - An immediate repeat using the same apparatus distinction, or basis, can return that result with certainty. - Repeated physical measurement can alter, and under suitable conditions inhibit, subsequent evolution. - The quantum Zeno effect is real experimental physics, not a claim that conscious watching controls reality.
One-line summary. Inspect a quantum state often enough in the right physical way, and the inspection itself can help keep it where it was.

prosody.emphasis: Chapter 5: Physics Notes: The Schrödinger Equation and Lawful Evolution

p.prosody: In one breath. Between measurements, an isolated quantum system changes by a precise rule: smoothly, predictably and reversibly. The strangeness enters when it physically interacts with a measuring device or its surroundings, not because the ordinary evolution has stopped obeying a law.

Start here. Think of a perfectly made clockwork toy under a glass cover. If nobody touches it, each wheel makes the next one turn in a particular way; run the motion backwards and, in principle, every wheel could retrace its route. The difficult moment is not the clockwork itself. It is opening the cover, prodding a wheel with a ruler, and then asking why the arrangement has changed.

The idea, step by step. 1. A quantum state is the best complete description available of a small system, including the possible results of a later measurement. 2. Left alone, that state does not wait around for a decision; it changes continuously according to a fixed rule. 3. That rule is the Schrödinger equation, which uses the system’s energy and interactions to determine its next state from its present one. 4. For a genuinely isolated system, this evolution is deterministic and reversible: the starting state fixes the later state, and the earlier state could in principle be recovered. 5. A measurement is not a conscious person looking; it is a physical interaction with an apparatus or environment, which must itself be included in the story. 6. The measurement problem concerns how definite recorded outcomes arise from that wider interaction, not a failure of the law governing the evolution beforehand.

What this chapter was actually showing you. Dr Fainrose sees that Mrs Chain’s domestic stabiliser has selected a cheap-looking result rather than allowing the rich pattern of her home to develop by its proper history. Her phrase, “they’re vandalising the evolution”, is the chapter’s physics lesson in miniature. Lolly’s note — “Need law of change” — is the corrective: knowing the possible home-states is not enough if the Ministry has imposed an end point while discarding the lawful relations that lead there. Houses are not isolated laboratory systems, mercifully, but the contrast is exact as an analogy.

Where the popular version goes wrong. Quantum mechanics is often presented as though the system is mysterious and random all the time, until a person looks at it and makes it real. That reverses the emphasis. Between measurements, the standard quantum rule is exceptionally orderly; nor does human attention have a special physical job. “Observation” means an interaction that can leave a record, such as a detector absorbing light or an environment becoming correlated with a system. The unresolved part is how to understand a single definite recorded result, not whether the pre-measurement state was lawless.

Going deeper (skip freely). This block can be skipped. In 1926 Erwin Schrödinger gave the time-evolution law for a non-relativistic quantum state. In words, the Hamiltonian is the operator representing the system’s energy, and it tells the state how to change.

When Ĥ does not explicitly change with time, this produces unitary evolution, |ψ( t )⟩ = e −iĤt/ℏ |ψ(0)⟩, which preserves total probability and can be reversed mathematically. A measurement is instead a physical coupling to apparatus and environment; treating that whole enlarged system quantum mechanically is precisely what makes the later question of outcomes so demanding.

What the reader learns. - A quantum state needs a law of change as well as a list of possible measurement results. - The Schrödinger equation gives smooth, deterministic and reversible evolution for an isolated system. - A measurement is a physical interaction, never an act of conscious attention. - The measurement problem concerns definite outcomes, not a gap in ordinary quantum evolution.
One-line summary. Quantum theory is not strange because nothing obeys a law; it is strange because the law is so orderly until a record is made.

prosody.emphasis: Chapter 6: Physics Notes: Hawking Radiation

p.prosody: In one breath. A black hole is not perfectly black: quantum physics predicts that it emits thermal radiation and therefore loses mass. The smaller it becomes, the hotter it gets and the faster the loss proceeds, while what happens to the information in everything it swallowed remains a deep problem.

Start here. Picture a wide, quiet river gathering speed as it nears a waterfall. Far upstream, a swimmer can easily tell calm water from a ripple. Right at the edge, though, the current itself is moving as fast as ripples travel, so a patch of water that a swimmer treading water there would call perfectly calm looks, to someone watching safely from the slow water upstream, indistinguishable from a ripple heading away from the falls. Nobody at the edge did anything to make a wave; the two observers simply disagree about what “no ripple” means once the water itself is moving that fast. A horizon does this to the quantum vacuum: what looks like ordinary empty space up close comes out, translated into the language of a distant, stationary observer, as a steady trickle of outgoing warmth. No small factory manufacturing particles at one special spot is required. A black hole is not a river, and the analogy should not be pressed past this point, but the disagreement between the two observers is the actual mechanism, not decoration on top of it.

The idea, step by step. 1. A black hole is a region whose gravity is so strong that, once past its event horizon, light cannot return to a distant observer. 2. In quantum field theory on curved spacetime, a distant observer predicts that a black hole emits faint thermal radiation, called Hawking radiation. 3. Radiation carries energy away, and energy has mass-equivalent, so an isolated black hole loses mass. 4. A smaller black hole has a higher Hawking temperature, so it emits more strongly than a larger one. 5. The loss therefore accelerates as the hole shrinks; very large astrophysical holes change absurdly slowly, while a hypothetical small engineered one would be less patient. 6. If the final radiation looks only thermal, we must ask how the detailed quantum information about what formed and entered the hole can still be preserved.

What this chapter was actually showing you. Fainrose’s two curves — Asset four C’s mass descending and its temperature rising — are the distinctive linked signs of Hawking evaporation. The Ministry has not mislaid a civic object; its black hole is shrinking by law, which is why “within projected envelope” is such a poor comfort. When Lolly notices that thermal radiation does not plainly reveal what fell in, she reaches the black-hole information problem. Mrs Chain’s home, the queue records and the overflowed alternatives give that question human stakes: if a system has stored irreplaceable structure in four C, it matters fiercely whether that structure is recoverable. In the novel, that makes the black hole a deadline rather than merely a scientific curiosity: when the anchor evaporates, information that has not been recovered may no longer be recoverable by any ordinary intervention.

Where the popular version goes wrong. The usual tale says that a pair of “virtual particles” appears at the horizon, one falls in and one escapes. It can gesture towards the answer, but it is only a heuristic and is widely criticised as a literal account; it suggests little particles popping out at one special place and can get the energy bookkeeping badly wrong. The better framing is about quantum fields in curved spacetime. What counts as an empty vacuum, and even what counts as a particle, is not observer-independent there; comparing the field’s distant past and distant future around a black hole yields radiation for a far-away observer. No little horizon factory is required.

Going deeper (skip freely). This block can be skipped. Stephen Hawking’s 1974 paper, “Black hole explosions?”, applied quantum field theory to a black-hole spacetime and found a thermal spectrum at infinity. In words, the temperature is inversely proportional to the mass: double the mass and halve the temperature.
T H = ℏ c 3 / (8π GMk B ).

In the semiclassical treatment, the evaporation time of an isolated, non-rotating, uncharged black hole scales as t evap ∝ M 3. That calculation creates the information problem: quantum evolution normally preserves distinctions between initial states, but exactly thermal final radiation seems not to display them. Most modern work expects information to be preserved, yet the complete mechanism requires quantum gravity and is not settled in a simple textbook picture.

What the reader learns. - Hawking radiation is a predicted thermal emission from black holes. - Smaller isolated black holes are hotter and evaporate faster as they lose mass. - The “particle pair at the horizon” story is a limited heuristic, not the mechanism to take literally. - Black-hole evaporation raises the question of how quantum information is preserved.
One-line summary. Asset four C is not going missing; it is becoming hotter, smaller and more difficult to forgive.

prosody.emphasis: Chapter 7: Physics Notes: Entanglement and the Beginning of Decoherence

p.prosody: In one breath. Entangled objects have one shared quantum description, so their correlations can be stronger than any set of separate local instructions allows, though they cannot send messages faster than light. When those delicate correlations leak into uncontrolled surroundings, decoherence makes interference effectively unavailable and the system begins to look ordinary and separate.

Start here. Forget gloves in boxes. Picture two slot machines, sealed in vaults on opposite sides of the planet, never wired together in any way. Pull either lever and you get a random number that tells you nothing useful on its own. But compare the two vaults’ printouts afterwards, for any of several different levers you might have pulled on each machine, and the numbers turn out to be stitched together more tightly than any pair of machines merely loaded at the factory with matching lists could manage — switch which lever you pull, and a pre-loaded pair would eventually get caught out. The stitching is not a number either machine was quietly carrying home in its gears; it exists only once both printouts are laid side by side, and only ordinary, unhurried travel can bring them together to be compared.

The idea, step by step. 1. A quantum state, as earlier chapters established, can specify possible measurement results without assigning a definite value in every measurement basis. 2. Two systems are entangled when the full pair has a quantum state that cannot be written as one independent state for each part. 3. The pair can then have definite shared correlations even though neither member has a definite individual value of the relevant property before measurement. 4. Measuring one side produces a result correlated with the other, but each local result is still unpredictable, so no usable message travels faster than light. 5. Real systems interact with air, light, apparatus and other surroundings; these interactions spread the system’s phase relations into an environment. 6. That spreading is decoherence: interference becomes practically inaccessible, though it does not by itself explain why one particular outcome is experienced.

What this chapter was actually showing you. At the Regional Compression Annex, Lolly discovers that Mrs Chain’s house, transport routes, identity links and the queue have been treated as though their connections could be cut off as optional “metadata”. Fainrose’s correlation budget is an analogy for the fact that the meaningful description may belong to the whole pattern, not to each component separately. By sending unresolved correlations into four C, Mr Voller’s system has coupled the district to a noisy, evaporating anchor. Fainrose’s warning — that the environment starts carrying away the phase relations — is the chapter’s first look at decoherence: the returning fragments will not simply recombine into their earlier coherent pattern.

Where the popular version goes wrong. Entanglement is regularly advertised as instant communication, or as a secret signal sent from one particle to another. It is neither. Entanglement can produce correlations that are revealed only when records from both sides are later compared by ordinary, slower-than-light means. Nobody at one end can choose the random local result needed to spell a message at the other. A second confusion is to say decoherence “solves” measurement. It explains why interference becomes unobservable in practice, but it does not on its own select the one outcome a person finds in a record.

Going deeper (skip freely). This block can be skipped. In 1964 John Bell derived inequalities obeyed by local hidden-variable theories; experiments beginning with Stuart Freedman and John Clauser’s 1972 test, and tightened by Alain Aspect’s 1981–82 experiments, found the quantum correlations instead. Bell’s result rules out local hidden variables, not every possible hidden-variable theory: pilot-wave theory, for example, is explicitly nonlocal. For a schematic entangled pair,

has a definite joint pattern but does not give either side its own definite 0 or 1 before a measurement in that basis. Decoherence is described by entanglement with many environmental degrees of freedom; after ignoring the environment, the interference terms of the system’s reduced density matrix are strongly suppressed.

What the reader learns. - Entangled systems are described by a shared state, not by complete independent states for their parts. - Entanglement produces strong correlations without faster-than-light communication. - Environmental interactions can disperse phase relations and cause decoherence. - Decoherence explains lost observable interference, not by itself a single chosen outcome.
One-line summary. When the Ministry treated connections as expendable, it learned that a shared quantum state shares the damage as well.

prosody.emphasis: Chapter 8: Physics Notes: The No-Cloning Theorem and Quantum Error Correction

p.prosody: In one breath. Physics forbids making a perfect duplicate of an unknown arbitrary quantum state, so Mr Voller’s “reference copy” cannot exist in the way he claims. Quantum error correction protects information by spreading it across a carefully arranged pattern, then checking for damage without reading out the protected state itself.

Start here. A wax seal on an unopened letter can be carried elsewhere without changing its pattern. You can also make many seals from a design you already know. What you cannot do is press a blank lump of wax against an unknown sealed letter, make a perfect second seal, and leave the first one untouched while learning every fine ridge. Some kinds of detail can be moved or reconstructed from a known recipe; they cannot all be duplicated from a single unknown original.

The idea, step by step. 1. An unknown quantum state can contain relations that no one has already written down as a complete classical recipe. 2. The no-cloning theorem says that no single physical procedure can make a perfect independent copy of every possible unknown state. 3. It does not forbid moving a state from one system to another; a transfer can leave the original changed or destroyed. 4. It also does not forbid preparing many copies of a state already known from its recipe, such as a repeatedly prepared laboratory state. 5. A measurement produces classical outcomes, but collecting those outcomes is not the same as retaining the full unknown state that produced them. 6. Quantum error correction encodes one logical state across several physical parts, so limited damage can be found and repaired without making a forbidden duplicate.

What this chapter was actually showing you. Mr Voller’s cold vault contains ticked boxes, classical representations and the fatal line “PHASE RECORD: NOT APPLICABLE”. It has preserved selected answers about Mrs Chain’s home, not an independent copy of its full quantum relations; Fainrose’s “photograph of a conversation” is exactly right. Her alternative is not a magical backup. When Lolly notices Mrs Chain’s sister represented across records, tokens, photographs and routes, she has found the story analogue of quantum error correction: the useful information lives in the pattern across the lattice. Fainrose’s left-hand/right-hand test is a syndrome measurement, designed to reveal an error without asking the encoded state to disclose itself.

Where the popular version goes wrong. “You cannot copy a quantum state” does not mean quantum information is uniquely doomed, or that every quantum state may exist only once. The theorem forbids a universal copier for an unknown arbitrary state. You may prepare another instance of a known state, and you may transfer a state rather than duplicate it. Nor does error correction evade the theorem by quietly copying the state into several boxes. The encoding distributes the one logical state in nonlocal correlations; no one component is a spare full original waiting in a cupboard.

Going deeper (skip freely). This block can be skipped. W. K. Wootters and W. H. Zurek, and independently Dennis Dieks, proved the no-cloning theorem in 1982. If one linear machine copied both |ψ⟩ and |φ⟩, it would have to turn |ψ⟩|0⟩ into |ψ⟩|ψ⟩ and likewise for |φ⟩, which requires ⟨ψ|φ⟩ = ⟨ψ|φ⟩ 2. That fails for general distinct, non-orthogonal states. Quantum error-correcting codes use extra physical systems and structured entanglement. In a stabiliser code, carefully chosen parity-like checks return a syndrome identifying an error pattern while commuting with, and therefore not revealing, the encoded logical information.

What the reader learns. - No physical process can perfectly copy an unknown arbitrary quantum state. - Moving a state and preparing a known state again are allowed; neither is forbidden cloning. - Measurement records are not automatically a full copy of the state that generated them. - Quantum error correction protects one state through distributed correlations and indirect error checks.
One-line summary. The Ministry built an impossible copy; Fainrose needs a recoverable pattern instead.

prosody.emphasis: Chapter 9: Physics Notes: The Uncertainty Principle—Position and Momentum

p.prosody: In one breath. A quantum thing cannot be prepared with arbitrarily exact answers to both “where is it?” and “how is it moving?” at once. This is a built-in feature of nature, not a complaint about inadequate equipment.

Start here. Think of a sound heard through a wall. A very brief click can be placed very accurately in time, but it contains a muddle of musical notes; a long, pure note has a clear pitch, but no equally clear beginning or end. Making one description tight makes the other spread out. No amount of better listening turns one sound into both a perfect click and a perfectly pure note.

The idea, step by step. 1. Position answers where a thing is, while momentum describes its motion, including its direction and how hard it is to stop. 2. A quantum state — the description introduced earlier in the book — behaves in key respects like a wave rather than like a tiny bead carrying a complete hidden docket. 3. A wave packed into a small region needs many wavelengths mixed together, and that mixture corresponds to a wide spread of possible momenta. 4. A wave with one very well-defined wavelength has a well-defined momentum, but it must extend over a wide region rather than having one sharply fixed position. 5. This unavoidable trade-off is the uncertainty principle: a state cannot supply arbitrarily sharp values of both properties at the same time. 6. A measurement can certainly disturb a system, but the principle remains even for an ideal measurement that adds no avoidable clumsiness.

What this chapter was actually showing you. Directive 11-C demands that each dwelling and person receive two certificates: Column A fixes its present configuration and Column B fixes its rate and direction of change. Fainrose sees why the demand is impossible before Miss Pike does. The scans and their correction factor dramatise one real difficulty — physical interventions can alter what they probe — but the deeper point is stronger: even an imagined perfectly gentle apparatus could not prepare arbitrary precision in both columns. When the Ministry insists otherwise, Miss Pike’s spreadsheet has to manufacture a Column B and then mistakes the manufacture for evidence against the people living in its rows. In the story, the temptation is to demand both columns at once: exact present state and exact future trajectory. Quantum mechanics refuses the request, and the Ministry’s paperwork does not change that refusal.

Where the popular version goes wrong. The usual story says that a particle secretly has an exact place and an exact motion, but an observer inevitably knocks it about while looking. That can happen in a real experiment, yet it is not what Heisenberg’s principle says. Quantum theory does not merely hide two exact pre-existing answers behind bad instruments; it sets a limit on how narrowly the two corresponding distributions can coexist in one state. Here and throughout the book, an observation means a physical interaction, never a person’s attention.

Going deeper (skip freely). This paragraph can be skipped. Werner Heisenberg stated the relation in 1927. For a collection of identically prepared systems, position and momentum have spreads measured by their standard deviations; quantum mechanics requires
Δ x Δ p ≥ ℏ / 2.

The symbol ℏ is Planck’s constant divided by 2π, a very small quantity, which is why the restriction is usually invisible for houses and people. The mathematical reason is a Fourier relation: narrowing a position wave pattern requires combining a broad range of wavelengths, while a narrow range of wavelengths makes the pattern spatially broad. The relation is about the state itself, not a procurement opportunity for a better scanner.

What the reader learns. - Position and momentum are linked quantum properties, not independent boxes that can both be filled to unlimited precision. - A sharply localised wave pattern necessarily has a broad spread of momenta. - The uncertainty principle is intrinsic to quantum states, not merely damage caused by crude instruments. - Directive 11-C turns an impossible demand into fabricated records and then punishes people by those records.
One-line summary. Quantum mechanics permits a precise location or a precise motion, but not two limitless certificates at once.

prosody.emphasis: Chapter 10: Physics Notes: Decoherence and Einselection

p.prosody: In one breath. Ordinary things look definite because they are continually jostled and marked by the world around them, not because a person has noticed them. That constant contact makes some familiar-looking states durable and makes quantum interference practically unavailable.

Start here. Imagine a muddy path after a busy morning. Shoes, bicycle tyres, rain, and a dog have each left traces of what passed through; by lunchtime there is no special official whose glance makes the path a path. The surroundings have been taking part all along, and some marks survive the traffic better than others.

The idea, step by step. 1. A superposition is a quantum state that does not yet have one definite value for the property being considered; it can produce interference between alternatives. 2. No large object is truly alone: light scatters from it, air molecules strike it, and it exchanges heat with its surroundings. 3. Those physical interactions entangle the object with its environment, leaving many outward traces correlated with its possible states. 4. Decoherence is the resulting loss of practically accessible interference between those alternatives; it does not require a mind to look at anything. 5. The environment does not preserve every possible state equally: einselection — environment-induced superselection — favours robust pointer states, such as stable, reasonably definite positions. 6. Decoherence explains why a moon behaves as though it has one settled location for all practical purposes, but it does not by itself answer why one outcome is experienced rather than another.

What this chapter was actually showing you. Mrs Prosser’s forty-one-person moon rota mistakes a civic quorum for a physical process. Outer Fenwick’s moon needs no clipboard holders: photons from the Sun and the moon, air, thermal radiation, and the rest of its surroundings are interacting with it continuously. Within the chapter’s extraordinary machinery, the decorative weathercock mast interferes with that settling contact and the Ministry bills residents to compensate for the damage. When the annex switches it off, the moon comes up at its ordinary time because the sky is again allowed to keep physically noticing it, whether or not anyone attends the whist drive.

Where the popular version goes wrong. “Observation makes reality” is a catchy phrase and almost wholly misleading. A conscious observer is not the missing ingredient; an observation in physics is a physical interaction, and the relevant interactions are already supplied in overwhelming numbers by photons, molecules, and radiation. The opposite overstatement is also wrong: decoherence does not simply prove that one unique outcome has been selected. It tells us why interference is absent for practical observers and why stable records arise, while the question of one experienced outcome remains for the next chapter.

Going deeper (skip freely). This paragraph can be skipped. H. Dieter Zeh set out the basic environment-entanglement account in 1970, and Wojciech Zurek developed einselection and the pointer-state programme from 1981 onward. In Zurek’s account, environmental coupling continually spreads information about especially robust states into many separate fragments of the surroundings, making them independently available to different physical systems. Experiments have watched this loss of interference in increasingly controlled systems; for example, Serge Haroche’s group reported direct monitoring of decoherence of field states in 1996. None of these results supplies a final, universally accepted solution to the measurement problem: they explain the effective classical appearance extremely well, not why exactly one result is experienced.

What the reader learns. - Large objects become classically stable through continual environmental interaction, not conscious observation. - Decoherence makes interference between macroscopic alternatives practically inaccessible. - Einselection favours robust pointer states rather than every possible quantum description. - Decoherence does not, by itself, settle why one definite outcome is experienced.
One-line summary. The moon stays definite because the whole sky keeps physically recording it, not because Mrs Prosser secures forty-one signatures.

prosody.emphasis: Chapter 11: Physics Notes: The Measurement Problem and Wigner’s Friend

p.prosody: In one breath. Quantum rules describe change smoothly, yet an experiment seems to end with one actual answer. The measurement problem is the unresolved question of what, if anything, turns the smooth description into that single experienced result.

Start here. Picture two singers holding one sustained chord, their pitches locked live to each other rather than two solo notes each decided in advance. Draw a curtain between the audience and singer A: singer A can tell you, this instant, exactly what note they are singing — for them nothing is remotely ambiguous. But that does not mean the chord itself — the full duet, as anyone hearing both voices together would have to describe it — has already settled into one fixed harmony sitting behind the curtain, waiting to be revealed. Until the curtain lifts and the two voices are heard as one performance, the honest description of the duet may still be an unresolved blend that has not finished becoming any one thing. Singer A’s certainty about their own note is completely real. It simply does not settle what the joint performance currently is.

The idea, step by step. 1. A quantum state evolves smoothly according to the same basic laws whether it describes a particle, a detector, or, in principle, the materials of a laboratory. 2. Yet a textbook measurement is usually said to yield one definite recorded result, with probabilities supplied by the quantum rules. 3. The measurement problem asks what physical feature licenses that change from a smooth superposition to one outcome, and where any boundary between system and apparatus could be. 4. In Wigner’s friend, a friend inside a sealed laboratory measures a system and obtains a definite result in their own record. 5. An observer outside can, before interacting with the laboratory, describe the friend, record, apparatus, and system together as one larger quantum system; that is the uncomfortable tension, not a parable about bad eyesight. 6. Decoherence — the environment-blabbing effect of Chapter 10 — makes records robust, but interpretations still disagree about whether collapse, branching, hidden variables, or some relational account supplies the final story.

What this chapter was actually showing you. Alfred Keinschein turns discarded outcomes into vampire nourishment, which is fiction with excellent table manners, but his arrival exposes the real difficulty. Phase Two asks a citizen to state a memory, then treats the completed form as if it merely retrieved a pre-existing official fact. Fainrose and Lolly see that the question, the person, and the paper form one physical intervention: the programme may be writing the record it claims to read. Alfred Keinschein’s “widening region of agreement” gives the chapter’s version of the Wigner’s-friend pressure: Mr Venn, Mrs Chain, the grid, and the Ministry need not all stand at one mythical instant outside the same measurement.

Where the popular version goes wrong. Wigner’s friend is often retold as proof that human consciousness magically causes collapse. It proves no such thing. Wigner did at one stage discuss consciousness in connection with measurement, but the thought experiment is valuable precisely because quantum theory has no agreed need for a conscious spectator: physical interactions create records. Nor does the scenario establish that one interpretation has won. It shows sharply why a universally smooth quantum evolution and one unambiguously definite outcome are hard to fit together without further interpretive work.

Going deeper (skip freely). This paragraph can be skipped. John von Neumann’s 1932 formulation made the tension vivid by allowing the quantum description to extend from a measured system through an apparatus and, in principle, to an observer. The smooth law is conventionally written
iℏ ∂/∂ t |ψ⟩ = H |ψ⟩,

which says that the state |ψ⟩ changes continuously under the system’s energy operator H. In his 1961 essay “Remarks on the Mind-Body Question”, Eugene Wigner imagined a friend who has measured inside a closed laboratory while Wigner remains outside. Collapse theories add a real stochastic collapse, Everett-style interpretations retain all branches, de Broglie-Bohm theory adds definite particle positions, and relational or agent-centred accounts characterise facts differently. These are live interpretive programmes, not experimentally settled winners.

What the reader learns. - Smooth quantum evolution and the appearance of one definite measurement result create the measurement problem. - Wigner’s friend makes the problem unavoidable by placing an observer and record inside the system described from outside. - Observation means physical interaction, not conscious attention. - Decoherence stabilises records but does not by itself choose one experienced outcome.
One-line summary. If quantum evolution applies to everything, the unanswered question is what makes one answer the one we live with.

prosody.emphasis: Chapter 12: Physics Notes: De Broglie Matter Waves and Pilot-Wave Theory

p.prosody: In one breath. Matter can show a wave-like pattern, and one interpretation says a particle is always somewhere definite while a real guiding wave directs its motion. That interpretation is deterministic, but its guidance reaches across distance in a way that is explicitly nonlocal.

Start here. Imagine a small toy boat in a canal. The boat is at one particular place, but ripples arriving from different parts of the water can still steer its next turn; the route depends on a wider pattern than the boat alone. The image is not a literal model of an electron, but it earns the central thought: something can have a definite location while being guided by an extended pattern.

The idea, step by step. 1. In 1924 Louis de Broglie proposed that material particles have an associated matter wave, extending the already puzzling wave-and-particle behaviour of light. 2. The de Broglie wavelength is shorter for greater momentum, so the wave aspect of a fast macroscopic object is far too fine to notice in daily life. 3. Electrons and other particles produce diffraction and interference patterns, showing that “a particle is only a tiny hard ball” is not an adequate account. 4. Pilot-wave theory, also called de Broglie-Bohm theory, adds a definite particle position at every moment and a real wavefunction that guides its path. 5. The particle occupies one path, but unoccupied or “empty” parts of the guiding wave can still affect its motion and produce interference; the wave does not collapse in this account. 6. The theory is explicitly nonlocal: the guidance of one particle can depend on the wider configuration, including distant entangled particles. That is not a defect concealed by the theory but the reason Bell’s theorem, next chapter, does not rule it out.

What this chapter was actually showing you. The Duc de Brévanne gives Lolly an alternative to Alfred Keinschein’s account. When he speaks of one actual wallpaper, a wave spread over other possible configurations, and “empty” alternatives that still steer, he is describing pilot-wave theory in the language of Mrs Chain’s house. On that interpretation Mr Venn’s scanner did not conjure a fact out of conscious observation; it physically changed the guiding conditions, while the actual configuration remained definite. Lolly’s proposal to remove the Ministry’s apparatus rather than restore a lost copy follows the Duc’s picture, whether or not nature ultimately uses that picture.

Where the popular version goes wrong. Matter waves do not mean that an electron is a miniature ripple of water, nor that standard quantum mechanics has simply been replaced by a classical hidden mechanism. Pilot-wave theory is a serious interpretation that reproduces the ordinary quantum statistics under its usual assumptions, but it pays for definite particle positions with genuine nonlocality. Bell’s theorem rules out local hidden-variable accounts, not every possible hidden-variable account; pilot-wave theory survives precisely because it does not pretend to be local. The guiding wave is a physical part of the theory, not a record waiting for a conscious observer to read.
Going deeper (skip freely). This paragraph can be skipped. De Broglie’s 1924 doctoral thesis proposed the relation
λ = h / p,

where λ is the matter wavelength, h is Planck’s constant, and p is momentum. Clinton Davisson and Lester Germer reported electron diffraction in 1927, and George Paget Thomson independently obtained electron diffraction that same year; de Broglie received the 1929 Nobel Prize. David Bohm gave pilot-wave theory its modern general formulation in two 1952 papers. Its guiding law is deterministic once the initial particle positions and wavefunction are fixed, while the usual probabilistic predictions arise from an unknown distribution of initial positions. In the normal quantum-equilibrium form, it makes the same tested predictions as standard nonrelativistic quantum mechanics, so it remains an interpretation rather than an experimentally established replacement.

What the reader learns. - Matter has a de Broglie wavelength and can produce wave-like diffraction and interference. - Pilot-wave theory gives particles definite positions guided by a non-collapsing real wave. - Empty parts of the guiding wave can affect the particle that is actually present. - Pilot-wave theory is nonlocal, which is why Bell’s theorem does not exclude it.
One-line summary. A pilot-wave particle is always somewhere, but the whole wave — including its empty possibilities — helps decide where it goes next.

prosody.emphasis: Chapter 13: Physics Notes: Bell’s Theorem and the C H S H Inequality

p.prosody: In one breath. Bell’s theorem says that if distant things carry pre-written local answers, their joint results can only agree up to a fixed limit. Experiments exceed that limit, so nature cannot be explained by local hidden variables, even though it still cannot be used to send a message faster than light.

Start here. Imagine two restaurants at opposite ends of a city, each choosing at random whether to serve tea or coffee. Two friends have agreed in advance how to answer either question, but cannot phone one another after they leave home. Their answers can match rather cleverly, yet there is a maximum cleverness possible when all the agreement was packed into the plan at breakfast. If the matches are better than that maximum, the friends did not merely bring a local plan.

The idea, step by step. 1. A pair of particles can be prepared in an entangled state, meaning that separate measurements show a pattern of joint results that cannot be reduced to two independent descriptions. 2. A hidden-variable account says each particle carries additional, pre-existing instructions that determine its result for every measurement that might be chosen. 3. Locality adds that the result here cannot depend on which measurement is freely chosen far away, except through influences no faster than light. 4. Bell showed that local pre-written instructions put a numerical ceiling on the correlations between the two sets of results. 5. The C H S H test uses four alternative settings, chosen after the pair has separated, and experiments find correlations above that ceiling. 6. Each result seen at either end remains unpredictable on its own, so the shared pattern cannot be turned into a faster-than-light telephone.

What this chapter was actually showing you. Jack Bellew gives Mr Pilbeam a number rather than a favourite account of reality. The Ministry calls its surveys of nine thousand dwellings separate local acts; Lolly sees that a Bell-style test across Fainrose’s correlation lattice can test that claim. Heitmann, Tegnér and Bellew disagree about what quantum mechanics means, but all three can be bound in advance by the reading from the timing rack in Sub-District 6. Mrs Chain’s correction matters too: even if Tegnér’s branches are part of an interpretation, harm in her branch is not made cost-free by an account of other branches.

Where the popular version goes wrong. The slogan is not that Bell proved that “nothing is real”, nor that a conscious observer reaches across space and changes a distant particle. A measurement is a physical interaction with an apparatus, not an act of human attention. Bell’s result rules out the combination of local influence and pre-existing hidden instructions under the usual assumption that the setting choices are not secretly coordinated with the source. It does not rule out every hidden-variable theory: the pilot-wave theory met in Chapter 12 has definite particle positions but is explicitly nonlocal, and so it survives Bell’s theorem. Nor does a Bell violation settle the competition among Copenhagen-style accounts, many-worlds, and pilot-wave theory; those interpretations are not currently experimentally distinguished.

Going deeper (skip freely). This block is optional. In John Bell’s 1964 argument, and in the 1969 C H S H form due to John Clauser, Michael Horne, Abner Shimony and Richard Holt, each side chooses one of two settings, a, a′ and b, b′. If the outcomes are recorded as +1 or −1, a local-hidden-variable model must obey

Quantum mechanics predicts up to 2√2 for suitable entangled states, while its individual outcomes remain random. Stuart Freedman and Clauser reported an early Bell-inequality violation in 1972; Alain Aspect’s 1981–82 experiments changed analyser settings during the photons’ flight. In 2015, independent loophole-free tests led by Ronald Hanson in Delft, Marissa Giustina in Vienna, and Lynden Shalm at NIST addressed the major locality and detection concerns in different implementations. Clauser, Aspect and Anton Zeilinger received the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics for pioneering entangled-photon experiments and Bell-inequality violations. These tests support the precise conclusion, not a mystical extra one: local hidden-variable models cannot reproduce the observed correlations.

What the reader learns. - A Bell test compares observed joint correlations with a ceiling required by local hidden-variable theories. - Quantum experiments violate the C H S H ceiling, although they do not transmit usable information faster than light. - Bell’s theorem excludes local hidden variables, not nonlocal pilot-wave theory or every possible interpretation. - A pre-agreed measurement can constrain a committee’s story without choosing a metaphysics.
